23-Aug-2017: CFPB resolution with two Amex banking subsidiaries for discriminating against consumers in Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands and other territories by offering card terms inferior to those in the 50 states. Amex remediated approximately $95-96m to 221,932 consumers. No civil penalty was assessed because Amex self-reported and fully cooperated. Note this post-dates the 30-Jun-2017 anchor.

gate1.note: Sells enterprise and service-provider switches, routers, wireless, security, collaboration and the attached services/maintenance contracts; product versus service revenue and deferred revenue are broken out clearly. Understandable unit economics for a generalist.

gate2.note: Through fiscal 2016 Cisco held roughly 55-60% share of the enterprise Ethernet switching market, sustained gross margins above 60%, and benefited from genuine lock-in: IOS/CLI operator training, a certification ecosystem (CCNA/CCIE), a two-tier channel, and multi-year maintenance contracts that made rip-and-replace expensive. The Q2 FY2014 revenue drop of 8% year over year (reported Feb-2014) was an emerging-market and service-provider order shock, not share loss - FY2015 revenue recovered to about $49.2bn, so it should not be read as a moat change at the 2014 anchor.

By the Q3 FY2017 report (May-2017) Cisco had posted year-over-year revenue declines for seven consecutive quarters, with the weakness concentrated in the core switching and routing lines rather than in peripheral segments. FY2014 switching revenue had already fallen 5% ($711m), driven by a 12% ($656m) drop in modular switches as the Catalyst 6000 base aged. Management publicly attributed compressing product gross margin to pricing pressure on standalone hardware. The visible cause was merchant silicon and white-box competition plus Arista in the data centre and Huawei internationally: durable, but no longer a price-setting franchise. Still NARROW rather than NONE because share, 60%+ gross margins and the services annuity all held.

gate3.note: 23-Dec-2013: Cisco publicly disclosed (blog post by deputy general counsel Roxane Marenberg) that it was investigating alleged FCPA violations in Russia and certain CIS states, including discounting practices, at the request of the SEC and DOJ. Investigation only - no finding at this date. Resolution for dating discipline: both DOJ and SEC formally declined to bring enforcement actions, announced 09-Sep-2016.

31-Jul-2019: Cisco agreed to pay $8.6m to settle a False Claims Act whistleblower suit (US ex rel. Glenn) alleging it sold its Video Surveillance Manager product to federal, state and local government agencies from 2007 to 2014 while knowing it was susceptible to cyber-attack. Believed to be the first FCA cybersecurity payout. Post-dates all CSCO anchors.

Oct-2020: a federal court (EDVA) found Cisco liable for wilful patent infringement in Centripetal Networks v. Cisco, awarding roughly $1.9bn in damages and royalties. Well after all CSCO anchors; recorded for completeness.

gate1.note: Four reported segments (Additives & Functional Products, Advanced Materials, Chemical Intermediates, Fibers) with volume, price and raw-material spread disclosed per segment; economics are propylene/olefin feedstock in, differentiated and commodity chemicals out. Heterogeneous but not opaque - a generalist can trace each segment's driver.

gate2.note: Genuine specialty positions with pricing power - Saflex PVB interlayers and Crystex insoluble sulfur (both acquired with Solutia, closed Jul-2012 for about $4.7bn), Tritan copolyester, coatings and tire additives - sit alongside a large commodity Chemical Intermediates book that is a pure spread business with no pricing power. The Fibers segment (acetate tow) was the clearest demonstration that the franchise was NARROW not WIDE: it contributed roughly 15% of sales and about 30% of profits in 2013-2014, then de-rated hard as Chinese acetate tow capacity was built out and Chinese cigarette demand fell for the first time ever in 2015 (down 8% in Q1-2016). Eastman closed its Workington, UK tow plant in 2015 and the Fibers earnings reset was fully visible in the FY2015 and FY2016 10-Ks, i.e. well before the 30-Jun-2018 anchor. Returns on capital in the high-single to low-double digits are consistent with NARROW. The FY2019 earnings decline (customer destocking, weak auto and durables end-markets) and the 2020 COVID trough are cyclical, not a further moat change.

gate3.note: 04-Oct-2017: two explosions and a fire in the coal gasification area of Eastman's Kingsport, Tennessee site (a process upset traced by the company's internal memo to a blocked 30-year-old valve). No injuries beyond first aid. The Tennessee Occupational Safety and Health Administration subsequently cited Eastman for four 'serious' violations (report released 2018). Regulator finding of safety violations at the company's largest manufacturing complex; became public the day of the incident.

Context, not a mark against Eastman: on 25-Jul-2013 a federal jury in Austin, Texas found that PlastiPure and CertiChem had made false and misleading claims about the estrogenic activity of Eastman's Tritan resin. Eastman was the PLAINTIFF and won; the defendants appealed. Recorded so a later reader does not mistake the Tritan docket for adverse litigation against Eastman.

Ordinary-course environmental exposure disclosed in the legal proceedings and environmental notes of each 10-K across the period: Superfund/state remediation obligations and accrued environmental reserves at legacy sites. No regulator finding of misconduct.

gate1.note: Designs, makes and distributes watches, leathers and jewellery under the owned Fossil/Skagen brands and licensed fashion brands (Michael Kors, Emporio Armani, DKNY, Diesel, Kate Spade). Unit economics are simple: gross margin on accessories less royalty payments to licensors, less SG&A across wholesale and its own retail stores.

gate2.note: Through fiscal 2014 Fossil ran on a genuine but rentable advantage: design and global distribution scale in fashion accessories, gross margins in the mid-50s%, and a licensed-brand portfolio - above all Michael Kors watches - that carried the growth. FY2014 worldwide net sales rose about 8% to roughly $3.5bn. NARROW rather than WIDE because the brand equity that drove the volume belonged to the LICENSORS, was rented under finite contracts, and depended on a fashion cycle Fossil did not control.

The break is dateable to the FY2015 results released 16-Feb-2016 and confirmed by the Q1-2016 results released 10/11-May-2016, both before the 30-Jun-2016 anchor. FY2015: worldwide net sales fell about 8% to roughly $3.23bn and operating margin roughly halved (mid-teens% to high-single-digits%). Q1-2016: net sales fell 9% year over year (7% constant currency) to about $660m, with WATCHES down 10% (8% constant currency) and jewellery down 13%; management cut FY2016 revenue guidance to a range implying a decline; the stock fell as much as 34% in a day on 11-May-2016. CEO Kosta Kartsotis described 'persistent headwinds pressuring the traditional watch category.' Cause was visible and structural, not cyclical: the Apple Watch shipped 24-Apr-2015 and consumed the same wrist and the same $200-400 price point. Fossil's own response - the $260m Misfit acquisition announced Nov-2015 and the Fossil Q connected line - was an admission that the traditional watch franchise was being displaced, and it did not arrest the decline (FY2016 net sales down about $186m or 6%; FY2017 net sales down about $254m or 8%, with roughly $407m of goodwill and trade-name impairment and a diluted loss of $9.87 per share reported 13-Feb-2018).

gate1.note: Specialty glass and ceramics across five reported segments - Display Technologies (LCD substrate glass), Optical Communications (fibre and cable), Specialty Materials (Gorilla Glass), Environmental Technologies (ceramic substrates for auto emissions), Life Sciences. Capital-intensive manufacturing with clearly reported segment sales and margins; readable by a generalist.

gate2.note: Corning holds a leading share of an LCD substrate oligopoly (Corning, AGC, NEG) and Gorilla Glass had a dominant position in smartphone cover glass with Gorilla Glass 4 shipping in 2015. But the defining fact of the Display business - roughly 40% of revenue and the bulk of profit - is that Corning disclosed SEQUENTIAL LCD GLASS PRICE DECLINES IN EVERY QUARTER of this window (moderate in Q2-2014 and Q1-2015, but always negative). A franchise that must give price back every quarter to hold volume, in a business needing continuous heavy capex on melting tanks, is NARROW, not WIDE. Gorilla Glass showed the same vulnerability from the other side: weak Gorilla sales in Q4-2013 (reported 29-Jan-2014) and price decline in Q2-2014 both compressed operating margin, so the cover-glass premium was not durable either. On 15-Jan-2014 Corning completed full ownership of Samsung Corning Precision Materials (announced Oct-2013), issuing about $1.9bn of convertible preferred to Samsung Display plus a further $400m purchase - roughly a 7.5% economic stake - which improved consolidated Display revenue and profit (about $2bn sales, about $350m profit) but also concentrated customer and shareholder exposure in a single counterparty. None of these changed the CLASS during 2013-2015.

gate3.note: Ordinary-course environmental exposure disclosed in each 10-K: Corning has been named by the EPA (Superfund) or state equivalents as a potentially responsible party at 17 active hazardous waste sites, with joint and several liability among contributors. Reserves accrued; no regulator finding of misconduct.

11-Dec-2015: Corning announced it would exchange its 50% equity interest in Dow Corning Corporation for 100% of a new entity holding roughly 40% of Hemlock Semiconductor plus about $4.8bn cash - unwinding the JV whose 1990s silicone breast-implant litigation and 1995 Chapter 11 had been Corning's largest historical legal exposure (long since charged off). Structural/portfolio action, not misconduct. Separately, in Sep-2019 Dow formally notified Corning of environmental remediation losses at a number of sites.

gate1.note: Two businesses after the 01-Nov-2015 separation from Hewlett Packard Enterprise: Personal Systems (notebooks, desktops) and Printing (hardware plus supplies). The classic razor-and-blades structure is fully disclosed - printer hardware near or below cost, with supplies carrying roughly two-thirds of Printing operating profit. Easy for a generalist to explain.

gate2.note: The moat was never the PC business - that is a commodity assembly business where HP competes on scale and channel against Lenovo and Dell. It was the installed-base supplies annuity: an installed printer only takes HP cartridges, giving high-margin recurring revenue at a price the customer has already sunk cost into. Honest read on the supplies economics: this is a captive-aftermarket toll, not a customer-preference moat, and its enforcement mechanism was already technical rather than competitive. The FY2016 supplies collapse (Printing net revenue down 14.3% and supplies down 17.8% for the three months ended 31-Jul-2016; FY2016 was the segment's biggest revenue drop, with Printing about 38% of total sales) should NOT be read as the moat break at the 30-Jun-2017 anchor: HP attributed most of it to a deliberate change in the supplies sales model plus channel-inventory reduction and unfavourable FX, and supplies did stabilise (FY2017 supplies revenue down only 0.6%, and supplies grew again in FY2018).

Visible on 27-Feb-2019 (Q1 FY2019 results), before the 30-Jun-2019 anchor: HP warned supplies revenue would decline about 3% for the rest of FY2019 and the stock fell as much as 17% in a day. Critically, management's stated cause was not FX or channel timing but MARKET SHARE AND PRICING LOSS as customers shifted supplies purchases online to third-party and compatible cartridges, plus weak EMEA demand. That is the annuity itself leaking. Confirmed 03-Oct-2019 when incoming CEO Enrique Lores announced a restructuring cutting 7,000-9,000 of roughly 55,000 jobs to save $1bn by end-2022, explicitly abandoning the razor-and-blades model in favour of services and higher up-front printer pricing for machines usable with non-HP ink. When a company publicly retires the pricing structure that WAS its moat, the classification is NONE.

gate3.note: 20-Nov-2012: HP took an $8.8bn goodwill write-off on Autonomy and publicly alleged 'serious accounting improprieties' and 'outright misrepresentations' at the acquired company, with more than $5bn of the charge attributed to accounting missteps. The fraud alleged was Autonomy's, but HP's own diligence and disclosure were challenged: a securities class action on behalf of purchasers between 19-Aug-2011 and 20-Nov-2012 settled in Jun-2015 for $100m paid by HP's insurers. Entity note: HP Inc. is the continuation of the original Hewlett-Packard Company (HPE was the entity spun off 01-Nov-2015), so this history attaches to HPQ.

09-Apr-2014: Hewlett-Packard and three subsidiaries paid more than $108m to resolve parallel SEC and DOJ FCPA actions - $74.2m in criminal fines to DOJ, $29m disgorgement ($26.47m SEC, $2.53m IRS forfeiture) and $5m prejudgment interest. The conduct: more than $3.6m in bribes to Russian, Polish and Mexican government officials to win or keep public contracts, including over $2m routed through agents and shell companies to a Russian official for a contract with the federal prosecutor's office, and over $600,000 in gifts and cash to a Polish official for national police contracts. The SEC found HP's books recorded the payments as legitimate commissions and expenses. Adjudicated bribery with an accompanying books-and-records failure.

Mid-Sep-2016: an HP firmware update containing an undisclosed 'Dynamic Security' feature activated in the field and bricked third-party ink cartridges in OfficeJet, OfficeJet Pro and OfficeJet Pro X printers (HP 934/935, 950/951, 970/971 cartridges), leaving customers' printers unusable without genuine HP supplies. Customers had received no warning. HP apologised on 28-Sep-2016 ('we should have done a better job of communicating about the authentication procedure') and committed to an optional firmware update removing the feature. Covert, unilateral disabling of already-purchased goods to protect the supplies margin - directly relevant to the Gate 2 assessment above, not merely a legal item.

Decision dated 17-Nov-2020, announced Dec-2020: the Italian Competition Authority (AGCM) fined HP Inc. and HP Italy EUR 10m for MISLEADING AND AGGRESSIVE COMMERCIAL PRACTICES over Dynamic Security. The authority found HP failed to inform consumers at purchase that non-original cartridges would be blocked, leading them to believe cartridges were faulty or empty, and separately recorded consumption and cartridge-origin data without prior notice in order to refuse free warranty assistance to printers that had used non-original cartridges. HP's appeal was denied. A regulator finding of systematic consumer deception. Well after all HPQ anchors - dated here only so the 2016-09 conduct can be seen for what a regulator later concluded it was; do NOT let this colour the 2017/2018/2019 evaluations.

Aug-2024: HP reached an agreement in principle to settle the US class action over firmware updates blocking third-party ink and toner, with the Mar-2025 settlement including a commitment to make such firmware updates optional. Far outside all anchors; recorded for completeness of the Dynamic Security thread.

gate1.note: Assisted tax preparation: ~10,000 US retail offices plus DIY software; fee-per-return economics, seasonal working capital, franchise/company-owned mix. A generalist can model returns prepared x net average charge less office cost. Not opaque.

gate2.note: Brand, physical office density and high client retention gave real repeat-purchase economics and pricing power (net average charge rose most years through FY2015). But the substitution threat was already in reported results before the first anchor: FY2016 (announced 2016-06-14) showed 23.2m returns worldwide, -4.1% y/y, and US assisted returns -5.8% through 2016-04-19, with Intuit publicly estimating the DIY category took ~2 points of share from assisted as of Feb 2016. Credit Karma Tax launched genuinely free federal+state filing in Jan 2017, and the IRS Free File Alliance channel was already free for ~70% of filers.

Pricing power visibly gone. On 2018-12-06 (Q2 FY2019 release) H&R Block announced 'upfront, transparent pricing' -- an explicit price cut for assisted clients to defend volume. FY2019 results (2019-06-11) confirmed the trade: US returns +1.5% to 20.3m but total revenue -2.1% to $3.1bn and EPS from continuing ops down to $2.15 from $2.98. Cutting price to hold share against a free substitute is the definition of an absent moat.

gate3.note: NY AG Eliot Spitzer sued H&R Block on 2006-03-15 for fraudulent marketing of 'Express IRA' accounts to low/middle-income tax clients (hidden fees, near-certain loss for ~30,000 New Yorkers). Settled by AG Cuomo in Jan 2010: refunds of $11.4m-$19.4m of fees nationwide plus $750k in fines/costs.

SEC charged H&R Block subsidiary Option One Mortgage (n/k/a Sand Canyon) on 2012-04-24 with misleading investors in >$4.3bn of subprime RMBS sold in early 2007 -- promising repurchase of breaching loans while concealing that it could not fund those obligations without discretionary parent support. Settled same day for $28.2m ($14.25m disgorgement, $3.98m interest, $10m penalty) without admitting or denying.

ProPublica reported (2019-04-22 for Intuit, H&R Block confirmed in follow-ups ~2019-04-26) that H&R Block, like Intuit, used robots.txt code to hide its IRS Free File product from Google and other search engines, steering Free File-eligible consumers into paid products. NY Gov. Cuomo called for a DFS investigation 2019-05-01; the LA City Attorney sued H&R Block and Intuit in early May 2019 alleging fraudulent, deceptive and unfair practices. Systematic consumer deception, credibly alleged and largely conceded on the facts.

New York Department of Financial Services concluded its investigation and publicly found that Intuit and H&R Block used 'unfair and abusive practices' to divert Free File-eligible taxpayers into paid products -- a regulator finding of misconduct, not merely an allegation.
LA City Attorney announced a $1.6m restitution settlement with H&R Block for California customers who paid despite being Free File-eligible.

FTC filed an administrative complaint (2024-02-23) alleging H&R Block deceptively marketed 'free' online filing and deleted consumers' entered tax data to coerce downgrade calls; resolved by consent order in 2024 (~$7m plus injunctive relief).

gate1.note: Integrated design + manufacture of x86 CPUs sold to PC OEMs and datacenter operators. Unit economics are legible: fab capex and depreciation against ASP x unit volume, with gross margin as the direct read-out of process leadership. Technically demanding but not a black box.

gate2.note: Through the 2015-2017 anchors the moat was intact in reported results: ~99% x86 server share (AMD server share was 0.8% at end-2017 per Mercury Research), gross margins in the low-60s%, and a manufacturing process lead over TSMC/Samsung. The first crack was public but not yet in results: on the Q2 2015 call (2015-07-15, i.e. AFTER the 2015-06-30 anchor but before 2016-06-30) CEO Krzanich pushed first 10nm product (Cannon Lake) to 2H2017, formally breaking tick-tock. Restructuring and ~12,000 layoffs followed 2016-04-19. Neither had yet dented share or margin.

By the 2019-06-30 anchor the process-leadership moat was demonstrably gone and it was showing up in third-party share data. Intel slipped 10nm again on the 2018-04-26 Q1 call (volume production pushed to 2019, third public delay); TSMC ran 7nm in high volume during 2018, ending Intel's node lead; AMD launched Ryzen (Mar 2017) and EPYC (Jun 2017) and Mercury Research data published in early 2019 showed AMD server share going 0.8% (end-2017) to 3.2% (end-2018). Intel still earned enormous returns, so NARROW rather than NONE.

gate3.note: European Commission fined Intel EUR 1.06bn (2009-05-13) for abuse of dominance 2002-2007 -- exclusivity rebates to OEMs/retailers and payments to delay AMD-based product launches. A regulator finding of misconduct, and it was a live, affirmed finding at all three anchors: the General Court upheld it in full on 2014-06-12. Only later was it unwound -- ECJ set aside the General Court judgment 2017-09-06 (after the 2017-06-30 anchor) and the General Court annulled the fine 2022-01-26. REGRADED 2026-07-27 from DISQUALIFYING to SERIOUS: this is pure competition law (exclusivity rebates), with no deception element, so it fails the dishonesty test the corrected Gate 3 rubric applies. It was also upheld by the General Court 2014-06-12 but SET ASIDE by the ECJ 2017-09-06 and the fine annulled in 2022 -- a finding that did not survive review should not permanently disqualify.

FTC consent order (Aug 2010) settling charges that Intel used anticompetitive tactics against AMD and Nvidia; no admission of liability. Follows Intel's 2009-11-12 $1.25bn settlement of AMD's private antitrust suit.

Meltdown/Spectre disclosed 2018-01-03. Reporting the following day showed CEO Krzanich had exercised and sold ~900,000 shares for ~$24m on 2017-11-29 under a 10b5-1 plan adopted 2017-10-30 -- months after Google notified Intel of the flaws in June 2017 -- leaving him at his contractual 250,000-share minimum. Two members of Congress called for an SEC investigation; no enforcement action resulted.

Krzanich resigned as CEO 2018-06-21 after an investigation confirmed a past consensual relationship with an employee that violated Intel's non-fraternization policy. Governance/character event, not financial misconduct.

gate1.note: Conventional supermarket retail plus fuel centers and pharmacy: identical-store sales, gross margin, and inventory turns are all disclosed and easy to model. Understandable.

gate2.note: Local scale density, private label (Simple Truth/Our Brands), and a genuinely long operating record: 52 consecutive quarters of positive identical-supermarket sales through fiscal 2016 and 12 consecutive years of market-share gains as of the FY2016 report. But the underlying economics were always thin (~1.5-2% net margin, ~10-11% ROIC) and grocery is a price-transparent commodity, so NARROW not WIDE.

Three dated events all landed before the 2017-06-30 anchor. (1) 2017-03-02: Q4 FY2016 identical-supermarket sales came in at -0.7% ex-fuel, ending the 52-quarter/13-year streak, driven by food deflation and Walmart price investment. (2) 2017-06-15: Kroger cut FY2017 adjusted EPS guidance from $2.21-$2.25 to $2.00-$2.05 and withdrew long-term guidance altogether; the stock fell ~19%. (3) 2017-06-16: Amazon announced the $13.7bn Whole Foods acquisition and KR fell another ~9%, ~$7bn of market value lost over the two days. A retailer that cannot forecast its own economics one year out and must match a structurally lower-cost entrant on price has no durable pricing advantage.

gate3.note: Kroger was one of many victims of the Accellion FTA file-transfer breach (Dec 2020, notifications Feb 2021) exposing employee and pharmacy customer data; $5m class settlement proposed later. Ordinary-course third-party vendor breach.

Kroger announced a nationwide opioid settlement charge of ~$1.2bn (2023-09) with states, subdivisions and tribes over pharmacy dispensing practices, without admission of liability. Far after all anchors.

gate1.note: Branded consumer staples sold through retail: volume x price less advertising and manufacturing cost, with segment-level disclosure. About as legible as a large company gets.

gate2.note: Across all three anchors (2013/2014/2015) the moat held on every measurable test. Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Oral-B and Always carried category-leading share; gross margin stayed near 49-50% and operating margin in the high teens/low 20s; ROIC remained well above cost of capital; and P&G continued to take price. Organic growth did decelerate -- FY2013 organic sales +3%, guidance of +3-4% for FY2014, and quarters in FY2015 running ~+2% -- and on 2014-08-01 A.G. Lafley announced the divestiture/discontinuation of 90-100 brands to concentrate on 70-80 brands representing ~90% of sales and >95% of profit. That was portfolio pruning to raise returns, not evidence of lost pricing power, and margins subsequently expanded. No downgrade is warranted from dated evidence at these anchors. (Emerging threats visible but not yet in results: Dollar Shave Club/Harry's pressure on Gillette from ~2014-2015, and later e-commerce private label.)

gate3.note: European Commission decision of 2011-04-13 fined P&G EUR 211.2m (Unilever EUR 104m; Henkel immunity) for a powdered-laundry-detergent cartel across eight EU countries running Jan 2002 - Mar 2005: agreeing market shares and agreeing not to cut prices when package sizes shrank under a joint environmental initiative. Classified DISQUALIFYING strictly per the rubric -- it is an adjudicated regulator finding of misconduct (price fixing). Mitigating facts for the caller's calibration: it was resolved under the EC cartel settlement procedure with a 10% fine reduction for cooperation, the conduct ended in 2005, the fine was ~0.3% of annual sales, and the matter was closed and fully paid well before the 2013-06-30 anchor. No comparably material regulatory finding against P&G surfaced in the 2013-2015 window. REVIEWED 2026-07-27 and RETAINED as DISQUALIFYING: unlike an abuse-of-dominance case, a secret cartel is collusion concealed from customers and regulators, which is squarely the dishonesty Gate 3 tests. Mitigation noted: conduct ended 2005, settled with a cooperation discount.

gate1.note: Handbags and accessories sold through owned retail, outlets, department stores and wholesale. Comparable sales, gross margin and store count are all disclosed; the economics are simple even if fashion demand is not predictable.

gate2.note: Coach's pre-2014 economics were genuinely excellent -- ~30%+ operating margin and high returns on capital on an 'accessible luxury' brand. But the mechanism of dilution was already visible in the filings: factory-outlet channel contribution rose from ~40% of sales a decade earlier to ~70% by the end of fiscal 2013, meaning the brand was being discounted faster than the full-price stores could build it. Never WIDE by Buffett standards -- a fashion brand whose price realization depends on outlet traffic is not durable.

Pricing power broke in reported results, visibly, before the 2014-06-30 anchor and long before Coach/Tapestry's first anchor here. North America comparable sales fell 13.6% in the December-2013 quarter (reported Jan 2014) and roughly 21% in the following quarter, after four straight quarters of declines; FY2015 net sales fell ~20% to ~$4.2bn and operating margin roughly halved. Management itself conceded the diagnosis: on 2014-06-19 Coach presented a multi-year transformation plan cutting promotional events and closing ~70 North American stores, and the stock fell ~9%. Comps did turn positive again in FY2017 and the Kate Spade acquisition (announced 2017-05-08, closed 2017-07-11) added scale, but the demonstrated need to reset the brand every cycle is the opposite of a durable advantage.

gate3.note: Consolidated 'fictitious pricing' class action (Marino v. Coach, filed Feb 2016) alleging Coach outlet tags compared prices to an MFSRP at which manufactured-for-outlet goods were never sold. Coach settled for $4.6m without admitting wrongdoing; the class period ran 2011-12-23 to 2020-08-24. Industry-wide outlet practice, ordinary-course consumer litigation.

CEO and chairman Jide Zeitlin resigned abruptly on 2020-07-21 after a board investigation into personal misconduct allegations (a woman alleged he posed as a photographer to induce a relationship roughly a decade earlier), amplified by a ProPublica investigation. Post-dates the 2020-06-30 anchor by three weeks. Follows Victor Luis's departure as CEO effective 2019-09-03, weeks after Tapestry cut its full-year forecast and warned on Kate Spade.

gate1.note: Core group disability and group life are analyzable, but a very large closed block of long-term-care policies is not: its adequacy depends on unobservable 40-50 year morbidity, policy-termination and reinvestment-rate assumptions that outsiders cannot check, and the reported figure moved by billions on management's own assumption changes. This is the textbook unanalyzable financial black box, and it was structurally true at every anchor, not just with hindsight -- confirmed later when the Maine Bureau of Insurance concluded (8-K filed 2020-05-04, 10-Q 2020-05-05) that Unum America's statutory LTC reserves were $2.1bn deficient as of 2018-12-31, three years after Unum's own GAAP reviews said otherwise.

gate2.note: Unum was the largest US group disability writer with entrenched employer/broker distribution, high case persistency and decent core-line underwriting margins, producing low-double-digit ROE. That is a distribution and scale advantage in a slow-moving product, not pricing power -- benefit costs are set by competitive bidding and the closed blocks are pure legacy liability.

The LTC block proved the franchise had been mispricing risk for decades. On 2018-05-01/02 (before the 2018-06-30 anchor) Unum disclosed a Q1 LTC interest-adjusted loss ratio of 96.6% versus 88.6% a year earlier and against 85-90% guidance, and the stock fell ~17% in a day. Then on 2018-09-18 (after the 2018 anchor, before the 2019 anchor) Unum announced the results of its LTC reserve review: a ~$750m pre-tax / $593.1m after-tax charge ($2.71 per diluted share) taken in Q3 2018. A business whose largest legacy liability can be revalued by that much is earning no economic rent. Confirmed again on 2020-05-04 by the Maine BOI $2.1bn statutory deficiency finding (7-year phase-in from year-end 2020, ~$200-250m in 2020).

gate3.note: UnumProvident settled a multistate market conduct examination on 2004-11-18 with insurance regulators from 48 states, joined by the US Department of Labor and supported by the NY AG: a $15m fine and mandatory reassessment of roughly 200,000 previously denied long-term disability claims. Regulators found inappropriate construction of medical reports to claimants' detriment and a significant number of denials for lack of 'objective evidence' where no such policy requirement existed. Systematic consumer harm found by regulators -- and it goes to the same claims-reserving culture that produced the later LTC problem.

California, which opted out of the multistate deal, reached its own settlement under Insurance Commissioner Garamendi, including an $8m fine, after finding the company's claims process itself unlawful.

Securities class actions filed beginning 2018-06-13 (Pittman v. Unum Group, E.D. Tenn.) for a 2018-01-31 to 2018-05-02 class period, alleging Unum concealed rising LTC claim incidence and unfavorable policy terminations. Plaintiffs ultimately lost. Kept MINOR because no fraud was established.

gate1.note: Integrated oil and gas: upstream volumes and realizations, downstream and chemical margins, reserve replacement and return on capital employed are all disclosed on a consistent basis. Commodity-exposed but not opaque.

gate2.note: Judged honestly, Exxon at the 2013/2014/2015 anchors had a real but limited advantage: an AAA credit rating held since 1949 (last non-AAA in 1930), the industry's best capital discipline and ROCE (~19% in 2013 versus mid-single-digit peers in bad years), an integrated downstream/chemicals hedge that cushioned the crude cycle, and 21 consecutive years of 100%+ reserve replacement through 2014. It is still a price taker in a commodity -- no pricing power, and the resource base depletes -- so NARROW, never WIDE. Note the 2013 and 2014 anchors both precede the OPEC-driven crude collapse that began in late 2014.

Three dated disclosures, all before the 2016-06-30 anchor, showed the advantage was cyclical rather than structural. (1) 2016-02-02: FY2015 results put ROCE at ~7.9% against ~19% in 2013, with capex and the dividend no longer covered by operating cash flow. (2) 2016-02-19: Exxon announced 2015 reserve additions of 1.0bn oil-equivalent barrels, a 67% reserve replacement ratio -- the first sub-100% year in over two decades. (3) 2016-04-26: S&P stripped the AAA rating, cutting to AA+ on low oil prices and high dividend payments. The 2016 reserve report (Feb 2017) then de-booked billions of barrels of Canadian oil sands. A business that cannot replace its own inventory or earn its cost of capital through a cycle has no durable advantage.

gate3.note: Pegasus pipeline rupture at Mayflower, Arkansas on 2013-03-29 spilled Wabasca heavy crude into a residential subdivision. Resolved with federal and state settlements (~$5m civil penalties plus remediation) in 2015. Ordinary-course operating/environmental liability for a pipeline operator.

NY AG Eric Schneiderman subpoenaed Exxon on 2015-11-04 (public 2015-11-05) for four decades of climate research, communications and financial records, investigating whether the company misled the public and investors about climate risk. Massachusetts AG followed in April 2016. Investigation, not a finding, at this date.

Reported 2016-09-20 that the SEC was investigating Exxon's refusal to impair reserves and assets while crude fell ~60% from mid-2014 (Chevron and Shell had impaired), and its use of proxy carbon-cost assumptions in project economics. No enforcement action followed; the probe was reported closed in 2018.

OFAC imposed a $2m civil penalty on 2017-07-20 for Ukraine-related sanctions violations: Exxon executed May 2014 legal documents with Rosneft countersigned by Igor Sechin, an individually designated SDN. Exxon sued within hours; the Northern District of Texas vacated the penalty on 2019-12-31.

NY AG filed a securities-fraud suit on 2018-10-24 alleging Exxon kept two sets of proxy-cost-of-carbon books to overstate asset values. After trial, Justice Ostrager ruled for Exxon on 2019-12-10, finding no material misrepresentation. Kept SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING because the fraud claim was adjudicated in Exxon's favor -- but at the 2018-2019 dates it was a live, credibly-pled AG fraud allegation.

gate1.note: Rate-regulated electric utility: revenue is rate base times a state/FERC-allowed ROE, plus recovery of fuel and capex through riders - a generalist can follow the unit economics from the rate cases and rate-base growth disclosures. Complicated in 2013-2014 only by the ~8 GW of unregulated Ohio/PJM merchant generation still on the books, which AEP had already announced it intended to divest.

gate2.note: Legal monopoly over service territory in 11 states (~5.4M customers, largest US transmission network) is a real barrier to entry, but the moat is granted and priced by regulators, not by the customer: authorized ROEs in the 9.5-10.5% band, earned ROE around 10%, no independent pricing power, and periodic regulatory lag (Ohio ESP litigation, Texas/Virginia/Kentucky rate cases 2013-2014). Merchant generation exposed to weak PJM capacity/energy prices in 2013-2014 was explicitly NOT moated - AEP announced in 2013-2014 it would sell or transfer those competitive assets (sale to Lightstone/Blackstone-Arclight closed 2017-01). Substitution threat low in the period; distributed solar was immaterial to load.

gate3.note: 2007-10-09: DOJ/EPA, 8 states and 13 citizen groups announced a Clean Air Act New Source Review consent decree covering 16 coal plants (46 units) - the largest environmental settlement in US history at the time: ~$4.6B of pollution controls, $15M civil penalty, $60M mitigation. Settled without adjudication of liability. Third joint modification entered 2013-05-14 (Rockport FGD deadline extension in exchange for tighter SO2 caps).

2020-07-21: arrest of Ohio House Speaker Larry Householder in the $60M HB6 bribery case put AEP's own political spending in the frame - AEP was the sole funder of the 501(c)(4) Empowering Ohio's Economy (approximately $8.7M over the period), which routed $150K to Generation Now and $200K to a Householder-aligned coalition. AEP was never criminally charged; its 2020-07 press release denying involvement was later found misleading by the SEC.

2021-06: AEP disclosed it had received an SEC subpoena (issued 2021-05) for documents relating to HB6 and to its dark-money contributions; a second subpoena followed in 2022-08. Shareholder securities class action and derivative suits filed in the same period.

2025-01: SEC administrative order - AEP agreed to pay $19M to settle findings that it issued a materially misleading press release about its role in funding Empowering Ohio's Economy, failed to disclose the related-party payments, and violated the books-and-records/internal-controls provisions of the Exchange Act. A regulator finding of misconduct against the issuer itself.

gate1.note: Health insurer: premiums in, medical costs out, with the medical benefit ratio and reserve development as the two things that matter - analyzable from the 10-K, not a black box. Reserve estimation and heavy dependence on government program rules (Medicare Advantage rates, ACA risk adjustment) make it harder than a retailer but not opaque.

gate2.note: Scale advantage in provider-network contracting and claims administration (about 23M medical members after the Coventry acquisition closed 2013-05-07, third-largest US insurer), sticky national-account and ASC relationships, and regulatory licensing barriers. But pricing power is statutorily capped: the ACA medical loss ratio floors effective 2011 (80% individual/small group, 85% large group) force rebates above a fixed underwriting margin, state regulators approve rates, and employer plan sponsors re-bid annually. Net margin ~4-5%, ROE ~13-15% in 2013-2014. New in the 2014 anchor year: public exchange participation from 2014-01 with unproven risk pools, risk-corridor receivables, and the health insurer fee - all downside skew to the pricing side of the moat (Aetna exited most exchange markets 2016-08 after large losses).

gate3.note: 2010-04-05: CMS imposed intermediate sanctions on Aetna, suspending marketing and enrollment for all Medicare Advantage-PD and standalone Part D contracts effective 2010-04-21, citing serious deficiencies in formulary/benefit administration, coverage determinations and appeals, and low-income-subsidy best-available-evidence handling. Sanctions lifted 2011-06.

2012-12-07/18: announced $120M proposed class settlement of out-of-network reimbursement claims (use of the discredited Ingenix usual-and-customary database to underpay non-network providers and members), New Jersey federal court. No admission of liability. Aetna terminated the settlement in 2014-03 when participation thresholds were not met, and the litigation continued.

Humana merger saga: announced 2015-07-03 ($37B); DOJ sued to block 2016-07-21; Judge John D. Bates permanently enjoined the deal 2017-01-23 under Clayton Act sec. 7 and, notably, found Aetna's stated public rationale for withdrawing from 17 ACA exchange markets in 2016-08 was not the real one - the court concluded Aetna withdrew at least in part to improve its litigation position, i.e. a judicial finding that the company's public explanation was pretextual. Deal terminated 2017-02-14; Aetna paid Humana a $1B break fee 2017-02-16. No fraud adjudication.

2018-01-17: $17M class settlement over an 2017-07/08 mailing whose oversized envelope windows disclosed up to ~12,000 members' HIV medication status; followed by state AG penalties (including a DC AG fine and a $935K California settlement) through 2018.

2018-02-11: CNN published deposition testimony from a former Aetna Southern California medical director (in the role 2012-2015) that he never reviewed patient medical records before approving or denying coverage; the California Insurance Commissioner opened an investigation the same day and other state regulators widened it within the week. Aetna settled the underlying suit in 2019-03/04 before trial.

gate1.note: Single-format retail: sell hard parts and maintenance items out of ~5,500-6,000 US stores at ~53% gross margin, hold enormous slow-turning inventory financed largely by vendor payables, and convert the cash into buybacks. Store-level economics are fully transparent in the filings.

gate2.note: Best-in-class economics sustained for two decades: company-reported after-tax return on invested capital in the low-30s (32.1% for fiscal 2018; ~31-32% fiscal 2017), gross margin 53.2% in fiscal 2018, operating margin high-teens. The durable advantage is inventory density, not price - a hub and mega-hub network that puts hard-to-find SKUs within same-day reach of satellite stores, which is exactly what a DIFM commercial customer with a car on the lift and a DIY customer with a dead vehicle will pay up for. Demand is failure-driven and non-discretionary, and the aging US vehicle fleet (average age rising past 11 years through 2017-2018) is a tailwind. Substitution threat tested in real time: auto-parts equities sold off hard in 2017 when Amazon expanded into parts (AZO shares fell roughly 40% from 2016 highs into 2017), yet fiscal 2018 domestic comps still turned positive (Q4 fiscal 2018 same-store sales +2.2%) and commercial/DIFM kept taking share, because delivery time and installation service are the binding constraints, not shelf price. Classification unchanged across both anchor dates.

gate3.note: 2014-11-17/24: San Diego federal jury in Juarez v. AutoZone Stores awarded $872,719 compensatory and $185,000,000 punitive damages for pregnancy discrimination, harassment and retaliation - one of the largest single-plaintiff employment verdicts on record. Parties jointly moved to dismiss on 2015-07-20 after a confidential settlement; no adjudicated finding survived.

2019-06-19: California AG announced an $11M settlement ($8.9M civil penalties, $1.35M supplemental environmental projects, $750K costs) covering illegal disposal of hazardous waste and of customer records with unredacted personal information at AutoZone stores in 45 counties. The underlying investigation covered conduct in 2013-2015, but the enforcement action and its facts only became public in 2019-06 - after both anchor dates.

gate1.note: Two understandable segments: metal beverage/food packaging (a converting business with aluminum cost passed through contractually) and a smaller aerospace/defense unit sold on cost-plus and fixed-price government contracts. Heterogeneous but not a conglomerate black box; the can business is ~85-90% of revenue.

gate2.note: Structural advantages are real but shallow: aluminum can making is a consolidated oligopoly (Ball, Rexam and Crown accounting for the large majority of North American capacity in 2013-2014), plants are capital-intensive and typically sited beside the filler's line, and multi-year supply agreements pass through metal cost. Against that, the can itself is a commodity spec, the customer list is concentrated and powerful (Coca-Cola, AB InBev, PepsiCo, MillerCoors), North American CSD volumes were shrinking roughly 2-3% per year through 2013-2014, and returns reflect it - EBIT margins in the high single digits and ROIC around 10-11%, well below what a wide-moat franchise generates. Substitution from PET and glass is live. The Rexam deal (announced 2015-02-19, completed 2016-06-30 with FTC-mandated divestiture of 8 US plants plus European/Brazilian assets to Ardagh for $3.42B) increased scale and specialty-can mix but also added leverage and goodwill; classification stays NARROW - scale in a commodity converting business is not pricing power.

gate3.note: 2011-03-24: SEC settled FCPA books-and-records and internal-controls charges against Ball Corporation - its Argentine subsidiary Formametal S.A. paid roughly $106,000 in bribes to Argentine government employees in 2006-2007 to import prohibited used machinery and export raw materials at reduced tariffs. Ball paid a $300,000 civil penalty, settled without admitting or denying, and no DOJ criminal action followed. Flagged explicitly as an FCPA matter, though at the smallest end of the FCPA resolution range and remediated (employees terminated) more than two years before the first anchor date.

2016-07: FTC consent order in In the Matter of Ball Corporation and Rexam PLC required divestiture of seven beverage-can plants and one can-end plant in the US (plus European and Brazilian assets) to Ardagh to cure horizontal overlap in three US regional markets and in specialty cans. An ordinary merger remedy, not a finding of misconduct.

gate1.note: Specialty mall retail with transparent store-level economics. The complication is not opacity but composition: through this period L Brands was two opposite businesses stapled together - Victoria's Secret (declining comps, collapsing segment margin) and Bath & Body Works (mid-to-high single and later double-digit comps) - so consolidated figures average a shrinking franchise with a compounding one and must be read at the segment level.

gate2.note: Through fiscal 2015 the franchise looked genuinely wide: Victoria's Secret held roughly a third of the US intimates market with brand-driven pricing power and the Fashion Show as a marketing moat, Bath & Body Works was the dominant US personal-care specialty chain, consolidated operating margin ran ~17-18% on record fiscal 2015 sales of ~$12.2B, and returns on capital were well above 20%.

Only the Bath & Body Works half of the moat survived, and this was visible in reported results before the 2018-06-30 anchor. Victoria's Secret comparable sales turned sharply negative in fiscal 2017 - Q1 fiscal 2017 comps -14% (reported 2017-05, versus +2% in Q1 fiscal 2016), declines in essentially every month of 2017, full-year comps down mid-single digits with about 5 points attributable to the April 2016 exit of swim, apparel and the catalogue - while share migrated to Aerie, ThirdLove and DTC entrants. Bath & Body Works meanwhile comped above +5% across 2016-17 and +11-13% in fiscal 2018 with operating profit up 29%. The pricing power that defined the old classification (VS full-price brand) was gone, replaced by heavy promotion; a chain that must discount to hold traffic is not wide.

gate3.note: 2018-11-08: Vogue published chief marketing officer Ed Razek's remarks dismissing transgender and plus-size models in the Fashion Show, triggering a public backlash and an apology - reputational rather than legal, but the first public crack in the brand's governance story. Razek left the company in 2019-08.

2019-07-06: Jeffrey Epstein's federal sex-trafficking indictment put chairman/CEO Leslie Wexner's decades-long financial relationship with Epstein - who had held Wexner's power of attorney in the 1990s - under public scrutiny. L Brands' independent directors retained outside counsel in 2019-07 to review any company ties to Epstein. Wexner told shareholders in 2019-09 he was 'embarrassed' by the association and said Epstein had misappropriated vast sums from him. Post-dates the 2019-06-30 anchor by days.

2020-02-01: New York Times investigation described an entrenched culture of misogyny, bullying and harassment inside Victoria's Secret, including allegations against Razek and a board that failed to act; shareholder derivative suits against Wexner and the board followed. 2020-02-20: L Brands announced Wexner would step down as CEO and chairman alongside the sale of a 55% stake in Victoria's Secret to Sycamore (Sycamore terminated the deal 2020-05). 2020-07: L Brands announced a $90M fund for former employees and contractors plus a governance overhaul.

gate1.note: Medical consumables and instruments: needles, syringes, blood-collection tubes, infusion systems and diagnostics sold into hospitals and labs on GPO contracts, with a razor-and-blade consumable stream. Unit economics are straightforward to explain.

gate2.note: At the 2013 and 2014 anchors BD was a consumables near-monopoly in its core: global leader in vacuum blood collection (BD Vacutainer) and hypodermic needles/syringes, with switching costs anchored in lab automation compatibility, clinician training, 510(k)/validation barriers and multi-year GPO contracts. Gross margin ~50%, operating margin ~19-20%, ROE ~25% and mid-teens ROIC in fiscal 2013-2014, with 40+ consecutive years of dividend increases. Pricing power is real but bounded by hospital cost pressure and safety-syringe competition (Retractable, Terumo, Greiner) - Morningstar rated the moat narrow rather than wide over this period, and BD's own returns on capital sit below true wide-moat compounders, so the classification is at the boundary.

Two large debt-funded acquisitions changed the economics of the enterprise, and the effect was visible in fiscal 2018 results reported 2018-11: CareFusion (closed 2015-03, $12.2B) and C.R. Bard (announced 2017-04-23, closed 2017-12-29, $24B) left a goodwill-heavy balance sheet on which return on invested capital fell to high single digits, gross margin was diluted, and BD inherited mass-tort liabilities and device-quality problems it had not previously carried. The core Vacutainer/needle franchise still earns its keep, but the consolidated entity is a leveraged roll-up rather than an intact compounder.

gate3.note: 2013-07-30: BD settled hypodermic-products antitrust class actions brought by hospitals and pharmacies (cases filed Tennessee 2005, New Jersey 2006, New York 2007) alleging exclusionary bundling and exclusive dealing through GPOs and PBMs to maintain monopoly power in home-use insulin syringes - $22M into a settlement fund, no admission. Follows an earlier $45M direct-purchaser (distributor) settlement agreed 2009-04-27.

2013-09-19: federal jury in the Eastern District of Texas found for Retractable Technologies on attempted monopolization of the safety-syringe market and on Lanham Act false advertising, awarding $113,508,000 in antitrust damages (subject to trebling to roughly $340M). This was live and adverse at both anchor dates. The Fifth Circuit reversed the antitrust judgment and rendered judgment for BD on 2016-12-02, while affirming Lanham Act liability and remanding on disgorgement.

2017-12-29: closing of the C.R. Bard acquisition transferred to BD Bard's mass-tort inventory - hernia mesh, pelvic mesh and IVC filter litigation involving thousands of claimants. Bard IVC filter bellwether trials began 2018-03 with plaintiff verdicts; reserves and claim counts have been disclosed in BD filings since.

2020-02: BD disclosed remediation and recall activity on Alaris infusion pumps (inherited from CareFusion) and a delayed 510(k) clearance, cutting guidance. A product-quality and regulatory-clearance failure rather than a finding of misconduct.

gate1.note: Diesel and natural-gas engines, components, aftertreatment, power generation and distribution, sold mostly to a short list of truck and equipment OEMs plus a large aftermarket parts and service stream. Cyclical and segment-heavy, but every line is explainable from unit volumes, content per engine and parts attach.

gate2.note: Cummins is the leading independent engine maker - roughly 40% of the North American heavy-duty truck engine market plus the exclusive diesel for Ram 2500/3500 pickups - and the installed base feeds a high-margin aftermarket parts and service annuity through several hundred distributors and thousands of dealers. Successive emissions rules (EPA 2010, GHG Phase 1 and the Phase 2 rule finalized 2016-08) raised the R&D and aftertreatment scale required to compete, which favors the largest independent. What keeps this from wide: the buyers are a handful of OEMs with real leverage, several of whom vertically integrated against Cummins (Daimler/Detroit Diesel, Volvo, PACCAR MX), demand is violently cyclical - North American Class 8 orders collapsed in 2016 and Cummins revenue fell about 9% that year to ~$17.5B with EPS down sharply, exactly across the 2016 and 2017 anchors - and returns, while good through the cycle (ROIC mid-to-high teens, ROE above 20%), are not fortress-stable. Long-run substitution risk from alternative powertrains was visible but not yet material in 2016-2017.

gate3.note: 2019-04-29: Cummins publicly disclosed it was conducting a formal internal review, with external advisers, of its emissions certification process and compliance for pickup-truck applications, following conversations with EPA and CARB about certification of engines in model year 2019 Ram 2500/3500 trucks, and voluntarily reported the review to EPA, CARB, DOJ and the SEC. Nothing about this - and nothing about the underlying conduct, which reached back to model year 2013 engines - was public before the 2016-06-30 or 2017-06-30 anchor dates.

2023-12-22: DOJ, EPA and CARB announced an agreement in principle (consent decree lodged 2024-01-10) resolving findings that Cummins installed defeat devices on engines in roughly 630,000 model year 2013-2019 Ram 2500/3500 trucks and undisclosed auxiliary emission control devices on roughly 330,000 model year 2019-2023 trucks. Civil penalty of $1.675B - the largest ever under the Clean Air Act - with total obligations, including recall 67A (announced 2023-11, ~560,000 trucks) and mitigation, valued above $2B; Cummins booked a ~$2.04B charge. Adjudicated-equivalent regulatory finding of systematic emissions defeat-device conduct.

gate1.note: Class I railroad: revenue = carloads x revenue-per-unit, costs tracked by a single published metric (operating ratio), capital spending on track/equipment is disclosed line by line. Capital-intensive but a generalist can explain how it earns money.

gate2.note: Eastern US duopoly with Norfolk Southern over an unreplicable right-of-way; post-Staggers (1980) rate freedom. Pricing power is visible in reported results: core pricing +1.3% in 2013 and continued same-store price gains across nearly all markets in 2014-2016 even while volumes fell. Operating ratio improved from ~71% (2013) to a record 66.8% in Q2 2015 (reported July 2015) and a Q3 record 68.3% (reported Oct 2015); ROIC ran low-to-mid teens 2013-2015. Substitution risk is limited for bulk/intermodal length-of-haul (rail cost per ton-mile far below truck). Coal was a demand shock, not a moat loss: export coal tonnage -8% (2013) and -11% (2014), coal revenue per carload -2% (2013) and -7% (2014), and management guided 2015 coal revenue down ~$450M (Jan 2015) on cheap natural gas -- yet price realization on the remaining book stayed positive, which is the moat test, not the volume.

gate3.note: In re Rail Freight Fuel Surcharge Antitrust Litigation (MDL 1869), filed 2007 against CSX, BNSF, NS and UP after the STB's Jan 2007 ruling barred rate-based fuel surcharges: shippers alleged a price-fixing conspiracy on fuel surcharges. Class certified June 2012; D.C. Circuit VACATED certification on 2013-08-09 (Comcast v. Behrend); on remand certification was DENIED and the D.C. Circuit AFFIRMED that denial 2019-08-30. No conspiracy was ever proven and no admission was made; direct-action suits by individual shippers continued for years afterward with CSX winning summary judgment in the long-running matter. Graded SERIOUS (competition-law allegation, unproven) rather than DISQUALIFYING because no cartel finding was ever entered.

Mount Carbon, West Virginia crude-oil train derailment and spill on 2015-02-16 (before the 2016-06-30 anchor; after the 2013 anchor); no fatalities. DOJ/EPA/West Virginia lodged a consent decree 2018-07-24: $1.2M federal civil penalty, $1.0M to West Virginia, plus $500K escrowed for a Kanawha Falls water-treatment upgrade. Environmental/safety violation, no deception element, and the penalty is immaterial to CSX's earnings.

EEOC sued CSX Transportation 2017-08-01 alleging its physical-ability tests had an unlawful disparate impact on female applicants; CSX agreed to a $3.2M consent decree announced 2018-06-13. Post-dates both anchors.

DOL/OSHA (announced 2024-10-11) obtained a federal court order requiring CSX to reinstate and pay $453K to two employees illegally terminated after raising safety concerns in 2017; OSHA had previously found similar Federal Rail Safety Act whistleblower retaliation at a locomotive shop (2016) and a Selkirk NY dispatch office (2010). Pattern of retaliation against internal safety reporting; well after both anchors.

gate1.note: Sells and finances agricultural/construction machines: units x price less material and manufacturing cost, plus a captive lender (John Deere Capital) whose economics are interest spread minus credit losses. Both halves are disclosed separately and are easy for a generalist to explain.

gate2.note: Dealer network (roughly 1,500 North American dealers), brand, parts/aftermarket annuity and precision-ag data lock-in. The decisive dated evidence is behaviour in a violent downturn: USDA net farm income fell from ~$124B (2013) to ~$108B (2014) to $73.6B (2015, USDA estimate published during 2015, the lowest since 2009). Deere's net sales and revenues fell 20% to $28.9B in FY2015 (reported 2015-11) and equipment sales fell 22%, yet FY2015 sales still carried POSITIVE price realization of +1% (i.e., Deere raised prices into a 22% volume collapse) and the company stayed profitable every quarter: net income $3.16B FY2014, $1.94B FY2015, ~$1.5B FY2016 (guided ~$1.4B in mid-2016). That combination -- price up while volume craters -- is the pricing-power proof; the earnings decline is cyclical demand, not moat erosion. Competitive set in high-horsepower North America is narrow (CNH, AGCO), and DOJ itself later described high-speed precision planting as a two-player market.

gate3.note: DOJ Antitrust Division sued 2016-08-31 (two months AFTER the 2016-06-30 anchor) to block Deere's purchase of Precision Planting from Monsanto, calling it a merger-to-monopoly in high-speed precision planting systems; trial was set for 2017-06-05 and Deere/Monsanto abandoned the deal on 2017-05-01. Graded MINOR because this was a prospective merger-review challenge with no allegation of wrongful conduct, deception, or abuse of an existing position, and no penalty.

SEC charged Deere with FCPA violations on 2024-09-10; Deere paid ~$9.93M ($4.3M disgorgement, ~$1.1M interest, $4.5M penalty). Wirtgen Thailand employees bribed Royal Thai Air Force, Department of Highways and Department of Rural Roads officials (cash, massage-parlour visits, international travel) plus private-company employees to win contracts, from at least late 2017 through 2020. Bribery = dishonesty, so DISQUALIFYING -- but note the conduct began late 2017 at a subsidiary acquired with Wirtgen in Dec 2017, i.e. entirely AFTER both the 2015-06-30 and 2016-06-30 anchors, and was unknown publicly until 2024. Deere fired the employees involved and remediated controls.

FTC, with the Illinois and Minnesota attorneys general, sued Deere on 2025-01-15 alleging unlawful restriction of independent repair (withholding the full Service ADVISOR tool) to monopolize repair of Deere agricultural equipment. Pure competition-law/monopolization theory with no deception element; far past both anchors and unresolved as of the latest information available here.

gate1.note: Clinical laboratory: requisitions x revenue per requisition, against a largely fixed cost base of labs, couriers and patient service centres, with the payer mix (Medicare/Medicaid, commercial, client bill, patient) disclosed. The one thing a generalist must accept is that price is set by payers, not by Quest -- but that is a moat question, not an opacity question.

gate2.note: Largest US clinical lab: national logistics network, ~2,200 patient service centres and the lowest cost per test in the industry -- a real scale advantage that gives it a place in every payer network. But it has no pricing power and the record says so with dates: 2013 revenue fell ~3% to $7.15B with revenue per requisition down 3%, roughly 2 points of it from reimbursement pressure (reported 2014-01-30); Medicare clinical lab fee schedule rates were being cut administratively; and PAMA was signed 2014-04-01, mandating that Medicare CLFS rates be reset to market-weighted private-payer medians (cuts eventually effective 2018) -- a statutory price cut Quest could not resist. Payer power was demonstrated earlier when UnitedHealthcare moved its exclusive national lab contract to LabCorp (announced 2006, effective 2007), an event that cost Quest volume it took years to recover. Substitutes are real: hospital outreach labs, physician-office testing, and a direct competitor of comparable scale in LabCorp. Durable but capped: NARROW, not WIDE.

gate3.note: On 2009-04-15 Quest's subsidiary Nichols Institute Diagnostics pleaded guilty in EDNY to a felony misbranding charge under the FDCA and Quest/NID paid $302M total ($40M criminal fine plus $262M-plus-interest to resolve False Claims Act allegations) -- at the time one of the largest medical-device recoveries ever. The government alleged NID marketed its Nichols Advantage Intact PTH immunoassay as having 'excellent correlation' with the IRMA assay while knowing it produced elevated readings. That is affirmative deception of customers and regulators, hence DISQUALIFYING; conduct ran to 2006 and the NID kit business was exited. Roughly four years stale at the 2013-06-30 anchor and under a different CEO (Stephen Rusckowski took over 2012-05), but the plea itself is a corporate felony conviction for misbranding.

Quest disclosed an agreement in principle 2011-05-09 and finalized on 2011-05-19 a $241M settlement with the California AG, DHCS and qui tam relator (Hunter Laboratories/Chris Riedel) -- the largest recovery in the history of the California False Claims Act. Allegations: overcharging Medi-Cal for more than 15 years versus the 'best price' rule and giving kickbacks in the form of discounted or free testing to physicians, hospitals and clinics. Settled without admission of liability, so SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING; two years before the 2013 anchor.

DOJ announced 2017-05-01 that Quest would pay $6M to resolve FCA allegations that Berkeley HeartLab (acquired by Quest with Celera in 2011) paid kickbacks to referring physicians disguised as 'process and handling' fees and waived patient copayments to drive blood-test referrals, plus medically unnecessary testing. No admission; Quest had ended the conduct. Post-dates both anchors.

Disclosed 2019-06-03: American Medical Collection Agency, a third-party billing-collections vendor to Quest's revenue-cycle contractor, was breached, exposing data on approximately 11.9M Quest patients. Vendor security failure, no deception by Quest; well after both anchors.

gate1.note: Diversified industrial run as four reported segments (Energy, Engineered Systems, Fluids, Refrigeration & Food Equipment), each a collection of niche equipment and consumables businesses with disclosed segment revenue and margins. Conglomerate breadth makes it tedious, not opaque -- a generalist can explain any single unit's economics (sell the machine, then sell the parts and consumables).

gate2.note: Portfolio of #1/#2 positions in small niches (artificial-lift pumps, fluid transfer/dispensing, marking and coding, retail refrigeration cases) with aftermarket and consumable attach rates that give real switching costs, and returns on capital in the low teens. But durability is limited on two dated counts. First, end-market dependence rather than pricing power: after oil crashed from ~$100 (June 2014) to under $50 (Jan 2015), Energy segment revenue fell from ~$2.05B (2014) to ~$1.48B (2015) and then a further 25.3% in 2016 (organic -24.4%), explicitly attributed in the FY2016 10-K to lower US rig count and customer capex -- Dover could not price through it, and took $55.2M of restructuring charges in 2015, $30.8M of it in Energy. Total revenue fell from $7.75B (2014) to ~$6.96B (2015) to ~$6.79B (2016). Second, the moat is bought rather than built: Dover is a serial acquirer and serial divestor (Knowles spun off Feb 2014), so goodwill is heavy and the franchise is a rotating portfolio rather than one enduring economic castle. NARROW is the honest class at both the 2015 and 2016 anchors.

gate1.note: Consolidated Edison is a HEAVILY RATE-REGULATED utility -- explicitly the simplest unit economics in this set: earnings are approximately the allowed return on equity applied to an approved rate base, with fuel and purchased-power costs passed through to customers under New York Public Service Commission multi-year rate plans. A generalist can compute it from the rate order.

gate2.note: REGULATION IS THE MOAT AND ALSO THE CEILING, and that is why this is NARROW rather than WIDE. CECONY holds a state-granted monopoly franchise for electric, gas and steam delivery in New York City and Westchester: substitution is effectively nil, customers cannot switch wires, and the barrier to entry is legal rather than economic -- there will never be a second set of Manhattan feeders. But the NYPSC, not Con Edison, sets the price: the 2013 electric rate plan (covering 2014-2016) used a 9.2% allowed ROE, and the 2016 electric/gas rate order (Cases 16-E-0060 / 16-G-0061, approved 2016, effective 2017-01-01) reset the allowed ROE to 9.0%. Con Edison therefore has no independent pricing power, earns a regulated spread on rate base, and bears asymmetric downside: safety penalties and imprudence disallowances fall on shareholders, not ratepayers (the East Harlem settlement costs were explicitly shareholder-borne). Durable, low-return, regulator-capped: NARROW.

gate3.note: MANAGEMENT-DISCONTINUITY FLAG. In Nov 1994 Con Edison pleaded guilty to federal FELONY charges of concealing the extent of an asbestos release from regulators and making false statements, arising from the 1989-08-19 Gramercy Park steam explosion where the company did not report for four days that ~200 lbs of released insulation contained asbestos; it paid a $2M fine, was placed on court-supervised corporate probation, and spent ~$54M settling private claims. The underlying conduct IS dishonesty (concealment plus false statements to regulators), which is why it is recorded here rather than omitted -- but it is 20 years stale at the 2014-06-30 anchor and every relevant decision-maker had turned over (CEO Eugene McGrath 1990-2005, Kevin Burke 2005-2013, John McAvoy from 2013), so it is graded SERIOUS with the discontinuity flagged rather than treated as live disqualifying conduct at the 2014/2015 anchors.

2007-07-18 Lexington Avenue steam-main rupture in midtown Manhattan: one death, asbestos in the debris, extensive private litigation and a PSC/DPS review. Infrastructure failure, no deception alleged; seven years before the 2014 anchor.

East Harlem gas explosion 2014-03-12 (three and a half months BEFORE the 2014-06-30 anchor): two buildings at 1644/1646 Park Ave levelled, 8 killed, ~50 injured. NTSB's report (June 2015, i.e. just before the 2015-06-30 anchor) attributed it to a faulty fusion joint between two Con Edison plastic gas pipes together with a long-known city sewer breach. The NY Department of Public Service investigation (2015) found Con Edison violated close to a dozen state gas-safety requirements -- failing to train employees and contractors to fuse plastic gas pipe properly, failing to supervise the work, failing to install emergency shut-down valves -- several of which it said contributed to the explosion. The NYPSC issued a show-cause order in Nov 2015; the matter settled for $153.3M approved 2017-02-17 (largest gas-safety settlement in New York history, including a $25M+ gas-customer benefit fund), borne by shareholders. Serious operational and safety failure with regulatory findings, but no dishonesty element, hence SERIOUS not DISQUALIFYING.

2019-07-13 West Side Manhattan blackout (~72,000 customers) caused by a relay-protection/transmission failure, followed by a DPS investigation and further outages during the July 2019 heat wave. Reliability failure, no deception; well after both anchors.

gate1.note: Two businesses, both explicable: Automotive (units x average transaction price less material, labour, warranty and fixed plant cost) and FORD CREDIT, a captive lender whose economics are receivables x net financing margin less credit losses, run at roughly 8-9x leverage and reported as its own segment with its own balance sheet. The captive finance arm adds a bank inside a manufacturer, which matters for the balance-sheet gate, but it is disclosed clearly enough that a generalist can explain it.

gate2.note: Mass-market auto manufacturing is the archetype of a no-moat business and Ford's own reported numbers say so. Structural facts visible at both anchors: enormous fixed capital and product-cycle spend, a unionized cost base reset upward by the UAW contract ratified 2015-11-20, chronic industry discounting, and buyers with near-zero switching cost. The single durable franchise is F-Series (best-selling US pickup since 1977/1981 and best-selling US vehicle since 1982), and it carried essentially all the profit: of Ford's record 2015 pre-tax profit of ~$10.8B (reported 2016-01-28), North America contributed roughly $9.3B, while Europe was around break-even, South America was LOSS-making in both 2015 and 2016, and Ford Credit earned a steady but unremarkable ~$1.9B. Consolidated automotive returns on invested capital sat below any reasonable cost of capital measured across the cycle even at a cyclical peak, and Ford required an unbroken product-spend treadmill to stand still. Pricing power exists in one truck line, not in the enterprise: NONE.

gate3.note: Ford cut published EPA fuel-economy ratings twice. Aug 2013: the 2013 C-Max Hybrid's advertised 47 mpg was reduced. 2014-06-12 (just before the 2015 anchor and squarely public): Ford relabelled SIX 2013-2014 models downward -- the C-Max Hybrid to 40 mpg combined (42 city / 37 highway) and the C-Max Energi to 38 mpg combined -- after finding errors in lab measurement and calculation of aerodynamic drag and road-load inputs, and paid customers ($550 to C-Max owners, $325 to lessees). Ford characterized it as testing error; EPA imposed no penalty at the time. Graded SERIOUS: material misstatement of a headline advertised metric across multiple model years, corrected voluntarily.

Takata inflator recalls: NHTSA's May 2016 expansion swept in tens of millions of US vehicles including Fords, and Ford recalls continued expanding through 2020 (NHTSA ordered a further ~3M-vehicle Ford recall in Jan 2020). The underlying dishonesty was TAKATA's -- Takata pleaded guilty to wire fraud and paid $1B in Jan 2017 for falsifying inflator test data -- not Ford's, so this is a supplier-defect recall for Ford's purposes.

Emissions/fuel-economy CERTIFICATION matter, precisely dated: an anonymous employee hotline report in Sept 2018 led Ford to open an internal probe in Feb 2019 and voluntarily disclose to EPA on 2019-02-18 and to CARB on 2019-02-21; Ford then disclosed in a late-April 2019 SEC filing (public 2019-04-26) that DOJ had opened a CRIMINAL investigation. The issue was 'road load' estimation -- analytical modelling and physical track testing that feed fuel-economy and emissions certification -- and expressly NOT defeat devices. LATER RESOLVED IN FORD'S FAVOUR: DOJ dropped its criminal probe and CARB closed its investigation in Feb 2021 with no charges, though EPA and Environment and Climate Change Canada reviews remained open.

DPS6 PowerShift dual-clutch transmission. Class litigation over 2011-2016 Fiesta and 2012-2016 Focus shuddering, bucking, hesitating and slipping had been public since 2012 and reached first final approval on 2017-10-18 (Vargas v. Ford). What became public on 2019-07-11 was the documentary proof: the Detroit Free Press 'Out of Gear' investigation published internal Ford documents and emails showing Ford launched the cars in 2010-11, and kept selling them for years, while knowing the transmissions could slip into neutral or lurch -- against 4,300-plus complaints to federal safety regulators. Two US senators demanded a federal investigation within days (July 2019). Knowing concealment of a safety-relevant defect from customers is dishonesty, hence DISQUALIFYING, but the KNOWLEDGE evidence dates to 2019-07, three years after the later anchor. Settlement history afterward: 9th Circuit VACATED the settlement 2019-09-13, the district court reaffirmed it 2019-10-22, and a revised final approval followed in March 2020.

2022-05-24: Ford paid $19.2M to settle a 41-state, Oregon-led multistate consumer-protection action over false advertising of MY2013-2014 C-Max hybrid real-world fuel economy and MY2011-2014 Super Duty maximum payload capacity -- the payload figure having been computed on a hypothetical configuration (no spare wheel/tire/jack, mini console, no radio) that only fleet buyers could actually order while it was advertised to everyone. Settled without admission, hence SERIOUS, but note the deception element is explicit in the AGs' allegations and the conduct spans model years 2011-2014, i.e. BEFORE both anchors even though the finding came in 2022.

gate1.note: Engineering and construction: win backlog, execute, recognize revenue percentage-of-completion. Explicable to a generalist -- but with the honest caveat that reported profit is not observed, it is ESTIMATED by management from cost-to-complete forecasts on multi-year projects, which is exactly where this company later blew up. Explicable, not opaque, so PASS.

gate2.note: An E&C contractor has no durable competitive advantage worth the name: work is won by competitive bid, backlog is repriced every cycle, switching costs for owners are low, and on FIXED-PRICE/lump-sum work all cost overrun risk sits with Fluor. Returns look respectable only because the asset base is thin, and even those returns turned out to be estimate-dependent rather than real -- the SEC later found (2023-09-06 order) that Fluor's bids on two large fixed-price projects rested on 'overly optimistic cost and timing estimates,' that internal accounting controls failed when overruns arrived, and that reported net earnings were overstated by $51M (22%) in 2016, $38M (25%) in 2017 and $43M (25%) in 2018. Dated visibility of the damage: SEC found certain Fluor personnel realized in EARLY 2016 that the flawed prior design on the Radford project was driving major cost and delay, but the first public charge came in Q1 2017 ($25M pre-tax on three southeastern US fixed-price gas-fired power plants, reported May 2017 -- just before the 2017-06-30 anchor); then $194M pre-tax / $124M after-tax in Q2 2017 (reported 2017-08-03), then $41M in Q4 2017, then the larger Q2 2019 charges that triggered the SEC inquiry. Also live from 2016: the Santos GLNG cost dispute. NONE at both the 2016 and 2017 anchors -- and note that at 2016-06-30 the impairment of this thesis was already forming inside the company but was NOT yet public.

gate3.note: 2011-06-17: Fluor agreed to pay the US $4M to resolve False Claims Act and Anti-Kickback Act allegations that it knowingly submitted false claims and paid and received kickbacks in connection with a contract to operate and manage mixed radioactive waste at DOE's Hanford site. Settled without admission of liability.

2015-01-29 (before BOTH anchors): Fluor Hanford LLC agreed to pay $1.1M to resolve False Claims Act allegations that roughly $670K of DOE funds were improperly used between 2005 and 2009 to lobby Congress and executive-branch officials for more appropriations and contracts for the Volpentest HAMMER training facility; whistleblower Loydene Rambo received $200K. Fluor's public statement emphasized that it admitted no improper conduct.

ACCOUNTING MANIPULATION, and the date it became public matters: on 2020-02-18 Fluor disclosed an SEC investigation (document requests and a subpoena covering the projects charged in Q2 2019) and said it could not file its 2019 Form 10-K on time; it received an NYSE delayed-filing notice, and an internal investigation with outside counsel and forensic accountants ran under a board Special Committee. Fluor finally filed the 2019 10-K on 2020-09-25, RESTATING fiscal 2016, 2017 and 2018 and interim periods from Q1 2018 through Q3 2019, with material weaknesses attributed to control failures on the Radford and Penguins projects. Net earnings had been overstated by 22-25% per year and by as much as 37% in one period. Nothing about this was public at either the 2016-06-30 or 2017-06-30 anchor.

2023-09-06: SEC charged Fluor with improper accounting and inadequate internal accounting controls on the two fixed-price projects; Fluor consented, without admitting or denying the findings, to cease-and-desist and a $14.5M civil penalty. Five current and former officers and employees also settled -- including former Chief Accounting Officer/Controller Robin K. Chopra, business-line CFO Bradley R. Scott and former business-line president James F. Brittain -- with individual penalties of $15,000 to $25,000. Same conduct as the 2020 restatement; recorded separately because this is the date a regulator's finding attached.

2025-08-11: Fluor acknowledged an Australian court decision awarding Santos over $450M in the long-running Gladstone LNG (GLNG) dispute over a 2011 EPC contract, a matter that had been live since 2016. Large but ordinary-course commercial contract litigation with no deception element -- which is itself the point about this business model: fixed-price and disputed-cost project risk is the recurring feature, not the exception.

gate1.note: Industrial flow control: engineered pumps, valves, seals sold as original equipment into oil/gas, chemical, power and water plants, then serviced for decades through a global network of Quick Response Centers (177 QRCs disclosed in the FY2013 10-K). Unit economics are simple to state: low-margin OE placement buys an installed base that generates higher-margin aftermarket parts and repair revenue.

gate2.note: Installed-base economics, not brand or network effects. FY2013/FY2014 10-Ks describe aftermarket as a distinctly higher-margin business tied to a worldwide installed base and 177 QRCs, and identify it as the source of stability across the cycle; roughly half of revenue was aftermarket in this period. Switching costs are real but bounded (API-spec products, credible rivals in Sulzer, ITT, KSB, SPX, Weir), and pricing is set project-by-project against competitive bids. Returns: FY2013-FY2014 operating margins ran low-to-mid teens on ~$4.8-4.9bn of sales with modest capital intensity, so returns on tangible capital were good but not fortress-grade. Cyclicality is the binding constraint: bookings track customer capex, and by the 2015-06-30 anchor the oil-price collapse that began H2 2014 was already visible in reported bookings declines (Q4 2014 and Q1 2015 releases). The subsequent 2015-2017 deterioration (2015 sales -6.5%; nine-month 2016 bookings -7.6% y/y driven by oil and gas; 2016 adjusted operating margin down 130bp; a decentralized 50+ P&L legacy operating model later admitted to and targeted by the multi-year 'Flowserve 2.0' realignment) confirmed the moat is cycle-exposed rather than pricing-power-based, but did not change the classification: aftermarket attachment survived the downturn.
