gate3.note: Announced (2004-02-06 disclosure of an SEC informal inquiry) the restatement of annual results for 2000-2003 plus 2003 quarterly and Q1 2004 results, accompanied by an unusually long list of admitted material weaknesses (non-U.S. pension accounting, period-end close and reporting, inventory, derivatives, control environment, receivables factoring/securitization, M&A accounting, unconsolidated investments, intangibles, accrued liabilities). Outcome reduced the severity: the SEC staff concluded its investigation on 2006-06-01 WITHOUT recommending any enforcement action against the company. Conduct predates the 2009 arrival of CEO Mark Blinn, i.e. different management at both the 2013 and 2015 anchors.

Public 2008-02-21/22: Flowserve resolved DOJ and SEC actions arising from the U.N. Oil-for-Food Program for about $10.5m total ($4.0m DOJ criminal fine plus a three-year deferred prosecution agreement for the French subsidiary; SEC disgorgement $2,720,861, prejudgment interest $853,364, $3.0m civil penalty). Substance is dishonesty, not a technical lapse: between 2001 and 2003 the French and Dutch subsidiaries paid $646,488 and authorized a further $173,758 in kickbacks to Iraqi government entities across twenty contracts, funding them through a bogus 10% 'after-sales service fee' routed to a Jordanian agent and recorded as a legitimate expense â€” deliberate falsification of the books to conceal payments to foreign officials. Not later reduced or reversed. Conduct and settlement both predate the 2013/2015 anchors and the 2009 management change, but the entity and the books-and-records injunction are continuous.

Disclosed in the FY2014 Form 10-K (filed February 2015, therefore public before the 2015-06-30 anchor) and repeated in the Q1 2015 10-Q: Flowserve terminated an employee of an overseas subsidiary after uncovering conduct that violated its Code of Business Conduct and 'may have violated the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act,' completed an internal investigation and self-reported to both the DOJ and the SEC. Escalation became public 2015-08 when the company disclosed an SEC subpoena for additional documents (reported 2015-08-04). Graded SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING because no charge or finding ever followed â€” no DOJ or SEC enforcement action against Flowserve was announced on this matter. Aggravating context for a repeat: this is the second FCPA episode at the same issuer inside eight years.

Continuous ordinary-course product-liability exposure as a former maker and distributor of asbestos-containing components used with its pumps and valves; mesothelioma suits are disclosed as recurring in every 10-K across the anchor period, with many resolved on summary judgment in Flowserve's favor. Date shown is the anchor period rather than an event: this is background litigation, not a discrete finding.

gate1.note: Post-spin Fox is deliberately simple: FOX News Channel and FOX Business, the FOX broadcast network, 28 owned-and-operated television stations, and FS1/FS2/Big Ten Network/FOX Deportes. Two revenue lines a generalist can explain â€” affiliate/retransmission fees per subscriber per month, and advertising sold against live news and live sports â€” against one dominant cost line, long-dated sports rights.

gate2.note: CORPORATE DISCONTINUITY, FLAGGED: 'Fox Corporation' did not exist before 2019-03-19, when it began trading as a spin-off of 21st Century Fox's news, sports and broadcast assets; the Disney acquisition of the remaining 21CF (film/TV studios, FX, Fox Networks Group, Star India, the Hulu stake) closed 2019-03-20. At the 2019-06-30 anchor the entity had roughly one quarter of standalone reported results and its first fiscal year (FY ended 2019-06-30, revenue about $11.4bn) was largely carve-out accounting. Pre-2019 21CF history is context only, not this entity's record. Moat evidence on the assets themselves: FOX News was and is the ratings leader in cable news with the best affiliate-fee leverage in the category, and live NFL/MLB/college rights plus 28 O&O stations give real retransmission-consent pricing power â€” affiliate fee revenue grew through both anchor years and FY2020 revenue rose to about $12.3bn despite COVID. Against that, three facts already public before 2019-06-30 argue against WIDE: pay-TV subscriber decline had been visible industry-wide since 2015 and shrinks the per-sub base every year; the crown-jewel content (NFL, MLB, Big Ten) is leased on renewable contracts at auction, so the counterparty captures the economics on renewal; and the company sold its entertainment library and studio to Disney, leaving no owned IP to fall back on. NARROW at both anchors. COVID confirmed the concentration risk without changing the class: sports shut down in March 2020 and the Television segment's advertising revenue fell 29% in the quarter ended 2020-06-30, while affiliate fees held and the April 2020 Tubi acquisition (about $445m cash, plus roughly $45m deferred) was the hedge.

gate3.note: PREDECESSOR-ENTITY MATTER, DISCONTINUITY FLAGGED (conduct at FOX News Channel under 21st Century Fox, before Fox Corporation existed; note however that Rupert and Lachlan Murdoch carried over as Co-Executive Chairman and CEO, so management continuity is only partial). Roger Ailes resigned as FOX News chairman 2016-07-21 following Gretchen Carlson's harassment suit (settled for $20m); the New York Times reported 2017-04-01 that about $13m had been paid to settle five O'Reilly harassment claims, and Bill O'Reilly was terminated 2017-04-19; the NYT reported 2017-10-21 a further, previously undisclosed $32m settlement with Lis Wiehl paid before his contract was renewed. The concealment element (settlements kept from investors and, per reporting, a private investigator hired to discredit claimants) is why this is graded above ordinary litigation; federal authorities in the SDNY examined whether 21CF had concealed the settlements from investors and no charges against the company were ever brought.

PREDECESSOR-ENTITY MATTER. 2017-11-20/21: 21st Century Fox settled shareholder derivative claims arising from the FOX News harassment scandal for $90m, with about $45m earmarked for a compliance council at FOX News. Defendants â€” including Rupert, Lachlan and James Murdoch and the Ailes estate â€” did NOT admit wrongdoing, which caps this at SERIOUS. Public well before both Fox Corporation anchors.

PREDECESSOR-ENTITY MATTER, DISCONTINUITY FLAGGED, and later REVERSED. 2020-04-06: DOJ (EDNY) charged former 21st Century Fox executives Hernan Lopez (ex-CEO of Fox International Channels) and Carlos Martinez, with Gerard Romy and Full Play Group SA, with wire fraud and money laundering conspiracies for bribing CONMEBOL/FIFA/CONCACAF officials to obtain confidential bid information and media rights, including U.S. rights to the 2018 and 2022 World Cups. Fox Corporation was NOT charged and denied involvement; the Fox International Channels business in which the alleged conduct occurred went to Disney in the March 2019 split, so this is predecessor conduct at an asset Fox Corporation does not own. Landed 2020-04-06, i.e. public before the 2020-06-30 anchor. Reversal history matters: Lopez was convicted at trial in March 2023, but the trial judge set the convictions aside in September 2023 in light of the Supreme Court's narrowing of federal fraud theories, and in December 2025 prosecutors moved to dismiss the case entirely as in the interests of justice.

POST-ANCHOR (after both 2019-06-30 and 2020-06-30). Smartmatic sued FOX News and Fox Corporation for defamation on 2021-02-04 seeking $2.7bn, and Dominion Voting Systems sued on 2021-03-26 seeking $1.6bn, over 2020 election-fraud claims broadcast in November-December 2020. Graded DISQUALIFYING on the dishonesty test because the Delaware court ruled at summary judgment (2023-03-31) that the challenged statements about Dominion were false, and discovery produced internal messages showing on-air talent and executives privately disbelieved the claims they aired; Fox settled 2023-04-18 for $787.5m and publicly acknowledged the court's finding that it had aired false statements. Nothing here was reduced or reversed on appeal â€” it was settled before opening statements. The Smartmatic action survived dismissal and continued after the Dominion settlement. Underlying broadcasts (November 2020 onward) also postdate both anchors.

gate1.note: Tire manufacturing and distribution: sell tires to automakers at thin or negative margin to seed the replacement market, then earn on replacement units through company-owned and independent retail. Capital-intensive, raw-material exposed (natural rubber, oil derivatives), and carrying a large legacy pension and asbestos tail â€” complex to value, but not opaque as a business.

gate2.note: Judged honestly, Goodyear is a price-taker in a global commodity with chronic overcapacity, and the reported numbers across the anchor period say so. FY2018 (reported 2019-02-08) sales of $15.5bn were up only 1% and Q4 original-equipment volume fell 22% on weak Chinese vehicle production; FY2019 nine-month sales fell 5% with tire volumes down 2%, OE volumes down 8%, and segment operating income falling every quarter (Q1 2019 $190m vs $281m; Q3 2019 $294m vs $362m). Management's own explanations of margin â€” higher raw material costs, lower volume, currency, weaker other-tire-related businesses, only partly offset by price/mix â€” describe cost pass-through with a lag, not pricing power. The brand supports a premium in some replacement segments, but low-cost Asian imports set the marginal price, distribution is not exclusive, and the company has not earned its cost of capital through a full cycle once pension and interest are charged. Substitution/disruption threat is structural rather than technological: tires are consumable and demand is durable, which is why this is NONE rather than a business in decline. No genuine change in class occurred at either the 2018 or 2019 anchor. On the break date recorded at gate 5: deterioration was visible but not yet a break at either anchor (2018 guidance cut on raw-material costs on 2018-02-08; a Q1 2019 net loss with a 9% volume decline reported 2019-04-30). The thesis was unambiguously broken on 2020-02-11, when Goodyear reported a FY2019 net loss of $311m ($1.33/share) against $693m of net income ($2.89) in 2018, a second consecutive year of falling segment operating income, and $205m of rationalization charges for modernizing two German plants and curtailing Gadsden, Alabama output â€” confirmed 2020-04-16 by the suspension of the quarterly dividend (about $37m per quarter) alongside an 18% Q1 2020 volume collapse. Both dates fall after both anchors.

gate3.note: 2003-10-22: Goodyear announced it would restate results for 1998-2002 and the first two quarters of 2003, with further restatement adjustments disclosed into 2004-2005; the SEC opened an inquiry into the circumstances and the company cooperated. Errors centred on overseas (notably European) accounting and account reconciliations. Graded SERIOUS, not DISQUALIFYING: no public enforcement action against the company was announced on this matter, and the conduct predates both anchors and the current management (Richard Kramer became CEO in 2010).

Court-found litigation deception over the G159 RV tire. In Haeger v. Goodyear (D. Ariz.), the district court in late 2012 sanctioned Goodyear roughly $2.7m for bad-faith discovery conduct â€” withholding internal heat-and-speed test data for the G159 that would have shown the tire was unsuited to the motorhome application in which it failed. The Ninth Circuit affirmed in 2016. The Supreme Court's decision in Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Haeger (2017-04-18) VACATED AND REMANDED on the amount, holding a sanction must be limited to fees caused by the misconduct; it did not disturb the finding of bad-faith concealment. Both the sanctions order and the Supreme Court decision were public before the 2018-06-30 anchor.

2015-02-24: SEC charged Goodyear with FCPA violations and the company agreed to pay more than $16m â€” $14,122,525 disgorgement plus $2,105,540 prejudgment interest. Its Kenyan subsidiary (Treadsetters Tyres) and Angolan subsidiary (Trentyre Angola) routinely paid officials, employees of state-owned entities and private-company purchasing staff a total of over $3.2m in bribes over four years to win sales, and recorded them in the books as legitimate business expenses. Falsified records to hide payments to officials is dishonesty on its face. Not later reduced or reversed; the SEC cited lax compliance controls and inadequate M&A diligence. Public more than three years before the 2018-06-30 anchor.

The G159 concealment matter escalated to the regulator and became broadly public before the 2018 anchor: NHTSA opened its investigation in December 2017, after a judge ordered the release of Goodyear claims and test data that the company had kept out of the agency's hands by settling suits confidentially and obtaining protective orders sealing the material; NHTSA issued an information request 2018-04-03. Dishonesty finding is the pattern of keeping failure data from the safety regulator, not the defect itself. Post-anchor continuation, dated for completeness: NHTSA formally requested a recall 2022-02-22, Goodyear refused 2022-03-08, and after NHTSA threatened a public hearing and court action Goodyear recalled about 173,000-175,000 G159 tires on 2022-06-07 â€” nearly two decades after the last one was made, with investigators concluding the tire's failures caused crashes killing 8 and injuring 69 between 1998 and 2009 and that Goodyear had itself concluded by 2002 the tire was unsuitable for Class A motorhomes.

gate1.note: Medicare Advantage is a legible per-member economic engine: CMS pays a county benchmark premium adjusted by each member's risk score, the plan pays claims (benefit ratio) and its own SG&A, and keeps the spread subject to minimum medical-loss ratios and Star-rating bonuses. Understanding it requires knowing the rules, not decoding the business.

gate2.note: Real advantages, all conditional on a single payer's rules. Scale in individual Medicare Advantage (the largest or second-largest MA plan through the anchor period), Star ratings that unlock bonus payments and continuous-enrolment marketing, owned/affiliated primary-care and pharmacy assets, and county-level network density that a new entrant cannot replicate quickly â€” average individual MA membership grew about 7% in 2013 and membership again beat plan in 2014. But there is no pricing power in the ordinary sense: CMS sets the benchmark, and the reported numbers show the exposure directly. CMS announced preliminary 2014 MA benchmarks in February 2013 implying a mid-single-digit decline in rates; sequestration took effect 2013-04-01; individual MA per-member premiums fell about 2.6% in Q1 2014 versus Q1 2013; Q1 2014 diluted EPS was $2.35 against $2.95 in Q1 2013. The ACA insurer fee and MLR floors compress the spread further. Government-administered revenue plus regulatory concentration caps this at NARROW at both the 2013 and 2014 anchors; no genuine change in class occurred between them.

gate3.note: POST-2014-ANCHOR by public-knowledge date. The DOJ Civil Division served an information request in December 2014 concerning Humana's Medicare Part C risk-adjustment practices â€” its oversight and submission of risk-adjustment data generated by network providers, medical-record reviews, health and well-being assessments and fraud-detection efforts. First publicly disclosed in the FY2014 Form 10-K filed February 2015, and repeated in the FY2015 10-K. Humana characterised it as part of a wider industry review touching multiple MA plans, providers and vendors. An investigation with no finding, so SERIOUS at most; nothing here was public before either the 2013-06-30 or 2014-06-30 anchor.

POST-ANCHOR. The qui tam filed in October 2012 by Dr. Mario Baez in South Florida â€” alleging that Humana knew of and profited from inflated risk-adjustment diagnoses submitted by network physician Isaac Kojo Anakwah Thompson â€” remained UNDER FEDERAL SEAL until 2016-02-26, so it was not publicly known at either anchor. Thompson was separately charged criminally with health-care fraud for submitting fraudulent diagnoses to Humana for MA beneficiaries. Humana also disclosed the related U.S. ex rel. Graves v. Plaza Medical Centers action (S.D. Fla., filed 2010) in its FY2015 10-K, where it obtained dismissal of several claims and later resolved the remainder. Allegations against Humana concerned inadequate oversight of provider-generated codes rather than proven deception by Humana.

FAR POST-ANCHOR, listed for completeness. Humana paid $90m to resolve a False Claims Act case alleging it submitted false bid information to CMS for a Medicare Part D prescription-drug plan (alleged conduct in the 2011-2017 window, i.e. spanning the anchor years, but not publicly known at either anchor). Separately, on 2025-05-01 the United States filed an FCA complaint against Humana, Aetna and Elevance alleging that from 2016 through at least 2021 they paid hundreds of millions of dollars in kickbacks to brokers for MA enrolments and discriminated against disabled beneficiaries â€” an unresolved allegation as of this writing, with no admission.

gate1.note: The deposit-funded lending and fee franchise (consumer banking, cards, asset and wealth management, treasury services) is explainable to a generalist: cheap sticky deposits funded at below market, lent or invested at a spread, plus recurring fee income. Passes with a stated caveat rather than a fail â€” the Corporate & Investment Bank's trading and derivatives book is genuinely hard for any outsider to mark, and the 2012 London Whale episode is the proof that it was hard for insiders too.

gate2.note: Deposit franchise plus scale, not a toll bridge. Through the 2016 and 2017 anchors JPMorgan combined the largest U.S. deposit base with #1 or #2 positions in investment banking fees, cards and treasury services, and the resulting funding-cost and technology-spend advantages are durable and visible in a consistently sector-leading return on tangible common equity. What holds it to NARROW: output is a commodity (money), pricing is set by markets and rate cycles rather than by the bank, capital and payout are decided by regulators through the annual stress tests (post-2013 CCAR), and the same scale that lowers funding costs invites the systemic-risk surcharge and the standing supervisory burden. Nothing in reported results between the two anchors changed the class; the 2016-2017 period was one of rising rates and improving net interest income, not of a change in competitive position.

gate3.note: 2013-07-30: JPMorgan Ventures Energy paid $410m ($285m civil penalty, $125m disgorgement) to settle FERC allegations of manipulative bidding strategies in California and Midwest power markets. Settled on a neither-admit-nor-deny basis, which caps this at SERIOUS despite the manipulation theory. Public well before both anchors.

THE LONDON WHALE. 2013-09-19: JPMorgan paid about $920m across the SEC, OCC, Federal Reserve and the U.K. FCA and â€” exceptionally, under the SEC's then-new admissions policy for egregious cases â€” ADMITTED it violated federal securities laws and that it misstated its financial results, giving the SEC an extensive set of factual admissions. Substance is dishonesty, not a trading loss: CIO traders mismarked positions and concealed more than $6bn of losses from senior management and, through the reported financials, from investors, for weeks. This is a company-level admission of misstated financials, which is the accounting-manipulation branch of the disqualifying test. Not reduced or reversed on appeal; the related criminal charges against two traders were later dropped, which does not disturb the firm's own admissions.

2013-11-19: $13bn global settlement with the DOJ, the RMBS Working Group and several states over the packaging and sale of residential mortgage-backed securities, including a $2bn civil penalty and $4bn of consumer relief. Accompanied by an agreed statement of facts in which JPMorgan acknowledged it made serious misrepresentations to investors about the quality of the loans in securitizations issued by JPMorgan, Bear Stearns and Washington Mutual. Acknowledged misrepresentation to investors is dishonesty; note the mitigating fact that a large share of the conduct sat in the Bear Stearns and WaMu books acquired in 2008. No appellate reduction.

2013-12-04: the European Commission fined JPMorgan about EUR 79.9m for participating in a cartel in yen interest-rate derivatives (Yen LIBOR), resolved under the Commission's settlement procedure with the standard 10% cooperation reduction. A secret cartel among competitors to distort a benchmark is squarely within the disqualifying category. Public before both anchors; not overturned.

2014-01-07: JPMorgan entered a two-year deferred prosecution agreement with the SDNY and paid about $2.6bn in total ($1.7bn DOJ forfeiture, $350m OCC penalty, plus civil settlements) over its role as Bernard Madoff's primary banker, admitting failures to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering programme and to file a Suspicious Activity Report in the United States even as its U.K. affiliate filed one. Graded SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING: the charged conduct is a Bank Secrecy Act compliance failure and non-reporting, not affirmative deception of a customer or regulator, though the asymmetry between the U.K. filing and the U.S. silence is uncomfortable. DPA expired without prosecution.

2015-05-20: JPMorgan Chase & Co. PLEADED GUILTY AT THE PARENT LEVEL to a felony violation of the Sherman Act for a conspiracy to manipulate the price of U.S. dollars and euros in the FX spot market, paying a $550m criminal fine, plus $342m to the Federal Reserve under a consent order. Four banks pleaded guilty the same day for collective criminal fines above $2.5bn. A criminal antitrust conspiracy â€” traders coordinating in a private chat room to fix benchmark rates and spreads â€” is a secret cartel by any reading. JPMorgan attributed the conduct principally to one dismissed trader. Public a year before the 2016 anchor; conviction stands.

2015-07-08: JPMorgan Chase Bank agreed with the CFPB and 47 states plus D.C. to pay about $216m ($136m in penalties and payments to states, $50m in consumer remediation, plus a separate $30m OCC penalty) over credit-card debt-collection practices, and was barred from reselling certain accounts. The conduct included robo-signed and sworn affidavits filed in court containing unverified or inaccurate information about consumer debts, and selling portfolios containing accounts it knew to be inaccurate or already settled. Filing false sworn statements with courts and passing bad information to buyers is deception of both a tribunal and customers.

2015-12-18: two JPMorgan wealth-management units (J.P. Morgan Securities LLC and JPMorgan Chase Bank N.A.) agreed to pay $267m to the SEC and ADMITTED WRONGDOING for failing to disclose conflicts of interest to advisory and brokerage clients, plus a $40m CFTC penalty ($307m total; $127.5m disgorgement, $11.815m interest, $127.5m penalty). They steered clients into the firm's own proprietary funds and into a more expensive share class of those funds, and preferred third-party hedge funds that paid a JPMorgan affiliate, without disclosing either preference â€” deprivation of information clients needed, admitted. Six months before the 2016-06-30 anchor.

BETWEEN THE TWO ANCHORS â€” public 2016-11-17, i.e. after 2016-06-30 and before 2017-06-30. JPMorgan paid more than $264m to resolve FCPA charges over its Asia-Pacific 'Sons and Daughters' referral-hiring programme: about $130m to the SEC, $72m to the DOJ under a non-prosecution agreement for the Hong Kong subsidiary, and $61.9m to the Federal Reserve. The entities acknowledged years of quid pro quo arrangements in which relatives and protÃ©gÃ©s of Chinese government officials and state-owned-enterprise executives ('princelings') were given well-paid jobs and internships outside normal hiring channels in exchange for banking mandates. Jobs-for-business is bribery of foreign officials; the DOJ gave limited credit because the violations were willful and widespread. Note the earlier public marker: press reporting of the SEC probe into the referral-hiring programme began in August 2013, so the existence of the investigation â€” though not the resolution â€” was already public at the 2016 anchor.

2016-12-07: the European Commission fined JPMorgan EUR 337.196m for participating in a cartel in euro interest-rate derivatives (Euribor), finding a single and continuous infringement between September 2006 and March 2007. JPMorgan did not settle and contested the decision. Appeal outcome, dated: in its December 2023 judgment the EU General Court annulled part of the decision for inadequate reasoning on the fine calculation but, exercising unlimited jurisdiction, re-imposed the identical EUR 337,196,000 â€” so no reduction for JPMorgan, while CrÃ©dit Agricole's fine was cut to EUR 110m and HSBC's was annulled. Further appeal to the Court of Justice followed. Public before the 2017-06-30 anchor and after the 2016-06-30 anchor.

POST-ANCHOR. 2020-09-29: JPMorgan agreed to pay about $920m (DOJ, CFTC and SEC combined â€” the largest spoofing resolution to that date) and entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement on two counts of wire fraud, over tens of thousands of episodes of spoofing in precious-metals futures and U.S. Treasuries markets between 2008 and 2016. Placing orders never intended to be executed in order to move prices is market deception; the conduct period overlaps both anchors but the enforcement action was not public until September 2020.

POST-ANCHOR, for completeness. JPMorgan settled Jeffrey Epstein-related claims in 2023 â€” about $290m with a class of victims (announced June 2023) and $75m with the U.S. Virgin Islands (announced September 2023) â€” over having retained Epstein as a client and allegedly ignoring internal warnings. Settled with no admission of liability, hence SERIOUS. Separately, in December 2021 JPMorgan paid $200m to the SEC and CFTC over years of unpreserved business communications on personal devices, a record-keeping failure rather than a deception.

gate1.note: Clinical laboratory testing: collect specimens through a patient-service-centre and courier network, run high volumes of standardised assays through automated core labs, and bill managed care, Medicare/Medicaid, hospitals and patients. Economics are pure operating leverage on fixed lab capacity â€” cost per test falls with requisition volume.

gate2.note: A genuine scale duopoly with Quest, and the scale is visible in the reported numbers: about $5.8bn of 2013 revenue across more than 220,000 clients, and Q3 2014 revenue of roughly $1.55bn, up 6.1% on 6.9% requisition growth described as primarily organic. Independent labs of LabCorp's size have unit costs, national payer contracts and in-network status that regional labs cannot match, and physician workflow integration creates modest switching friction. Held to NARROW because price is set by others: the payer mix disclosed around the Covance deal was managed care 32%, pharma/biotech 29%, commercial 22%, Medicare/Medicaid 12%, patients 5% â€” so a plurality of revenue is priced by government fee schedules or annual managed-care negotiation. Two dated reminders of that dependence bracket the anchors: Medicare clinical-lab fee-schedule cuts through 2013, and the Protecting Access to Medicare Act signed in April 2014, which replaced the 1984-85-based fee schedule with market-based rates and set up the later PAMA cuts. No genuine change in moat class between the 2013 and 2014 anchors; the 2014-11-03 agreement to acquire Covance for about $6.1bn (closed 2015-02) diversified revenue toward pharma services but was announced after both anchors.

gate3.note: 2011-07-14: LabCorp reached an agreement in principle to settle California ex rel. Hunter Laboratories LLC v. Quest Diagnostics et al. for $49.5m, recording $34.5m of settlement expense in Q2 2011 net of a $15.0m prior reserve and paying in Q3 2012. The state-law False Claims Act suit alleged LabCorp improperly billed Medi-Cal above the rates it charged other customers between 1995-11-07 and November 2009, with the relator claiming $97.5m including interest. NO ADMISSION of liability, which holds this at SERIOUS rather than disqualifying; LabCorp also accepted temporary pricing-reporting obligations or, at its election, a discount to Medi-Cal's maximum rate from 2011-11-01 to 2012-10-31. Public before both anchors.

October 2013: LabCorp received a Civil Investigative Demand from the Texas Attorney General for documents on its billing to Texas Medicaid, and cooperated. Ordinary-course payer/regulator billing inquiry of the kind the 10-K describes as recurring â€” subpoenas and CIDs from government agencies, Medicare/Medicaid payers and managed-care organisations reviewing billing practices â€” alongside periodic qui tam suits. Public between the 2013 and 2014 anchors; no finding.

POST-ANCHOR, listed for completeness. June 2019: LabCorp disclosed that roughly 7.7 million of its patients' payment records were exposed in the breach of American Medical Collection Agency, a third-party collections vendor also used by Quest; litigation and state-AG inquiries followed. A vendor security failure rather than misconduct by LabCorp.

gate1.note: Defense prime economics are legible even if the programmes are technical: win a government programme of record, then earn on decades of development, production lots and sustainment under cost-plus and fixed-price contracts whose margins and cash timing are set by contract type and milestone billing. The complexity is in the accounting for long-term contracts and the pension, not in the business model.

gate2.note: Moat is programme position, and at the 2013 and 2014 anchors it was as strong as it gets in this industry. Lockheed is prime on the F-35 â€” the only Western fifth-generation strike fighter in production, sole-sourced, with three variants, eleven-plus partner nations and a multi-decade sustainment tail â€” plus the F-22, C-130J, THAAD, PAC-3, Aegis combat system, Trident II D5, JASSM, Sikorsky helicopters from 2015, and classified space and missile-defence work. Barriers are not brand but a certified industrial base, security clearances, decades of qualification data and a customer that cannot switch mid-programme; incumbent primes also capture the aftermarket by design. Reported returns are exceptionally high on an accounting basis (equity is depressed by pension deficits), and cash generation supported large buybacks and consistent double-digit dividend increases through 2013-2014. Two honest qualifications that do not change the class: the customer is a monopsony that legislates the margin (the 2013 sequester and the October 2013 shutdown were live at the first anchor), and F-35 cost and schedule criticism was continuous. No genuine change in class between the anchors.

gate3.note: PREDECESSOR-ENTITY MATTER, DISCONTINUITY FLAGGED. In January 1995 Lockheed Corporation pleaded guilty to conspiring to violate the FCPA and to wire fraud over about $1m paid to an Egyptian legislator to help secure a C-130 sale, paying roughly $24.8m in criminal fines and civil penalties; a former executive was imprisoned. The conduct and plea predate the Lockheed Martin merger completed in March 1995 and are three management generations removed from the anchor dates (Marillyn Hewson became CEO in January 2013). Graded SERIOUS on the predecessor rule notwithstanding that the underlying conduct was bribery.

2012-03-23: Lockheed Martin paid $15.85m to resolve False Claims Act allegations that it passed on to the government inflated tool costs from subcontractor Tools & Metals Inc., which had marked up perishable tools sold for use on military aircraft including the F-22 and F-35 between 1998 and 2005; two relators shared $2m. TMI's former president had pleaded guilty in December 2005 and received a seven-year sentence. The fraud originated with the subcontractor; Lockheed's exposure was for passing the costs through. Resolved by settlement, no admission of liability by Lockheed. Public about fifteen months before the 2013-06-30 anchor.

POST-ANCHOR (after both 2013-06-30 and 2014-06-30). 2015-08-28: Sandia Corporation, a wholly owned Lockheed Martin subsidiary managing Sandia National Laboratories, agreed to pay $4.79m to resolve DOJ allegations under the Byrd Amendment and the False Claims Act that between 2008 and 2012 it used federal contract funds to lobby Congress and the Department of Energy for a non-competitive extension of its roughly $2.4bn-a-year management contract, aiming to prevent competitors from bidding. Settled WITHOUT any admission of wrongdoing. Using taxpayer money to lobby against competition for taxpayer money is a governance red flag even absent an admission.

POST-ANCHOR. 2019-02-08: the United States filed a False Claims Act and civil Anti-Kickback Act complaint in the Eastern District of Washington against Mission Support Alliance LLC (the joint venture holding the DOE Hanford infrastructure-support prime contract), Lockheed Martin Corporation, Lockheed Martin Services Inc. and a then-serving Lockheed Martin vice president, alleging inflated information-technology subcontract costs billed to DOE and kickbacks paid to secure the subcontract. Resolved 2021-04-05 for $6m from the defendants, with no admission of liability. Naming a sitting corporate officer distinguishes this from routine contract disputes.

gate1.note: Franchised QSR: ~81% of ~35,400 restaurants franchised at FY2013, so earnings are royalties (~4-5% of franchisee sales) plus rent on company-owned real estate, plus margins on the shrinking company-operated base. A generalist can explain the unit economics from the 10-K segment tables.

gate2.note: Brand plus real-estate/royalty model. FY2013 (reported 2014-01-23): system-wide sales ~$89B, consolidated operating margin ~31%, ROIC high-teens, positive global comparable sales every year 2003-2013. Franchisee capital funds most unit growth, so returns on McDonald's own capital are structurally high.

Traffic and share loss to fast casual visible in reported monthly/quarterly comps before the 2015-06-30 anchor: US comps negative from late 2013 onward (Q1 2014 US -1.7%, reported 2014-04-22), November 2014 US comps -4.6% (reported 2014-12-08), FY2014 US comps -2.1% and first negative annual GLOBAL comps since 2002 at -1.0% (reported 2015-01-23), May 2015 US comps -2.2% (reported 2015-06-08). Three consecutive years of declining US guest counts. Pricing power intact on menu price but the brand was losing units of demand; CEO change announced 2015-01-28 (Easterbrook effective 2015-03-01) and turnaround plan announced 2015-05-04.

All Day Breakfast launched 2015-10-06; Q4 2015 US comps +5.7% (reported 2016-01-25). Recovery was not immediately durable -- Q4 2016 US comps relapsed to -1.3% (reported 2017-01-23) -- but Q1/Q2 2017 US comps of +1.7%/+3.9% (reported 2017-04-25 / 2017-07-25) plus refranchising toward ~93% franchised restored both comps and margin, with FY2017 US comps +3.6% (reported 2018-01-30).

gate3.note: China supplier scandal. Shanghai Dragon TV aired footage on 2014-07-20 showing workers at Shanghai Husi Food (a subsidiary of US-based OSI Group, a McDonald's supplier) using expired meat and repackaging it with new expiry dates; the plant was shut immediately and five Husi managers were detained by 2014-07-23. McDonald's suspended Husi-sourced product in China and Japan within days. The deliberate relabeling was the SUPPLIER's conduct, not McDonald's own -- for McDonald's this is a supply-chain oversight failure, not company dishonesty. Impact: APMEA comparable sales turned sharply negative from August 2014 (monthly release 2014-09-09) and McDonald's quantified a material earnings drag in its 2014-10-21 Q3 release. Later penalties: a Shanghai court in February 2016 fined Husi/OSI units ~RMB 2.4M and jailed 10 employees; Shanghai FDA added ~RMB 17M (Husi) and ~RMB 7.3M (OSI China) fines in 2016.

On 2014-12-19 the NLRB General Counsel issued 13 consolidated complaints naming McDonald's USA, LLC as a JOINT EMPLOYER with franchisees for alleged retaliation against workers in the Fight for $15 protests. Labor-law dispute, no dishonesty alleged. Resolved by settlement approved by an ALJ in 2019 and affirmed by the Board on 2020-07-17; no joint-employer liability was ever established.

On 2015-12-03 the European Commission opened an in-depth state-aid investigation into Luxembourg tax rulings (2009) under which McDonald's Europe Franchising paid no tax on European franchise royalties. ANNULLED IN EFFECT: on 2018-09-19 the Commission concluded the non-taxation did not constitute illegal state aid -- no finding against McDonald's.

French tax authorities raided McDonald's France offices on 2016-05-18 in a transfer-pricing/tax-fraud investigation (royalties routed via Luxembourg/Switzerland). Resolved 2022-06-16 by a French CJIP (deferred-prosecution-style agreement) totalling ~EUR 1.245B (EUR 508M public-interest fine plus ~EUR 737M back taxes) with no criminal conviction. All post-anchor for the 2014/2015 dates.

gate1.note: Global packaged snacks: brands (Oreo, Cadbury, Milka, LU, Trident) sold through grocery/traditional trade; unit economics are volume x price/mix less cocoa/dairy/wheat/packaging input cost and A&C spend. Complicated by the corporate history (Kraft Foods Inc. split 2012-10-01) and heavy FX/emerging-market mix, but explainable from the segment disclosures.

gate2.note: Corporate history: Mondelez is the snacks half of Kraft Foods Inc., which split on 2012-10-01 (North American grocery spun off as Kraft Foods Group); Cadbury had been acquired by Kraft in February 2010. Real brand moat -- #1 globally in biscuits and #2 in chocolate, Power Brands ~70% of revenue with double-digit Power Brand growth in Latin America (+12.3%) and Asia (+20.3%) in 2013 -- but the moat is NOT wide on returns: FY2013 organic net revenue +3.9% with adjusted operating income margin only 12.0% (reported 2014-02-12), far below branded-food peers, and goodwill/intangibles of roughly $40B on ~$72B of assets from the Cadbury/Kraft deals keep ROIC in the mid-to-high single digits. Pricing power is real in chocolate and gum, weaker in biscuits against private label; the coffee business was contributed to the Jacobs Douwe Egberts JV (announced 2014-05-07, closed 2015-07-02), and margin gains from 2015 onward (adjusted OI margin to ~15.3% in 2016) came from the 2014-2018 restructuring program rather than from pricing, with volume/mix negative and organic growth only +1.3% in 2016 (reported 2017-02-01).

gate3.note: On 2015-04-01 the CFTC filed a civil complaint in N.D. Ill. alleging Kraft Foods Group and Mondelez Global LLC manipulated December 2011 wheat futures and cash wheat prices -- buying ~$90M (a six-month supply) of Dec-2011 futures they never intended to take delivery of, to depress cash prices and widen the Dec/Mar spread, earning >$5.4M. PREDECESSOR DISCONTINUITY: the December 2011 conduct predates the 2012-10-01 split, so it was Kraft Foods Inc. conduct for which both successors were named. Resolved by consent order entered 2019-08-14: $16M penalty and injunction, WITHOUT any admission of wrongdoing (the order also restricted the parties' public statements about it), so no manipulation was ever adjudicated.

European Commission opened formal antitrust proceedings on 2021-01-28 into Mondelez restricting cross-border trade in chocolate, biscuit and coffee products. Decision 2024-05-23: EUR 337.5M fine for 22 Article 101 agreements/concerted practices limiting parallel trade (2012-2019) and Article 102 abuse of dominance in chocolate tablets (2015-2019); fine reflects a 15% cooperation-procedure reduction after Mondelez acknowledged liability. Pure competition-law matter (market partitioning / abuse of dominance), no deception element alleged. Entirely post-anchor for the 2013/2014 dates.

gate1.note: Defense prime: revenue is US government contracts (~85-90%), earned as cost-type (fee on cost) or fixed-price work, with segment operating income and estimate-at-completion adjustments disclosed by segment. Classified programs limit visibility into specific businesses, but the economics -- backlog, book-to-bill, margin rate, cash conversion -- are explainable to a generalist.

gate2.note: Incumbency moat on long-life franchises (B-2 sustainment, E-2D, Global Hawk/unmanned, ICBM ground systems, classified space/restricted programs) with very high entry barriers, but a single monopsony customer that sets prices and audits profit rates -- there is no pricing power in the Buffett sense. Sequestration proved it: revenue fell from $26.4B (2011) to $24.7B (2013) to $24.0B (2014) to $23.5B (2015) after the Budget Control Act (2011-08) and sequester onset (2013-03-01), with segment operating margin roughly 12.5-13% (Q3 2014 12.9%). EPS growth in the anchor window came mostly from shrinking the share count -- 233.9M average diluted shares (2013) to 212.1M (2014) to ~187.9M (Q3 2015), completing the 60M-share retirement goal announced 2013-05 -- not from organic growth. Franchise strengthened later: LRS-B/B-21 award announced 2015-10-27, competitor protest denied by GAO 2016-02-16.

gate3.note: PREDECESSOR DISCONTINUITY: DOJ announced in April 2009 a $325M False Claims Act settlement covering defective heterojunction bipolar transistors supplied to the National Reconnaissance Office. DOJ's investigation concluded that Northrop and its predecessor TRW Inc. failed to test/qualify HBTs made 1992-2002 and 'made misrepresentations about, and concealed certain material facts regarding' their reliability -- conduct with a clear dishonesty element, but it was overwhelmingly TRW conduct (TRW was acquired by Northrop in December 2002) and was settled civilly without an admission of liability. Whistleblower Robert Ferro received $48.7M. Public and known well before the 2014/2015 anchors.

POST-ANCHOR DISCLOSURE OF IN-ANCHOR CONDUCT: DOJ announced in November 2018 that Northrop Grumman Systems Corp. would pay ~$27.45M in civil recovery (a $25.8M payment plus earlier repayments) to settle FCA allegations that it overstated employee labor hours billed to the Air Force on the BACN and DRC contracts between 2010-07-01 and 2013-12-31, plus a separate agreement with the US Attorney (S.D. Cal.) Criminal Division forfeiting $4.2M. The alleged conduct (knowingly false labor billing) straddles the 2014 and 2015 anchors but was NOT public then; the civil claims were resolved as allegations without a determination of liability.

gate1.note: Oilfield capital equipment: designs and builds drilling rig packages (derricks, drawworks, top drives, BOPs) plus consumables/spares and downhole tools; earnings track customer capex, so the drivers are new orders, backlog, and aftermarket attach rate -- all disclosed quarterly. Understandable, just violently cyclical. Distribution arm spun off as NOW Inc. on 2014-05-30.

gate2.note: Dominant position in offshore/newbuild rig packages (majority share of drilling packages on newbuild floaters and jackups) with a very large installed base feeding spares and service, giving a real but conditional advantage. FY2013 revenue ~$22.8B with operating margin in the mid-teens, and Rig Systems backlog peaking around $16B in Q3 2014 (reported 2014-10-27). Crucially, all of it is derivative demand from customer capex; NOV has no pricing power independent of the crude cycle.

The 2014-2016 crude collapse (WTI peaked ~$107 in June 2014, fell below $50 in January 2015 and to ~$26 in February 2016) went straight through orders and backlog, and this was visible in reported results BEFORE the 2015-06-30 anchor: Rig Systems new orders collapsed to $236M in Q1 2015 (reported 2015-04-28) from roughly $2B per quarter in 2014, with segment backlog $10.43B, down 17% sequentially and 31% year over year. It kept going: total backlog $7.0B at 2015-12-31 versus $14.3B a year earlier (-51%, reported 2016-02-03); Rig Systems backlog $6.08B at 2015-12-31 with only $89M of Q4 2015 orders; Rig Systems backlog $2.5B at 2016-12-31 with $115M of Q4 orders. Revenue $21.4B (2014) to $14.8B (2015) to ~$7.25B (2016) with large goodwill impairments and a multi-billion 2016 net loss -- no durable earning power through a cycle.

gate3.note: US trade-sanctions and export-control violations by NOV and subsidiaries Dreco Energy Services and NOV Elmar involving Cuba, Iran and Sudan between 2002 and 2009. The ~$25M penalty was PRELIMINARILY AGREED AND FULLY ACCRUED IN 2010 and the matters were disclosed in NOV's Form 10-K/10-Q filings from at least the FY2010 annual report (filed February 2011), so the existence and size of the matter was public before both the 2013 and 2015 anchors. Final resolution 2016-11-09: $25M total across a non-prosecution agreement with the US Attorney (S.D. Tex.), Commerce/BIS, OFAC (~$5.98M) and ICE. Aggravating detail in the public settlement documents: senior-management awareness/'willful blindness' and approval of the sanctioned business by overseas units; OFAC recorded it as NOT a voluntary self-disclosure. Resolved by NPA without criminal conviction.

gate1.note: Class I railroad: ~20,000 route miles in the eastern US; revenue is carloads x revenue per unit across coal, intermodal and merchandise, and the cost side is readable through the operating ratio. Capital intensity and maintenance capex are explicit in the filings.

gate2.note: Eastern US duopoly with CSX over a network that cannot be rebuilt at any price, protected by post-Staggers pricing freedom; same-store price gains ran ~3-4% a year through 2011-2015. FY2014 (reported 2015-01-27): railway operating revenue ~$11.6B, operating ratio 69.2%. The moat held through a genuine secular shock: coal fell from ~26% of revenue in 2011 to ~21% in 2013 to ~16% in 2015 as cheap gas displaced utility coal, and 2015 revenue fell ~9.5% with the operating ratio deteriorating to 72.6% (reported 2016-01-27) -- yet the franchise was never contested, and the December 2015 five-year plan (announced 2015-12-04, ~$650M of cost reductions, sub-65 OR target) delivered OR 68.9% in 2016 and 65.8% in 2017. Independent market evidence of franchise scarcity: Canadian Pacific disclosed an unsolicited takeover approach on 2015-11-17 (exploration reported 2015-11-09), NS's board rejected it on 2015-12-04 and rejected sweetened offers on 2015-12-08 and 2015-12-16, and CP abandoned the ~$28B bid on 2016-04-11 after DOJ urged the STB to reject its voting-trust structure -- i.e. regulatory protection of the network is itself part of the moat.

gate3.note: In re Rail Freight Fuel Surcharge Antitrust Litigation: complaints filed in 2007 and consolidated as an MDL in D.D.C. in November 2007, alleging that Norfolk Southern, CSX, Union Pacific and BNSF conspired to impose standardized fuel surcharges as a disguised rate increase (2003-2008). A price-fixing ALLEGATION that was never established: class certification was granted in June 2012, VACATED by the D.C. Circuit on 2013-08-09, DENIED on remand on 2017-10-10, and that denial was AFFIRMED by the D.C. Circuit on 2019-08-30 (plaintiffs' own regression showed negative damages for 2,000+ putative class members). Individual shipper suits continued afterward; no liability finding against NS.

POST-ANCHOR: East Palestine, Ohio derailment of NS train 32N on 2023-02-03 with hazardous-material release and controlled vinyl chloride burn. Resolutions: ~$600M class settlement with area residents (announced April 2024, approved September 2024) and a DOJ/EPA consent decree announced 2024-05-23 of ~$310M including a $15M Clean Water Act penalty. Safety/environmental failure with material regulatory action -- no finding of dishonesty by the company.

gate1.note: Personal auto insurance: premiums earned less losses/LAE less expenses (the combined ratio), plus investment income on float. Progressive discloses monthly results and its 96 combined-ratio target explicitly, so a generalist can audit the unit economics more easily than at almost any other insurer.

gate2.note: The moat is a low-cost direct-distribution and risk-segmentation advantage, not brand pricing power. Evidence at the anchors: underwriting profit inside the 96 target every year -- combined ratio 93.5% (FY2013) and 92.4% (FY2014), with the personal-lines CR 93.4% (2013) and 93.3% (2014) -- earned WHILE growing net premiums written 8% to $18.7B (2013) and 10% to $20.6B (2014); direct auto policies in force +9% in 2015 to 4.92M (reported 2016-01). Growth with underwriting profit is the signature of a genuine cost edge. But it is NARROW, not wide: auto insurance is a price-shopped commodity with a comparably-positioned direct rival in GEICO and much larger agency incumbents, no switching costs, and margins that move with industry frequency/severity -- the 2015-2016 loss-cost spike pushed the CR to 95.1% in both years, requiring double-digit rate increases. Bundling capability added via the ARX/American Strategic majority acquisition, closed 2015-04-01.

By FY2018 results (reported 2019-01) the cost advantage looked structural rather than cyclical: combined ratio improved to 93.4% (2017) and 90.6% (2018) while net premiums written grew from $20.6B (2014) to ~$32.6B (2018) and personal-auto market share moved from roughly 8-9% to above 11%. Taking large share and improving margin simultaneously, for several consecutive years, is the evidence a wide cost moat leaves in reported results.

gate3.note: Reputational episode: an August 2011 blog post ('My Sister Paid Progressive Insurance to Defend Her Killer') went viral over Progressive's role in a Maryland UM case where its interests aligned with the at-fault driver's defense. Ordinary claims-practice controversy, no regulatory finding.

Ordinary-course claims/policy-form class actions disclosed and settled in the 2013-2015 10-Ks: reimbursement of insureds' legal fees in recoveries from other Progressive insureds (settled 2013), application of a preferred-provider discount to medical-payment claims (settled 2013), premium charging and total-loss handling on commercial stated-amount policies (settled 2013), steering insureds to Service Centers/network repair shops (settled 2014), and an uninsured-motorist rejection form challenge (accrued 2014, settled class-wide 2015). No fraud allegations, no regulatory penalties.

POST-ANCHOR: $61M Michigan settlement (November 2024) over failure to include sales tax, title certificate and registration transfer fees in total-loss payments from 2013 through 2024 -- a claims-measurement dispute of a type common across the industry, not a dishonesty finding.

gate1.note: GATE 1 TESTS EXPLAINABILITY, NOT ETHICS. The unit economics are unusually simple: sell premium-priced cigarettes (Marlboro ~10% of world market ex-US/China) at prices that pass through excise tax and add real price, on low capital intensity and near-total-payout free cash flow. Reported results are distorted by currency, which the company strips out in disclosed currency-neutral figures -- readable, not opaque.

gate2.note: Pricing power is genuinely exceptional and dated in the reported numbers: FY2014 cigarette volume -2.8% ex-acquisitions and FY2015 volume -1.0%, yet FY2015 favorable pricing was +$2.1B and adjusted operating-income margin ROSE 0.3pp to 42.6% on a currency- and acquisition-neutral basis (reported 2016-02-04) -- price fully outruns secular volume decline. Reported EPS is the noisy part: FY2015 adjusted diluted EPS $4.42, -12.0% as reported, with an unprecedented $1.20-per-share currency headwind, i.e. double-digit currency-neutral growth reported as a decline. Threats to the moat are regulatory/substitution rather than competitive: Australia plain packaging (in force 2012-12-01) and PMI's investment-treaty challenge to it dismissed on jurisdiction 2015-12-17 (costs order against PMI 2017-03); EU Tobacco Products Directive 2 adopted April 2014, applicable 2016-05-20; PMI's ICSID claim against Uruguay's packaging rules dismissed 2016-07-08; illicit trade a permanent leak. Reduced-risk substitution was self-funded: iQOS launched in Nagoya in November 2014, expanded through Japan and Italy in 2015-2016.

gate3.note: On 2004-07-09 Philip Morris International signed a 12-year cooperation agreement with the European Commission and 10 member states, paying $1.25B, to combat contraband and counterfeit of its cigarettes -- a material regulatory settlement resolving smuggling-facilitation concerns WITHOUT admission of liability. The agreement expired 2016-07-09 and the Commission decided not to renew it (its own assessment published February 2016 was unfavourable to renewal).

PREDECESSOR DISCONTINUITY: on 2006-08-17 Judge Kessler (D.D.C.) held in United States v. Philip Morris USA that the US cigarette makers violated RICO through decades of coordinated fraudulent concealment and misrepresentation about smoking, addiction and 'light' cigarettes -- conduct squarely in the dishonesty category, affirmed by the D.C. Circuit on 2009-05-22 with certiorari denied 2010-06-28. The defendants were Altria/Philip Morris USA (the US business); PMI was separated from Altria by spin-off on 2008-03-28 and was not itself an adjudicated defendant, so the finding attaches to the predecessor group and the historical corporate DNA rather than to PMI's own post-2008 conduct.

PREDECESSOR DISCONTINUITY: on 2008-07-31 Canada's Rothmans, Benson & Hedges resolved federal/provincial contraband claims relating to 1989-1996 cigarette smuggling, pleading guilty and agreeing with its then-parent to total payments of ~CAD 550M (a criminal fine plus civil payments over ten years). PMI acquired Rothmans Inc. (and thereby full ownership of RBH) in 2008, i.e. essentially contemporaneously with and after the conduct and its resolution -- an admitted dishonesty matter, but pre-acquisition conduct of the acquired entity.

On 2015-06-01 the Quebec Superior Court gave judgment in the Blais and Letourneau class actions, assessing ~CAD 15.6B of damages against three manufacturers -- ~CAD 3.1B against PMI's subsidiary RBH (CAD 10.5B Imperial Tobacco, CAD 2B JTI-Macdonald) -- on findings that the companies knowingly withheld and trivialised health and addiction risks. Visible just before the 2015-06-30 anchor. Conduct period was largely 1950-1998, i.e. mostly before PMI's 2008 ownership of RBH (discontinuity). UPHELD on appeal 2019-03-01 (~CAD 13.5-14B); RBH obtained CCAA creditor protection on 2019-03-22 and PMI deconsolidated RBH from that date.

In January 2016 Thai prosecutors indicted Philip Morris (Thailand) Ltd and seven employees for under-declaring the customs value of cigarettes imported from the Philippines (2003-2007), with headline exposure reported at up to ~$2B. Outcome and reductions: in November 2019 the Bangkok Criminal Court convicted the COMPANY and fined it THB 1.2B (~$39.7M) while ACQUITTING all seven employees for lack of evidence; the appeals court lowered the fine (2022-06) and the Supreme Court cut it by ~85% in October 2025. Material mitigation: WTO panels/Appellate Body in Thailand -- Cigarettes (Philippines) (2011, and again in 2018-2019 compliance proceedings) found Thailand's customs valuation of these same imports inconsistent with its WTO obligations.

gate1.note: Specialty apparel/home retailer operating three owned brands (Urban Outfitters, Anthropologie Group, Free People) plus a wholesale segment and, from 2019, the Nuuly rental service. Unit economics are fully legible to a generalist: buy or design merchandise, mark it up, sell through stores and direct-to-consumer; profit turns on markdown rate, delivery cost and store-occupancy leverage.

gate2.note: Own-design vertical brands with real customer affinity and a debt-free balance sheet; peak economics reported for FY2014 (year ended 2014-01-31, reported March 2014): revenue $3.09B, net income ~$282M (~9% net margin), no borrowings. The advantage is brand/merchandising taste, not structural cost or switching cost - i.e. it can be lost by missing a fashion cycle, which is exactly what followed.

Four consecutive years of margin erosion were on the tape by the anchor. Net income fell from ~$282M (FY2014) to ~$232M (FY2015) to ~$224M (FY2016) to ~$158M (FY2017, reported March 2017). Q1 FY2018, reported 2017-05-22: total net sales $761M (flat), comparable Retail segment sales -3.1% (Urban -3.1%, Anthropologie Group -4.4%, Free People +1.5%), gross profit rate -284bp on higher markdowns, net income $12M / $0.10 per diluted share versus roughly $52M / $0.44 a year earlier. Results driven by markdowns demonstrate an absence of pricing power. Erosion continued after the 2017 anchor: FY2018 (reported March 2018) net income ~$104M, a ~2.9% net margin, and gross profit rate -291bp for the nine months to 2017-10-31.

Merchandising recovered: FY2019 (year ended 2019-01-31, reported 2019-03-05) revenue +10% to $3.98B with retail comps up high single digits and net income ~$298M - the brands regained traction, confirming the earlier decline was a fashion cycle, not terminal. But it did not persist: FY2020 (reported 2020-03-03) revenue was flat at ~$3.98B with comps ~+1% and net income back down to ~$168M. The occupancy-heavy operating leverage was then exposed by COVID - Q1 FY2021 (quarter ended 2020-04-30, reported 2020-05-19, i.e. before the 2020 anchor): net sales -31.9% to $588M, comparable Retail segment sales -28% (Free People -19%, Urban -24%, Anthropologie Group -33%), wholesale -74%, gross profit rate 2.0% versus 31.1%, preliminary net loss $138M / $(1.41) per share.

gate3.note: Navajo Nation sued Urban Outfitters and subsidiaries in D.N.M. (filed February 2012, after an October 2011 cease-and-desist) alleging trademark infringement and violations of the federal Indian Arts and Crafts Act for selling 'Navajo'/'Navaho' branded goods. Two counts were dismissed in May 2016; the parties settled at a settlement conference on 2016-09-29 (publicly reported November 2016) on undisclosed terms, together with a supply and license agreement to collaborate on authentic American Indian jewelry. Private IP/labeling dispute, no regulator involved, no admission.

Ordinary-course wage-and-hour class actions. California suits alleged uncompensated off-the-clock bag checks and 'on-call' shift scheduling (Charles v. Urban Outfitters - employees required to call two hours before a scheduled shift to learn whether they would work). The New York Attorney General wrote to major retailers about on-call scheduling in April 2015; URBN ended the practice. Routine retail employment litigation, no regulatory finding of dishonesty.

Le Tote Inc. sued URBN in June 2020 (E.D. Pa.) alleging misappropriation of trade secrets under the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act and the Pennsylvania UTSA plus breach of contract, in connection with the launch of URBN's Nuuly rental business. URBN ultimately won a favorable verdict (2023). Post-anchor for the 2020 date (filed after 2020-06-30 in most reports; ordinary-course commercial dispute either way).

gate1.note: At the 2013 anchor Amgen's earnings came from a small set of long-marketed biologics a generalist can name and price - Neulasta/Neupogen, Enbrel, Epogen/Aranesp, Prolia/Xgeva - with legible unit economics (~85% gross margin, R&D ~20% of sales, patent/biologic exclusivity as the pricing shield). The pipeline is genuinely unassessable by an outsider, but in 2013 the pipeline was upside, not the thesis: the marketed base carried essentially all of the $17.3B of 2012 revenue.

gate2.note: FY2012 results (reported January 2013): revenue $17.27B, net income ~$4.35B, ~25% net margin. Durability sources visible at the anchor: Enbrel protected by the '182 patent issued 2011-11-22 running to 2028; Neulasta a ~$4B franchise with no competitor and no US biosimilar approved in any category as of mid-2013 (the first, Sandoz's Zarxio, was not approved until 2015-03-06); large-scale mammalian-cell manufacturing and FDA process validation are genuine entry barriers. Visible counterweight already in the reported numbers by 2013: Epogen/Aranesp had been in decline since the FDA black-box warnings of March 2007 and the January 2011 CMS ESRD bundled-payment rule.

Biosimilars finally reached Amgen's own franchises. The first Neulasta biosimilar (Mylan/Biocon's Fulphila) was FDA-approved 2018-06-04 and launched July 2018; a second (Coherus' Udenyca) was approved Q4 2018 and launched January 2019. Neulasta sales fell from roughly $4.5B (2018) to ~$2.9B (2019) to ~$2.0B (2020, -29% y/y), visible in the FY2018 report (January 2019) and FY2019 report (2020-02-04). Enbrel held off US biosimilar launches but ground lower on rebate pressure. Amgen offset this by becoming a biosimilar seller itself, which is a lower-margin, competitive business - the moat narrowed from structural to portfolio-and-scale.

gate3.note: Securities fraud class action (lead plaintiff Connecticut Retirement Plans and Trust Funds) alleging Amgen and former executives made misleading statements and omissions about the safety and marketing of Aranesp and Epogen; class period 2004-04-22 to 2007-05-10. Pending and public well before the 2013 anchor. The Supreme Court held on 2013-02-27 that proof of materiality is not a prerequisite to class certification, allowing the case to proceed. Amgen settled for $95M a month before trial, expressly without admitting liability or wrongdoing (2016).

On 2012-12-18/19 Amgen pleaded GUILTY before the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York to a criminal information charging it with introducing a misbranded drug, Aranesp, into interstate commerce, and paid $762M total: a $136M criminal fine, $14M forfeiture and $612M civil False Claims Act settlement. DOJ's position was that Amgen sold Aranesp intending it be used at off-label doses the FDA had specifically considered and REJECTED, and for an indication the FDA never approved; the civil allegations also covered kickbacks to healthcare providers. Amgen entered a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement with HHS-OIG. This is an admitted criminal deception of prescribers and the FDA, public roughly six months before the 2013-06-30 anchor.

Post-anchor. Amgen disclosed in its Q2 2021 filing that the IRS had issued notices of deficiency seeking roughly $3.6B of additional tax for 2010-2012 and a further ~$5.1B plus penalties for 2013-2015, over transfer pricing on its Puerto Rico manufacturing operations - approximately $10.7B in dispute. A securities class action followed in 2022 alleging Amgen concealed the exposure. A tax controversy, not an established finding of dishonesty; no admission, and litigation in the U.S. Tax Court continued.

gate1.note: A deposit-funded lender plus wealth management and capital markets: gather roughly $1.4T of low-cost consumer and commercial deposits (FY2019 10-K), lend and invest at a spread, and earn fees at Merrill/GWIM and in the global markets business. The revenue model is explainable in a paragraph. The honest caveat: a $2.4T balance sheet with a large derivatives book cannot be independently verified by an outsider, so a generalist can explain how the bank makes money without being able to audit what it is carrying.

gate2.note: Through 2008-2014 BAC's reported results showed no durable advantage of any kind: it lost $2.2B in 2010, earned only $1.4B in 2011, $4.2B in 2012 and $4.8B in 2014 on a very large equity base, with acquired and own crisis-era liabilities consuming most pre-provision earnings. The quarterly dividend was held at $0.01 from 2009 into 2014; the Federal Reserve rejected BAC's 2011 capital-return request (March 2011); and BAC had to withdraw and resubmit its 2014 capital plan after disclosing a multi-year regulatory-capital reporting error on 2014-04-28.

A real, if commoditized, funding advantage became visible in reported results once litigation ran off. By the FY2016 report (2017-01-13) BAC held roughly $1.26T of deposits at a near-zero blended cost, the #1 or #2 US retail deposit share (~10-11% of US deposits), and had cut the efficiency ratio into the mid-60s from the high-70s in 2014. FY2018 (reported 2019-01-16) delivered ROTCE of ~15.5%; FY2019 (reported 2020-01-15) net income $27.4B ($2.75/share), ROTCE 14.9%, deposits above $1.4T, and a record $34B returned to shareholders. Scale plus the deposit franchise is genuine but it is not WIDE: banking is a leveraged, regulated, price-taking business with no product differentiation, and the same scale produced catastrophic outcomes a decade earlier.

gate3.note: BAC'S OWN CONDUCT (prior management). The SEC charged BAC over its proxy disclosures for the Merrill Lynch acquisition - failing to disclose the bonuses Merrill would pay and Merrill's mounting Q4 2008 losses. Judge Rakoff rejected the original $33M deal as a 'contrivance' and approved a $150M settlement on 2010-02-22. The New York Attorney General separately sued BAC, then-CEO Ken Lewis and CFO Joe Price in February 2010; that case settled 2014-03 for $15M from BAC, $10M from Lewis and a three-year officer-and-director bar for Lewis. Deception of BAC's own shareholders, but settled without admission and under management (Lewis) that left in December 2009 - Moynihan became CEO 2010-01-01.

BAC'S OWN SERVICING CONDUCT on an acquired platform. OCC and Federal Reserve consent orders of 2011-04-13 covered deficient mortgage servicing and foreclosure processing, including foreclosure affidavits sworn without personal knowledge of the underlying facts ('robosigning'). On 2012-02-09 BAC took the largest share - roughly $11.8B - of the $25B National Mortgage Settlement with DOJ, HUD and 49 state AGs. The affidavit practice was systematic deception of courts and borrowers occurring in 2009-2011, i.e. after the Countrywide acquisition and under BAC's own management of the servicing business, though the platform itself was inherited. Caveat: the NMS carried no admission of liability.

BAC'S OWN CONDUCT, current management. On 2014-04-09 the CFPB ordered Bank of America, N.A. and FIA Card Services to provide about $727M of relief to roughly 1.4M consumers for deceptively marketing credit card add-on products ('Credit Protection Plus' and 'Credit Protection Deluxe'), and for illegally charging approximately 1.9M accounts for credit monitoring and credit reporting services the customers never actually received. BAC also paid a $20M civil money penalty to the CFPB (plus $25M to the OCC). Consent order; deception of retail customers in the ordinary course of the card business.

BAC'S OWN CONTROL FAILURE. On 2014-04-28 BAC disclosed it had overstated its regulatory capital by roughly $4B for several years due to an error in accounting for structured notes assumed in the Merrill acquisition. It suspended the buyback and dividend increase it had announced weeks earlier following the 2014 CCAR, and resubmitted its capital plan. Self-disclosed and corrected; no enforcement action followed, but a multi-year misstatement of regulatory capital is not ordinary-course.

LARGELY INHERITED - DISCONTINUITY FLAG. On 2014-08-21 BAC agreed to pay $16.65B ($9.65B cash penalty including a record $5B FIRREA penalty, plus $7B of consumer relief) to resolve federal and state RMBS claims. DOJ's statement of facts covered Bank of America, Countrywide Financial and Merrill Lynch. The overwhelming bulk of the misrepresented securitizations were originated and sold in 2004-2008 by Countrywide (acquired 2008-07) and Merrill Lynch (acquired 2009-01) under those firms' own pre-acquisition management; BAC's own securitization desk was also included. Graded SERIOUS per the acquired-entity rule, with the caveat that BAC voluntarily bought both franchises and their liabilities.

Competition/market-conduct, no deception finding. On 2015-05-20 the Federal Reserve fined BAC $205M for unsafe and unsound practices in its FX trading business (deficient controls over traders' use of electronic chatrooms). Notably, BAC was NOT among the banks criminally charged that day - Citigroup, JPMorgan, Barclays and RBS pleaded guilty to FX antitrust conspiracy, and UBS to a LIBOR-related charge; BAC pleaded to nothing. BAC separately paid $187.5M to settle the private FX antitrust class action (2015). Pure competition-law/controls matter with no admitted customer deception.

ACQUIRED ENTITY, BUT THE CONDUCT CONTINUED UNDER BAC OWNERSHIP. On 2018-03-23 the New York Attorney General announced a then-record $42M settlement with Bank of America Merrill Lynch over a fraudulent 'masking' scheme: beginning in 2008 and continuing through 2013, BofAML routed client equity orders to outside electronic liquidity providers (Citadel, Two Sigma, Knight and others) and reprogrammed its systems to doctor the execution confirmations sent back to clients so they would not see it - over 16 million client orders representing more than 4 billion shares. BofAML acknowledged the conduct. Merrill was acquired 2009-01, so most of the masked orders were routed while the firm was owned and run by BAC. Systematic deception of institutional customers.

On 2019-03-22 the SEC announced Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith would pay over $8M to settle charges of improperly handling 'pre-released' American Depositary Receipts - it borrowed pre-released ADRs from brokers it should have known did not hold the underlying foreign shares. Part of an industry-wide SEC sweep touching most large prime brokers; settled without admission or denial.

POST-ANCHOR. Arising from BAC's administration of state unemployment-benefit prepaid debit cards during the pandemic - most visibly the California EDD program, where BAC froze roughly 350,000 accounts and was widely reported from October 2020 onward to have failed legitimate claimants. On 2022-07-14 the CFPB and OCC ordered BAC to pay about $100M in restitution plus $125M in penalties ($100M CFPB, $25M OCC) for an inadequate fraud-screening and error-resolution process. Conduct and public knowledge both post-date the 2020-06-30 anchor.

POST-ANCHOR. On 2023-07-11 the CFPB and OCC ordered BAC to pay roughly $250M ($100M restitution, $150M in penalties) for repeatedly charging multiple $35 insufficient-funds fees on the same re-presented transaction, withholding promised credit card cash and points bonuses, and enrolling customers in credit card accounts WITHOUT their authorization - using or obtaining consumer credit reports to open accounts customers never asked for. Unauthorized account opening is deception of customers in the same family as the Wells Fargo matter. Entirely post-anchor.

gate1.note: Closeout and discount retailer: buys manufacturers' overstock and closeout merchandise plus a growing base of manufactured-for-Big-Lots goods, and sells it through roughly 1,400 US stores. Unit economics are completely transparent - gross margin around 39-40%, with store occupancy, distribution and store labor the dominant costs.

gate2.note: Closeout retail carries no durable competitive advantage: no scale cost advantage against Walmart, Dollar General or Amazon; no brand pricing power (the customer comes for a price, not for Big Lots); and the closeout merchandise supply is opportunistic and shrinks whenever suppliers manage inventory well. Dated evidence available at the 2018 anchor: Big Lots entered Canada in July 2011 (Liquidation World) and exited entirely - announced with Q3 2013 results in December 2013, all 78 locations closed by February 2014, at a realized loss of about $0.47 per share. FY2017 (reported March 2018) revenue was $5.27B versus $5.20B in FY2016, a ~1.3% increase that included an extra 53rd week and came against a lower store count - i.e. flat to slightly down on a comparable basis. FY2017 income of $189.8M / $4.38 per diluted share versus $152.8M / $3.32 in FY2016 was driven substantially by buybacks shrinking the share count (from roughly 58M to 43M over four years) rather than by growth, and the stock fell on the March 2018 Q4 print because comps disappointed.

gate3.note: Securities class action and consolidated shareholder derivative actions (S.D. Ohio; derivative cases consolidated by order of 2012-08-10) alleging that CEO Steven Fishman and other officers and directors sold shares while in possession of undisclosed knowledge that results were deteriorating. Fishman sold 227,500 shares at about $45 for roughly $10.3M on 2012-03-20; on 2012-04-23 the company told investors sales had slowed and the stock fell 24% the next day to $34.71. The SEC and FBI both opened inquiries; the SEC closed its investigation WITHOUT bringing an enforcement action against the company (reported 2013). Big Lots agreed in May 2018 - before the anchor - to pay $38M to settle the securities class action, with insurers funding part of it and no admission of wrongdoing; the related derivative settlement (including a $3.5M insurance payment) was set for a settlement hearing on 2018-07-26 in Columbus. Graded SERIOUS: material settlement without admission, and the regulator declined to charge.

gate1.note: The accounting is simple - FY2018 (reported January 2019) revenue $13.45B, net income ~$4.43B, ~87% gross margin - but by the 2019 anchor a generalist could not assess the business, only describe it. Two unknowable binary events dominated the value: the fate of aducanumab in Alzheimer's disease, and whether the Tecfidera '514 patent would survive, with Tecfidera alone at $4.27B (about 32% of 2018 revenue). Explainable unit economics, unassessable durability, and no way for an outsider to handicap either question.

gate2.note: Leadership in multiple sclerosis with high returns but patent-term, not structural, protection. FY2018 (reported January 2019): Tecfidera $4.27B, Avonex plus Plegridy ~$2.73B, Tysabri ~$1.86B, Spinraza (FDA-approved 2016-12-23, orphan exclusivity) $1.72B; ~33% net margin. Erosion was already visible before the anchor: Avonex had been declining for years as oral MS therapies took share, and Mylan filed IPR2018-01403 in 2018 challenging the Tecfidera '514 patent as obvious, with parallel ANDA litigation in N.D. W.Va. PIPELINE EVENTS STRADDLING THE ANCHOR: on 2019-03-21 - BEFORE the 2019-06-30 anchor - Biogen and Eisai discontinued the Phase 3 EMERGE and ENGAGE aducanumab trials after a pre-specified futility analysis based on a 2018-12-26 data cut of 1,748 patients predicted both would miss their primary endpoint; the stock fell roughly 29% that day. The reversal came on 2019-10-22 - AFTER the anchor - when Biogen announced that a larger dataset including patients who completed 18 months between the December cut and the March halt showed EMERGE had met its primary endpoint, and that it would file for approval. At the 2019-06-30 anchor, only the failure was known.

The patent moat broke. The PTAB upheld the Tecfidera '514 patent against Mylan's obviousness challenge on 2020-02-05, but on 2020-06-18 the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of West Virginia (Judge Irene Keeley) invalidated 13 claims for failure to meet the written-description requirement of Section 112 - affirmed by the Federal Circuit on 2021-11-30, with certiorari denied in 2022. Generics launched in August 2020. US Tecfidera revenue collapsed from about $3.1B (2019) to roughly $1.5B (2020) to under $0.5B (2021), visible in the FY2020 report (February 2021) and FY2021 report (February 2022). Total revenue fell from $14.38B (2019) to $10.98B (2021). Aduhelm, approved 2021-06-07, generated approximately $3M of sales in all of 2021 and did not replace anything.

gate3.note: The qui tam United States ex rel. Bawduniak v. Biogen (D. Mass.), filed under seal in 2012, was UNSEALED on 2015-07-01 after the United States declined to intervene - so the allegations were public four years before the 2019 anchor. The relator, a former Biogen employee, alleged Biogen paid millions in speaker honoraria, speaker-training fees, consulting fees and meals to physicians between 2009 and 2014 to induce prescriptions of Avonex, Tysabri and Tecfidera, in violation of the Anti-Kickback Statute and False Claims Act. Allegation only as of the anchor; DOJ had affirmatively declined to join.

POST-ANCHOR. On 2020-12-17 Biogen agreed to pay $22M to resolve DOJ False Claims Act allegations that from 2011 to 2013 it used two 501(c)(3) charities - the Chronic Disease Fund and The Assistance Fund - as conduits to pay the Medicare copays of patients on Avonex and Tysabri, working through Advanced Care Scripts to route patients to the foundations and making contemporaneous donations that funded their copays. Settled with no admission; Biogen publicly maintained its conduct had been appropriate. A whistleblower received nearly $4M.

POST-ANCHOR. On 2022-07-20 Biogen agreed to pay $900M to resolve the Bawduniak kickback case - the largest recovery in the 150-year history of the False Claims Act obtained without the United States intervening. The relator received $266M, the largest whistleblower award on record. Settled without any admission of liability.

POST-ANCHOR. The FDA granted Aduhelm accelerated approval on 2021-06-07 over its own advisory committee's near-unanimous negative vote (10-0 against with 1 uncertain), after which three committee members resigned. The FDA's acting commissioner requested an HHS Inspector General investigation on 2021-07-09. A joint House Committee on Oversight and Reform / Energy and Commerce investigation reported on 2022-12-29 that the FDA-Biogen interactions had been 'atypical' and the approval process 'rife with irregularities,' including an off-the-books jointly prepared briefing document, and criticized Biogen's $56,000 annual launch price. No enforcement action against Biogen; findings concern improper closeness to the regulator rather than proven fraud. CMS restricted coverage to clinical trial participants in its final national coverage determination of April 2022 (draft 2022-01-11), and Biogen discontinued Aduhelm in January 2024.

gate1.note: Custody and asset-servicing bank: it safekeeps and administers securities for institutions - $37.1 trillion of assets under custody and/or administration at 2019-12-31 - charging basis-point fees on assets serviced, earning net interest revenue on the client cash that sits with it, plus issuer services, clearing and custody for advisors through Pershing, and $1.9 trillion of asset management. Fee-on-assets plus float; a generalist can explain every revenue line.

gate2.note: Global custody is a four-firm oligopoly (BNY Mellon, State Street, JPMorgan, Citi) with punishing switching costs - moving a fund complex's custodian means re-plumbing daily NAV production, accounting, and regulatory reporting - and BNY Mellon is the largest participant. FY2019 (reported 2020-01-16): $37.1T AUC/A, $1.9T AUM, net income applicable to common shareholders of about $4.3B or $4.51 per diluted share, on roughly $21B of tangible common equity. The honest counter-evidence, also on the record before the anchor: the moat converts poorly into growth. Total revenue was roughly $15.2B (2016), $15.5B (2017), $16.4B (2018) and $16.5B (2019) - essentially flat across the decade, as per-basis-point fee compression offset asset growth, and earnings swing with short-term rates rather than with any pricing decision management makes. A wide moat that protects a static earnings stream.
