POST-ANCHOR. The rate dependency the flat revenue line had hinted at became the whole story when the Fed cut to zero in March 2020: BNY was forced into money-market fee waivers and net interest revenue fell from about $3.35B (2019) toward $2.6B in 2020-2021. FY2021 (reported January 2022): revenue $15.93B and net income ~$3.55B, both BELOW 2019's $16.5B and $4.4B despite two more years of market appreciation. Structural switching costs intact; economic advantage demonstrably not translating into owner earnings growth.

gate3.note: On 2011-10-04 the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and the New York Attorney General sued BNY Mellon alleging a decade-long fraud in its 'standing instruction' foreign exchange service for custody clients; Virginia and Florida qui tams, a Department of Labor investigation, an SEC investigation and multiple customer class actions followed. Allegation stage - the settlement and admissions came in 2015.

On 2015-03-19 BNY Mellon agreed to pay $714M to globally resolve the United States' and New York State's lawsuits, the customer class actions, and the SEC and Department of Labor matters over its standing-instruction FX product provided to custody clients before early 2012. BNY Mellon ADMITTED the underlying facts: it promised custody clients the best interbank market rate of the day on their FX transactions and instead systematically gave them the day's worst or near-worst rate, without disclosing the pricing method. This is admitted, systematic, decade-long deception of the bank's own custody customers - the single most important entry in BNY's record and public more than four years before the 2019 anchor.

On 2015-08-18 the SEC announced that BNY Mellon would pay $14.8M ($8.3M disgorgement, $1.5M prejudgment interest, $5M civil penalty) for violating the anti-bribery and internal-controls provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. BNY Mellon provided valuable internships to family members of officials of a Middle Eastern sovereign wealth fund, bypassing the GPA and multi-interview standards of its own competitive internship program, because employees viewed the internships as important to retaining the fund's business; the officials made repeated follow-up requests about the placements. This was the SEC's first FCPA enforcement action built on internships rather than cash payments. Settled without admitting or denying. Bribery/FCPA is explicitly disqualifying conduct; note it settled without admission.

Operational failure, not dishonesty. A corrupted SunGard InvestOne operating-system upgrade crashed on 2015-08-24, and the backup instance corrupted concurrently, leaving BNY Mellon unable to strike net asset values for roughly 1,200 fund structures across 66 fund-accounting clients for several days. BNY Mellon settled the Massachusetts Securities Division's investigation for $3M in March 2016 for failing to oversee its third-party vendor and lacking a workable contingency plan; it reprocessed shareholder transactions at system-generated NAVs on request and waived reprocessing fees. Vendor-management and controls failure.

gate1.note: Tier-one automotive supplier: designs and manufactures turbochargers, emissions and thermal-management systems, and transmission components (dual-clutch modules, torque-transfer systems) that are engineered into specific OEM vehicle programs years before launch and then supplied for the life of the program. Unit economics are legible - content per vehicle multiplied by program volumes, less contractual annual price-downs to the customer.

gate2.note: Real but bounded. The advantage is engineered-in content: once BorgWarner wins a program, switching mid-cycle is prohibitively expensive for the OEM, and the company was the leading independent turbocharger supplier as European diesel penetration peaked. The ceiling is the customer. Per the FY2015 10-K (filed February 2016, the latest available at the 2016-06-30 anchor) and confirmed in the FY2016 10-K, three customers were each 10% or more of net sales - Volkswagen Group about 14%, Ford about 11%, Toyota about 11% - and OEMs extract annual price concessions as a matter of contract. The business is also cyclical and program-dependent: net sales fell from $8.31B (2014) to $8.02B (2015) even with the Remy International acquisition (closed 2015-11-10) contributing, before the FY2016 print reached $9.07B largely on that acquisition. A further structural overhang was already public at the anchor: the VW diesel emissions scandal broke on 2015-09-18 with the EPA's notice of violation against BorgWarner's largest customer, and Western European diesel share began a decline from roughly 50% (2015) toward 36% (2018), directly relevant to a diesel-weighted turbocharger mix. No BorgWarner misconduct was alleged in that matter.

gate3.note: Legacy asbestos product liability. BorgWarner, as successor to Borg-Warner Corporation, has for decades been one of many defendants in asbestos personal-injury actions arising from friction products (brake and clutch materials) sold before the 1980s. Disclosed at the anchor in the FY2015 10-K and continuing: in 2016 approximately 2,800 claims were resolved, of which 352 (13%) resulted in any payment by or on behalf of the company, and BorgWarner spent $45.3M on asbestos defense and litigation that year. Ordinary-course inherited product liability with no allegation of misconduct.

ACCOUNTING - PERIOD COVERS THE ANCHOR BUT NOTHING WAS PUBLIC UNTIL AFTER IT. BorgWarner first recorded a large charge for previously unasserted asbestos claims with its FY2016 results in early 2017 (i.e. after the 2016-06-30 anchor). On 2018-06-15 it announced it would RESTATE its consolidated financial statements for fiscal 2015 and 2016 as presented in the FY2017 10-K, having re-evaluated its accounting for the estimated value of asbestos claims not yet asserted and the associated defense costs. On 2020-08-26 the SEC issued a settled administrative order finding that from 2012 through 2016 BorgWarner materially misstated its financial statements by failing to record over $700M of liabilities for future asbestos claims - it performed no substantive quantitative analysis despite holding nearly 40 years of its own raw claims data, and relied on untested assumptions that its products were unique among asbestos defendants and that industry benchmarks did not apply. The restatement pushed $703.6M of charges back to 2012. BorgWarner paid a $950,000 penalty without admitting or denying the findings; the SEC did not charge fraud or scienter. Graded SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING because the order rests on a failure to estimate rather than on intentional manipulation - but note that the anchor-date financial statements were, as a matter of SEC finding, materially wrong, and an analyst at 2016-06-30 had no way to know it.

gate1.note: Caterpillar builds and sells construction, mining and energy equipment through ~160 independent dealers, and earns a large, higher-margin annuity on replacement parts and service tied to the installed base; a captive lender (Cat Financial) finances the machines. A generalist can state the unit economics: machine margin plus decades of parts pull-through, against a deeply cyclical volume line.

gate2.note: As of the 2015-06-30 anchor the moat is the dealer network and parts distribution, not the machine itself: Caterpillar was the world's #1 maker of construction and mining equipment, with independent dealers whose relationships and territories span generations and a parts system built to deliver most components anywhere within 24 hours. Downtime economics make an installed-base owner reluctant to switch. The 2012-2016 mining collapse is a VOLUME event, not share loss: revenue fell from the 2012 peak of $65.9B to $55.7B in 2013 (reported 2014-01) and $55.2B in 2014 (reported 2015-01), and Caterpillar's monthly retail-machine-sales 8-Ks had shown negative year-over-year world machine sales continuously from late 2012 through the anchor. Q1 2015 (reported 2015-04-23) showed Resource Industries down again. Post-anchor and excluded at this date: Q2 2015 (2015-07-23) Resource Industries sales $1.991B, -11% y/y, with segment profit at break-even vs $114M a year earlier; on 2015-09-24 Caterpillar announced a restructuring cutting up to 10,000 jobs and said 2012-peak-to-2016 sales would fall about $20B (~31%), roughly two-thirds of it mining. Sales troughed at $38.5B in 2016 and the franchise recovered strongly from 2017 -- which is the evidence that the moat was intact and the cycle, not the moat, was doing the damage.

gate3.note: Announced 2013-01-18: Caterpillar's audit committee concluded (2013-01-16) that senior managers at Zhengzhou Siwei / ERA Mining Machinery had run multi-year accounting misconduct -- improper cost allocation overstating profit and early, sometimes unsupported, revenue recognition. Caterpillar took a ~$580M non-cash goodwill impairment (Q4 2012), about two-thirds of the $886M purchase price, and removed several Siwei managers. DISCONTINUITY FLAG: the fraud was committed by the acquired Chinese company's own management BEFORE Caterpillar closed the deal in mid-2012; Caterpillar discovered it (inventory discrepancies, 2012-11), investigated, disclosed promptly and CEO Doug Oberhelman publicly accepted blame (2013-01-28). Graded SERIOUS as acquired-entity conduct under different management, with a genuine due-diligence failure attributable to Caterpillar.

Public 2014-04-01: Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations hearing (Levin) released a report finding Caterpillar had shifted more than $8B of US taxable income to a Swiss affiliate, Caterpillar SARL (CSARL), from 2000-2012 and deferred or avoided about $2.4B of US tax, under a structure designed by PricewaterhouseCoopers; by 2008 roughly 45% of consolidated revenue and 43% of profit was booked in CSARL while the parts business was physically run from Illinois. No finding of illegality -- Caterpillar and PwC testified the structure complied with law. This is aggressive-but-lawful tax planning made public by a hostile congressional forum, not an adjudicated wrong.

Both pre-anchor and both disclosed in the Form 10-K filed 2015-02-17, i.e. BEFORE the 2015-06-30 anchor: (a) on 2015-01-08 Caterpillar received a federal grand jury subpoena from the US District Court for the Central District of Illinois seeking documents on undistributed foreign profits and cash movements among US and non-US subsidiaries; (b) on 2015-01-30 Caterpillar received the IRS Revenue Agent's Report closing the 2007-2009 exam, proposing roughly $1B of additional tax and accuracy-related penalties on CSARL parts profits under substance-over-form / assignment-of-income doctrines. Caterpillar said it would vigorously contest and that the transactions complied with applicable law. An analyst standing at 2015-06-30 therefore knew a criminal grand jury and a billion-dollar IRS assessment were live.

POST-ANCHOR (excluded at 2015-06-30). On 2017-03-02 federal agents from the US Attorney's office for the Central District of Illinois, IRS Criminal Investigation, FDIC Office of Inspector General and Commerce Department export enforcement executed search warrants at three Caterpillar sites: Peoria headquarters, East Peoria offices, and the Morton parts distribution center, seizing documents and electronic records tied to the CSARL cash and equipment transfers. A government-commissioned report by Dartmouth accounting professor Leslie Robinson, reported 2017-03-07, alleged Caterpillar had brought back billions in offshore profits without paying required tax and had failed to comply with tax and financial reporting rules. Caterpillar denied wrongdoing; press reports say the DOJ criminal probe wound down after 2018.

RESOLUTION, post-anchor. On 2022-09-08 Caterpillar announced a settlement with the IRS covering tax years 2007-2016 for roughly $740M ($490M tax plus $250M interest) -- less than 35% of the ~$2.3B originally sought -- with NO penalties and, critically, NO adjustment based on the substance-over-form or assignment-of-income doctrines the IRS had asserted. No civil or criminal charges were ever filed against Caterpillar or any employee. The 2014-2017 allegations were therefore materially reduced on resolution; the tax structure was ultimately not held to be a sham. Any dated read of this company must not let the 2017 raid headlines colour the 2015 anchor, nor let the 2022 vindication colour the 2015 or 2017 dates.

gate1.note: NAMING DISCONTINUITY: at the 2014-06-30 anchor the ticker CB is ACE Limited, a Zurich/Bermuda-domiciled global commercial property and casualty insurer and reinsurer -- NOT The Chubb Corporation, which was then a separate NYSE company (ticker CB was Chubb Corp's; ACE traded as ACE). ACE acquired Chubb Corp and adopted its name and ticker only on 2016-01-14. The economics are Buffett's home ground: write premium, hold float, invest it, and make money only if the combined ratio stays below 100. Reserve estimation is judgmental, which is the one genuinely hard-to-verify input, but the business model is plainly explainable.

gate2.note: At the 2014-06-30 anchor ACE's advantage is underwriting discipline plus a hard-to-replicate global licensing and branch network (operations in ~54 countries) and AA-category financial strength ratings that large multinational buyers require. The evidence is the record, not the story: ACE ran a P&C combined ratio of 88.0% in 2013 (reported 2014-01-28) and had compounded book value per share for over a decade under Evan Greenberg (CEO from 2004-05). But commercial P&C is a capital commodity -- capacity is repriced annually by brokers, switching costs for the insured are near zero, and soft markets punish everyone. That is a NARROW moat: real, operator-dependent, and reversible if underwriting discipline slips. Not WIDE.

Change visible after the anchor: ACE agreed on 2015-07-01 to buy The Chubb Corporation for $28.3B and closed on 2016-01-14 at ~$29.5B ($14.3B cash, $15.2B stock), immediately adopting the Chubb name globally and the CB ticker -- creating the world's largest publicly traded P&C insurer. The addition of Chubb's high-net-worth personal lines franchise (a genuinely sticky, service-differentiated book) and greater scale in US middle market strengthened the moat, and the combined company kept posting high-80s combined ratios. It is still NARROW rather than WIDE: the core is still annually repriced commercial insurance, and the source of returns is management discipline over the cycle rather than a structural toll.

gate3.note: First public 2004-10-14, when NY AG Eliot Spitzer's civil complaint against Marsh & McLennan described a sham-bidding scheme in which insurers, ACE units among them, submitted deliberately uncompetitive 'B quotes' so a designated incumbent would win, in exchange for steered business paid for via undisclosed contingent commissions. Settled 2006-04-25/26 with the New York, Illinois and Connecticut attorneys general for $80M -- $40M restitution to policyholders whose excess casualty placements were rigged and $40M in penalties -- plus a bar on contingent commissions on excess casualty through 2008. The settlement also covered finite-reinsurance accounting: regulators found ACE had created the false appearance of risk transfer in at least six deals using SECRET SIDE AGREEMENTS whose wording contradicted the written contracts. Bid-rigging plus off-contract side letters that falsify risk transfer is exactly the dishonesty category, hence DISQUALIFYING, notwithstanding that ACE settled without admitting liability. PARTIAL DISCONTINUITY: the conduct ran roughly 1999-2004; Evan Greenberg became ACE's CEO in 2004-05 (having joined the company in 2001 and served as president/COO from 2003), so this is not a clean change of regime. LATER REDUCTION: the related criminal convictions of two former Marsh executives (February 2008, NY antitrust) were VACATED on 2010-07-02 by Justice James Yates, who found undisclosed evidence and cooperator testimony that contradicted the trial record; other defendants were acquitted or had charges dismissed. The civil/regulatory findings against ACE were never undone.

gate1.note: At the 2014-06-30 anchor Cigna is mostly a fee-based administrator: the majority of its US medical membership is self-funded employer business where Cigna is paid a per-member administrative fee and the employer carries the claims risk, alongside insured medical, group disability and life, and a fast-growing international supplemental health arm. Explainability improved materially on 2013-02-04 when Cigna paid Berkshire Hathaway Life of Nebraska about $2.2B (funded with ~$1.8B of supporting assets, $100M of parent cash and a ~$300M tax benefit) to reinsure its run-off variable annuity death-benefit and guaranteed-minimum-income-benefit books, taking a ~$500M after-tax charge -- removing the one genuinely opaque, equity-market-sensitive liability from the story.

gate2.note: The durable pieces at 2014-06-30 are entrenched national and middle-market employer relationships (multi-year, high switching cost once payroll, wellness and claims systems are integrated), specialty attach (behavioural, pharmacy, dental, stop-loss) on top of the ASO base, and a genuinely differentiated international supplemental business. Against that: rates are bid annually, provider networks are replicable within a market, and the Affordable Care Act (enacted 2010-03) imposed medical loss ratio floors from 2011 that cap insurer margin at 15-20% of premium, with exchanges opening 2013-10 adding a lower-margin individual channel. Cigna nevertheless compounded adjusted EPS through 2012-2014 and earned mid-to-high-teens ROE. That is NARROW, not WIDE -- a regulated scale advantage, not a toll.

gate3.note: Public 2009-02-17: as part of NY AG Andrew Cuomo's industry-wide investigation, Cigna agreed to stop using the UnitedHealth-owned Ingenix database to set 'usual and customary' out-of-network rates and to contribute $10M toward an independent replacement (which became FAIR Health, Inc., seeded with almost $100M across insurers). The AG's finding was that the Ingenix data understated prevailing charges, systematically shifting cost onto patients who used out-of-network care. Settled without admission of liability; Cigna's $10M was small relative to UnitedHealth's $350M. Graded SERIOUS: a regulatory action over systematic underpayment, but Cigna was a user of an industry utility rather than its architect.

Agreement dated 2013-05-13 with the insurance regulators of California, Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania over long-term disability claim handling. Cigna agreed to reopen and reassess claims denied in California from January 2008 through December 2010 and in the other four states from January 2009 through December 2010, to adopt enhanced claim documentation and disposition procedures, and to submit to two years of regulatory monitoring. Cigna recorded a $77M pre-tax ($51M after-tax) charge in Q1 2013: $48M of benefit costs and reserves on claims expected to be reopened (including $925,000 of fines, $750,000 of regulatory surcharges and $9.5M of claim handling expense) plus $29M of additional cost on open claims from the process changes. Material, dated, pre-anchor, no admission of wrongdoing.

POST-ANCHOR (excluded at 2014-06-30). On 2016-01-21 CMS imposed immediate intermediate sanctions suspending all enrollment and marketing for Cigna-HealthSpring and Bravo Health Medicare Advantage and Part D plans across eight states, citing 'widespread and systemic failures' in coverage determinations, appeals and grievances, Part D formulary and benefit administration, access to facilities and records, and compliance program effectiveness, which caused enrollees to face delays, denials and higher out-of-pocket cost. The sanctions were not lifted until 2017-06-16 after remediation in March-April 2017 and an independent audit.

POST-ANCHOR. On 2023-09-29 Cigna agreed to pay about $172M across two False Claims Act settlements and entered a five-year corporate integrity agreement with HHS-OIG. The core allegation concerned the '360' program, in which vendors performed in-home assessments of Medicare Advantage members and Cigna submitted the resulting diagnosis codes to CMS for risk-adjustment payment even though the visiting nurses had not performed the testing or imaging needed to support those diagnoses. Relator Robert Cutler received $8.1M. No admission of liability.

gate1.note: Clorox makes and sells low-priced, frequently repurchased household consumables -- bleach and cleaners, Glad bags, Kingsford charcoal, Hidden Valley dressings, Brita filters, Burt's Bees, Fresh Step -- through grocery, mass and club retailers. Unit economics are as simple as they get: raw material plus conversion plus roughly 10% of sales in advertising, sold at a branded premium over a store-brand alternative sitting on the same shelf.

gate2.note: Honest reading at the 2014-06-30 anchor, and against private label specifically. In favour: Clorox stated in its FY2014 10-K (fiscal year ended 2014-06-30, filed August 2014) that close to 90% of its brands hold the #1 or #2 share position in their categories, and it sustained gross margins in the low-to-mid 40s while pushing list price increases through 2011-2014 commodity inflation. Against: liquid bleach was ~13% of consolidated net sales in FY2014 (14% in FY2013 and FY2012) and is a chemically identical commodity where store brands compete openly on price; Glad bags and Kingsford face the same store-brand attack; and growth was thin -- FY2014 sales of about $5.6B were roughly flat with FY2013, so the pricing power that exists shows up as margin defence rather than volume growth, and it depends on continuous innovation and advertising spend to justify the premium. That combination -- real per-category leadership, no category-wide toll, private label always one shelf away -- is NARROW, not WIDE. Dated post-anchor event that tests the franchise's edges rather than its moat: on 2014-09-22 Clorox declared its Venezuelan business no longer viable and shut it, and on 2014-09-26 the Maduro government occupied the Santa Lucia and Guacara plants; Clorox took $60-65M of after-tax exit costs in FY2015 -- an expropriation loss, not a competitive one.

gate3.note: Reported 2011-12-01: Clorox settled a California district attorneys' consumer protection action, approved by Alameda County Superior Court, paying just under $200,000 and accepting an injunction against deceptive packaging headspace. The allegation was that Anti-Allergen Bleach and Cold-Water Bleach, sold in California from January 2008 to January 2010, were packaged in the same 3-litre bottles as regular bleach but filled to only ~80% versus ~95%, violating California's Fair Packaging and Labeling Act by making value comparison misleading. Settled without admission of liability; the products were discontinued. Ordinary-course consumer-protection housekeeping at trivial dollar size.

POST-ANCHOR, and flagged as only partially verified in this research. A proposed settlement agreement between the Consumer Product Safety Commission and The Clorox Company carrying a $14,150,000 civil penalty was published in the Federal Register on 2026-01-27 for public comment. CPSC civil penalties of this type customarily concern failure to report a product hazard within the statutory window rather than affirmative deception; the underlying product and conduct were not confirmed in this research and should be verified before being relied on.

gate1.note: Two businesses, both explainable. Comcast Cable owns physical coaxial/fibre plant passing roughly 57 million US homes and bills monthly subscriptions for broadband, video, voice and increasingly wireless; NBCUniversal owns broadcast and cable networks, a film studio and theme parks. The cable economics -- sunk plant, high incremental margin on each added broadband subscriber, capex driven by node splits and equipment rather than re-trenching -- are straightforward for a generalist.

gate2.note: At the 2018-06-30 anchor the moat is the pipe, and the evidence separates the two products cleanly. BROADBAND (pricing power intact): in the results reported 2018-01-24 Comcast added more than one million high-speed internet customers in 2017 -- the twelfth consecutive year above that mark -- while high-speed internet revenue grew roughly 8-9% a year on annual rate increases plus speed-tier mix, in most of its footprint against one telco DSL/partial-fibre alternative or none. Raising price every year while still taking share is the definition of demonstrated pricing power. Comcast's DOCSIS 3.1 upgrade (rolled out from 2016) delivered gigabit speeds over the existing plant, so it could match fibre marketing claims without a fibre rebuild. VIDEO (melting, and less important than it looks): video customers fell about 186,000 in 2017 (roughly 38,000 in Q4 2017 alone), with cord-cutting plainly visible since 2013 -- but video was the low-margin product, squeezed between rising programming fees and OTT substitutes, and its decline was already being more than offset by broadband ARPU and net adds. The correct 2018 judgement is that Comcast was converting a declining video monopoly into a durable broadband one, and the moat was WIDE.

The inflection became public on 2022-07-28, when Comcast reported that Q2 2022 broadband customers were flat at 32.2 million -- zero net additions, the first time ever, and the same quarter Charter also reported a decline, the first-ever drop for the two largest cable operators. The cause was competitive entry that had not existed in 2018: T-Mobile and Verizon fixed-wireless home internet (T-Mobile added 560,000 broadband customers that quarter) plus accelerating fibre overbuild. From this point the local broadband monopoly is a contested market: Comcast's pricing power now shows as an explicit ARPU-versus-volume trade-off rather than as both at once, and losses followed (for example about 167,000 broadband customers lost in Q2 2025). Still a good business with sunk plant and high incremental margins -- but NARROW, not WIDE. This entry is dated from 2023 because a June-30 anchor could not see the 2022-07-28 disclosure until the 2023 anchor.

gate3.note: Associated Press testing in October 2007 showed Comcast was interfering with BitTorrent peer-to-peer transfers by forging reset packets; Comcast initially denied blocking, then acknowledged the practice and characterised it as reasonable network management. On 2008-08-01 the FCC ruled that Comcast had violated its 2005 Internet Policy Statement by secretly degrading customer traffic and ordered disclosure and termination of the practice. REVERSED: on 2010-04-06 the DC Circuit vacated the order in Comcast Corp. v. FCC -- but on jurisdictional grounds (the FCC had failed to tie its ancillary authority to a statutory mandate), not on the underlying facts. Graded SERIOUS for the initial denial of conduct the company was in fact engaged in.

On 2016-08-01 Washington Attorney General Bob Ferguson sued Comcast for more than $100M, alleging it misrepresented the scope of its Service Protection Plan, charged for service calls that should have been free, and ran improper credit checks. Pre-anchor as a filed action; the FINDING is post-anchor: on 2019-06-11 King County Superior Court Judge Timothy Bradshaw ruled Comcast violated the Washington Consumer Protection Act more than 445,000 times, including enrolling roughly 31,000 customers in the Service Protection Plan without their consent, and imposed about $9.1M in penalties plus restitution -- the largest trial award ever in a Washington consumer protection case, though far short of the $100M sought, with substantial parts of the state's case rejected.

On 2016-10-11 Comcast agreed to pay the FCC $2.3M -- described by the FCC as the largest civil penalty ever levied on a cable operator -- and to a five-year compliance plan, resolving an investigation into 'negative option billing' or cramming. Triggered by subscriber complaints filed with the FCC during 2014 and 2015, the investigation concluded Comcast had charged customers for premium channels, set-top boxes and DVRs they never affirmatively requested, and refunded them only after persistent customer effort. Settled without an admission of liability. This sits at the boundary of the disqualifying category: it is unauthorised charging of customers at scale, but the FCC framed it as a systems and controls failure rather than an intentional scheme, so it is graded SERIOUS.

gate1.note: After spinning off its refining, marketing and chemicals arm as Phillips 66 on 2012-05-01, ConocoPhillips was a pure-play exploration and production company -- the largest independent E&P in the world at the 2014-06-30 anchor. The unit economics are transparent and brutal: revenue is a world price the company does not set, times barrels; profit is that price less finding, development and lifting costs, less depletion and taxes. Easy to explain, which is not the same as easy to own.

gate2.note: Crude oil and natural gas are undifferentiated commodities and ConocoPhillips is a price taker; there is no brand, no switching cost, no network, and no ability to raise price. What the company had at the 2014-06-30 anchor was scale, a long-lived reserve base and a stated plan to deliver 3-5% annual production and margin growth funded by roughly $16B of annual capital spending against roughly comparable operating cash flow at $100+ Brent -- i.e. the growth was contingent on a price it did not control, and the programme was barely self-funding at the top of the cycle. Brent peaked around $115 on 2014-06-19, days before the anchor, and fell to the $50s by December 2014 and the $30s by January 2016; ConocoPhillips's realisations, earnings and dividend all followed the price down, which is the practical proof that no moat existed. Low-cost acreage is an advantage of degree within a commodity, not a durable competitive advantage; the correct class is NONE.

gate3.note: Leaks at the Penglai 19-3 field in China's Bohai Bay, operated by ConocoPhillips China with CNOOC as partner, began in June 2011 but were not publicly reported until 2011-07-05, after a microblog tip-off -- the delay attributable in the first instance to China's State Oceanic Administration, which had withheld the news for about a month, a point that cuts against reading the whole episode as company concealment. Roughly 700 barrels of crude and about 2,500 barrels of oil-based drilling mud escaped, affecting some 6,200 square kilometres. The SOA ordered production suspended on 2011-09-02 and publicly accused ConocoPhillips China of failing to fully report the spill and of having represented that leak sources were sealed and cleanup complete when they were not; the company disputed the characterisation. Settlements followed: about RMB 1.09B for fisheries losses in Hebei and Liaoning agreed with the Ministry of Agriculture and SOA in January 2012, and a final April 2012 agreement bringing the total paid into compensation and marine-environment funds to roughly RMB 1.683B (on the order of $300M). Graded SERIOUS -- a material regulatory action with allegations of misreporting to a regulator, but a single operational incident with a contested factual record and a regulator that had itself suppressed disclosure, not a pattern of deception.

gate1.note: Campbell Soup makes and sells shelf-stable soup and broth, sauces (Prego, Pace), V8 beverages, Pepperidge Farm baked goods and snacks, and Arnott's biscuits in Australia, through supermarkets and mass retail. Unit economics are elementary: agricultural and packaging inputs plus conversion, sold at a branded premium, with a large share of the price gap given back as trade promotion to hold shelf space and features.

gate2.note: Judged honestly against private label at the 2013-06-30 anchor. The brand is genuinely dominant -- Campbell's held roughly 55-60% of the US wet soup category and condensed soup's red-and-white can is one of the most recognised marks in American retail, with real scale advantage in a low-price-per-serving product. But the pricing power is thin and the category was shrinking: FY2013 US soup sales rose only about 2.7% and did so on heavy promotional support, and the very next quarter reported (fiscal Q1 2014, released November 2013) showed condensed soup sales down 7% and ready-to-serve soup down 11%. Store brands compete directly on the shelf at a visible discount and take share whenever consumers trade down. Management's own behaviour confirms the read: rather than reinvest in soup, Campbell bought growth elsewhere -- Bolthouse Farms for $1.55B (announced 2012-07, closed 2012-08), Plum Organics (2013-06) and Kelsen (2013-08). Post-anchor, the pattern held and worsened: the 2018-05-18 results carried a $393M quarterly loss including $619M of Campbell Fresh impairments, and by 2022-09 the company was publicly acknowledging consumers switching to private label in condensed soup and broth. The soup brand never disappeared and the category share held, so the class remains NARROW throughout rather than falling to NONE -- but it was never WIDE at this anchor.

gate3.note: POST-ANCHOR (excluded at 2013-06-30). The House Oversight Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy released a staff report on 2021-02-04 on toxic heavy metals in baby food; Plum Organics -- acquired by Campbell in June 2013 and still owned by Campbell at the time -- was among the manufacturers that did NOT provide the requested internal testing data, and the subcommittee characterised the non-response as a refusal to cooperate. Campbell and Plum issued a public response on 2021-02-25. Campbell sold Plum to Sun-Maid in May 2021, and the subcommittee's follow-up report of 2021-09-29 published the withheld data, showing Plum finished products with up to 225 ppb inorganic arsenic, a majority above 5 ppb lead and nearly 40% above 5 ppb cadmium. Consumer class actions were filed against Plum, Gerber and Beech-Nut from 2021-02. Graded SERIOUS for the refusal to produce safety data to a congressional inquiry, which is a candour failure rather than ordinary product litigation; note that no US regulatory limit for these metals in most baby foods existed at the time and the issue was industry-wide.

gate1.note: Two understandable businesses at the 2018-06-30 anchor (pre-Aetna close): ~9,800 retail drugstores earning a spread on dispensed scripts plus front-store merchandise, and Caremark, a top-3 PBM earning administrative fees, retained rebates and mail/specialty margin. PBM rebate and spread economics are opaque in disclosure but the drivers (script volume, generic dispensing rate, reimbursement per script) are explainable to a generalist.

gate2.note: Scale-based, not franchise-based. Caremark (merged with CVS 2007) sat in a three-firm PBM oligopoly (ESRX, CVS, UNH/OptumRx) with high stated client retention and buying scale versus manufacturers; retail side had the largest US store count and roughly a quarter of US script share, plus regulatory/licensing barriers. Offsetting: drug retailing is commoditized, PBM contracts are rebid every ~3 years, and the payer, not the pharmacy, controls network access.

Moat visibly narrowed, class unchanged. 2016-08: Walgreens announced a strategic alliance with Prime Therapeutics (22M Blue Cross/Blue Shield lives) and CVS cut 2016 EPS guidance on network losses. 2016-09/12: CVS was dropped from the Tricare retail network effective 2016-12-01 (~9.4M members steered to Walgreens). 2016-11-08: CVS cut its 2017 outlook, quantifying roughly 40M prescriptions lost, disproportionately profitable ones. These flowed through 2017 reported results alongside negative front-store comps and reimbursement pressure, demonstrating that CVS could not defend its own script base against payer network design. 2017-12-03: CVS agreed to acquire Aetna for ~$69B (closed 2018-11-28, post-anchor) -- an explicit admission that standalone retail-pharmacy/PBM economics needed vertical integration to be defended. 2018-06-28, two days before the anchor: Amazon announced the PillPack acquisition; CVS fell ~8% and CVS/WBA/RAD lost ~$11B of combined market value in a day.

gate3.note: 2010-10-14: CVS agreed to pay $77.6M ($75M civil penalty, then the largest ever under the Controlled Substances Act, plus $2.6M forfeited profits) and accepted responsibility for illegally selling pseudoephedrine to methamphetamine traffickers, primarily in Los Angeles, Orange and Clark counties. The government agreed not to bring criminal charges; CVS agreed to a three-year compliance-and-ethics program. Compliance failure with acceptance of responsibility, not adjudicated deception.

2014-04-08: SEC charged CVS Caremark with misleading investors and committing accounting violations; CVS paid $20M, neither admitting nor denying. The SEC alleged CVS failed to disclose, during a $1.5B September 2009 bond offering, that it had lost significant Medicare Part D and PBM contract revenue (disclosed 2009-11-05, stock -20% that day), and that CVS changed the purchase accounting for the Longs Drugs acquisition -- writing $189M of personal property down to $0 and reversing $49M of previously recorded depreciation -- without disclosing it, which lifted Q3 2009 earnings past analyst estimates while the company was announcing bad news. Substance of the charge is accounting manipulation and investor deception. DISCONTINUITY: conduct was 2009 under CEO Tom Ryan; Larry Merlo became CEO in March 2011 and led the company at the 2018 anchor.

2015-05: CVS paid a $22M civil penalty (M.D. Fla.) and admitted that pharmacists at two Sanford, Florida stores knowingly filled thousands of prescriptions for oxycodone and other painkillers lacking a legitimate medical purpose during 2010-2011; DEA said the two stores ordered 1-2 million oxycodone pills a year, ~27x the national average. Admission of knowing illegal dispensing.

Repeat pattern of Controlled Substances Act settlements in the years immediately before the anchor: 2016-02-12, $8M (D. Md.) for dispensing controlled substances on prescriptions not issued for a legitimate medical purpose; 2016-10-20, $600,000; 2017-07-11, $5M (E.D. Cal.); 2018-06-28, $1.5M -- two days before the anchor; 2015-08, $450,000 (D.R.I.). Individually small, but the recurrence across districts is the relevant integrity signal at 2018-06-30.

POST-ANCHOR. 2018-11-19: Florida sued CVS and Walgreens over their role in the opioid crisis, opening the wave of state/municipal dispensing suits. 2022-11: CVS agreed to pay ~$5B over 10 years to settle state, municipal and tribal opioid claims. 2024-12-18: DOJ filed a nationwide complaint alleging CVS knowingly dispensed unlawful controlled-substance prescriptions in violation of the CSA and False Claims Act, alleging staffing/compensation metrics that 'emphasized speed over safety'; contested by CVS. 2025-08: a court entered a ~$290M FCA judgment against Caremark ($95M trebled plus penalties) over Medicare Part D drug-price misreporting, from a 2014 qui tam by an Aetna actuary.

gate1.note: A diversified industrial: process-automation instruments, valves and control systems (Rosemount, Fisher, DeltaV) sold into refineries, chemical and power plants, plus industrial automation, climate/HVAC components, tools and data-center power. Unit economics are ordinary manufacturing -- engineered hardware at high gross margin, with a large aftermarket/service tail on an installed base.

gate2.note: Process Management is the source: distributed control systems and field instrumentation are specified into multi-decade plant designs, are validated against safety and regulatory standards, and are expensive and risky to rip out, so replacement demand and service annuities recur. Emerson held #1 or #2 share across most of its product categories and Process Management ran segment margins near 19-20%. Corroborated by an unusually long consistency record -- Emerson had raised its dividend every year for 58 consecutive years by 2015, spanning multiple industrial recessions.

What changed and when it showed: the oil-price collapse that began late 2014 revealed that the wide-moat segment was concentrated in energy capex, not diversified across process industries. Reported 2015-05-05 (Q2 FY2015) and 2015-08 (Q3 FY2015): underlying declines from oil and gas weakness after a strong Q1. FY2015 results reported 2015-11: net sales -9%, underlying -2%, hit by lower oil prices, a global slowdown in industrial capital spending, emerging-market weakness and dollar strength. Separately, on 2015-06-30 -- the anchor date itself -- Emerson announced it would spin off Network Power and explore sale of power generation, motors/drives and residential storage, conceding that a large share of the portfolio had no defensible position; Network Power was ultimately sold to Platinum Equity for $4B on 2016-12-01, well below the capital sunk into building it. The durable moat is real but confined to process automation, not the consolidated company.

gate3.note: 1990-05: Emerson's Electronics & Space Corp subsidiary pleaded guilty to four counts of making false statements to the federal government -- submitting false and inflated cost and price data on US military contracts between 1983 and 1987 -- and Emerson paid $14M in civil settlement plus criminal fines. Conduct is dishonesty in substance, but DISCONTINUITY: it is 25 years before the 2015 anchor, at a defense subsidiary, under the Chuck Knight management era; David Farr had been CEO since 2000 with no comparable finding since. Graded SERIOUS rather than disqualifying on remoteness and management change.

POST-ANCHOR (filed 2015, tried 2018). A federal jury in N.D. Cal. found that Emerson Network Power misused BladeRoom Group's confidential modular data-center design information obtained under an NDA during acquisition talks, awarding ~$30M ($10M lost profits, $20M unjust enrichment); with interest and fees the figure rose to roughly $77M. Partially revisited on appeal -- the Ninth Circuit ruled on the case on 2021-08-30. Misappropriation under an NDA is a candor problem, dated after the 2015-06-30 anchor.

POST-ANCHOR. FTC consent order (In the Matter of Emerson Electric and Pentair) requiring divestiture of a switchbox business to Crane Co. to clear Emerson's $3.15B Pentair acquisition -- an ordinary merger-remedy matter, no deception alleged. Emerson also carries continuing ordinary-course asbestos product-liability litigation through subsidiaries including Fisher Controls and Crosby Valve (e.g., an adverse Rhode Island verdict in 2017).

gate1.note: Power management across four understandable franchises: electrical components and systems (breakers, switchgear, UPS, wiring devices), hydraulics (pumps, valves, hose), aerospace fuel and hydraulic systems, and vehicle drivetrain including heavy-duty truck transmissions. Sells engineered hardware through distributors and OEMs; economics are unit volume times price times a manufacturing margin, with an aftermarket tail.

gate2.note: The defensible franchise is Electrical: products are specified into building and utility designs, must carry UL/IEC and code approvals, are sold through entrenched distributor relationships, and generate long-tail service and replacement demand. Hydraulics, Vehicle and (to a lesser degree) Aerospace are cyclical, OEM-dependent and share-contested. Eaton is a serial acquirer -- the $13B Cooper Industries deal closed 2012-11-30 and was structured with an Irish domicile that dropped the effective tax rate toward the low teens, materially lifting reported EPS without any improvement in operating economics; investors should not read that step-up as moat.

Class unchanged but the source of the moat became visible in results. Revenue fell from $22.6B (2014) to $20.9B (2015, reported 2016-02) to $19.7B (2016, reported 2017-02) -- roughly -13% over two years -- driven almost entirely by Hydraulics, Vehicle and energy-exposed end markets, while Electrical segment revenue held far better and Electrical margins expanded. In 2017 management opened a public strategic review of the Hydraulics, Vehicle and Lighting portfolios. Read correctly, this confirms that the durable business is Electrical and that roughly 40% of the company was cyclical, low-moat content.

gate3.note: 2009-10-08: after a four-week liability trial in D. Del., a jury returned a verdict against Eaton in ZF Meritor LLC v. Eaton Corp., finding Eaton engaged in anticompetitive de facto partial exclusive dealing in North American heavy-duty truck transmissions (market-share-conditioned discounts with the four truck OEMs). Filed October 2006. Pure competition-law matter with no deception alleged. 2011-08-19: final judgment of liability entered but zero damages awarded. 2012-09-28: the Third Circuit affirmed denial of Eaton's JMOL, letting the liability verdict stand. 2014-06-23: Eaton agreed to pay Meritor $500M, paid 2014-07-16 (plaintiffs had claimed $800M, $2.4B trebled).

2010-01-06: Judge Yerger of the Hinds County (Mississippi) Circuit Court imposed a joint and several sanction of $1,560,642.83 against Eaton and three of its attorneys for intentional discovery violations. The core finding: Eaton had executed a consulting agreement with former Frisby employee Milan Georgeff on 2003-01-28, then on 2005-02-25 served a misleading interrogatory response describing it as merely a 'strictly limited indemnity'; the true agreement surfaced only on 2005-11-02 in parallel North Carolina litigation. Deliberate misrepresentation to a court.

2010-12-22: the Hinds County Circuit Court dismissed WITH PREJUDICE all of Eaton's trade-secret claims against Frisby Aerospace (later Triumph Actuation Systems) as a sanction for 'improper ex parte and fraudulent contacts' -- fraud on the court. Eaton had sued in 2004 alleging six engineers who left for Frisby stole aircraft hydraulic pump and motor trade secrets from its Jackson, Mississippi plant. On 2006-12-01 Eaton's Mississippi counsel recommended retaining former Hinds County District Attorney Ed Peters, describing him as 'the closest possible associate of Judge DeLaughter' -- the presiding judge. A special master's report of 2010-08-11 made the underlying findings of fact. Judge Bobby DeLaughter was separately indicted 2009-02-12, pleaded guilty 2009-07-30 to obstruction (lying to the FBI about his conversations with Peters) and was sentenced to 18 months on 2009-11-13; Peters received immunity. Triumph's counterclaims further alleged Eaton gave false information to prosecutors to procure criminal charges against the engineers it had accused.

2013-11-21: the Mississippi Supreme Court, unanimously, affirmed BOTH the $1.56M discovery sanction and the dismissal with prejudice (Eaton Corp. v. Frisby, 133 So.3d 735). Critically, it found 'clear and convincing evidence' that Eaton's own corporate officers knew Peters was making improper ex parte communications for Eaton's benefit, citing internal emails discussing Peters securing trial dates and postponing a sanctions ruling. This is not a rogue-outside-counsel finding -- it is an appellate court holding that corporate officers knew. NOT reduced or reversed on any later appeal.

2014-06-18: Eaton signed a $147.5M settlement resolving all remaining Triumph claims -- $135.3M to Triumph Group plus $12.2M into a fund for the six engineers Eaton had originally accused. Combined with the $500M Meritor payment three weeks later, Eaton paid out roughly $650M in mid-2014 across the two matters. All of the above is public well before the 2018-06-30 anchor.

gate1.note: Copper, gold and molybdenum mining -- unit economics reduce to ore grade, strip ratio and net cash cost per pound against a world price the company does not set. The oil and gas segment added in mid-2013 (deepwater Gulf of Mexico, onshore California) is a second, differently driven commodity business with its own reserve and finding-cost accounting, which complicates the story but does not make it opaque.

gate2.note: Pure price taker in a globally traded commodity, with no pricing power, no switching costs and no customer captivity. FCX's only genuine advantage is asset quality -- Grasberg in Papua, Indonesia, whose gold byproduct credits historically made it one of the lowest net-cash-cost copper mines on earth -- but an ore body is an asset advantage, not a durable competitive moat, it depletes, and it is not reproducible as a management skill. Earnings swing with copper: revenue ~$20.9B and net income ~$4.6B in 2011 versus ~$20.9B and ~$2.7B in 2013 on the same top line.

Weakened further, visible before the anchor. (a) Sovereign risk crystallized: Indonesia's raw-ore export ban and progressive export duty took effect 2014-01-12, halting FCX concentrate exports from Grasberg for roughly six months and costing close to $1B of revenue in a twelve-week span; Jakarta was simultaneously demanding conversion from the Contract of Work to a special license carrying higher taxes and royalties, divestment to 51% Indonesian ownership, domestic smelter construction, and surrender of international arbitration rights. An MoU restoring exports was reached 2014-07-25, just after the anchor. (b) Capital allocation: on 2012-12-05 FCX announced ~$9B of acquisitions (Plains Exploration & Production for $6.9B and McMoRan Exploration for $2.1B, ~$20B including assumed debt); FCX shares fell 16% that day -- its worst day since 2008 -- while PXP rose 23% and MMR rose 87%. The market priced the deals as a transfer from FCX shareholders on day one. Deals closed 2013-05-31 and 2013-06-03.

gate3.note: 2005-12-27: The New York Times, using company records, reported FCX paid nearly $20M between 1998 and 2004 directly to Indonesian military and police generals, colonels, majors and captains as well as to units. Payments to individual officers were illegal for those officers to accept under Indonesian law; the payments were disclosed to the SEC and drew FCPA scrutiny. No FCPA enforcement action was ever brought and the company characterized the payments as reimbursement for security in a remote operating area. Graded SERIOUS rather than disqualifying because it was never charged or adjudicated, but direct cash to named individual officers is bribery-adjacent conduct on the record before the anchor.

RELATED-PARTY SELF-DEALING ALLEGATIONS. The December 2012 PXP/MMR acquisitions were conflicted on their face: FCX chairman James R. Moffett was co-founder and chairman of McMoRan Exploration, FCX CEO Richard Adkerson was co-chairman of MMR, directors and financial advisers overlapped across the three companies, and FCX's largest shareholders publicly attacked the deal. Derivative and stockholder suits followed in Delaware Chancery from December 2012 (In re Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. Derivative Litigation, No. 8145-VCN; In re Plains Exploration & Production Company Stockholder Litigation, where the Chancery Court denied a preliminary injunction). RESOLUTION, POST-ANCHOR: settlement announced 2015-01-15 for $137.5M -- then the largest derivative settlement in Delaware history -- funded $115M by D&O insurers and $22.5M by FCX, approved by the Chancery Court 2015-04-07, with proceeds net of fees paid out to shareholders as a special dividend. Not an admission, but the size is the finding.

2013-05: the roof of a non-operational underground training tunnel collapsed at Grasberg, killing 28 workers and injuring 10; operations were suspended for roughly six weeks. Further fatalities followed in September 2014. Graded MINOR on this scale because it is a safety and operating-culture failure rather than a dishonesty finding, but it is material context for a business whose single most valuable asset sits in a jurisdiction where the operator's social license is contested.

POST-ANCHOR, and FCX is the solicited party rather than the wrongdoer. 2015-11: the 'Papa minta saham' recordings became public in Indonesia, in which House Speaker Setya Novanto was heard soliciting shares in FCX's Indonesian unit in connection with the contract extension; the recording was made by FCX Indonesia's own chief executive. Novanto was forced to resign the speakership. Included for completeness on the Indonesian political-risk thread.

gate1.note: Four legible segments: Aerospace (Gulfstream large-cabin business jets plus jet services), Marine Systems (Electric Boat nuclear submarines, Bath Iron Works destroyers, NASSCO), Combat Systems (Abrams, Stryker, munitions) and Technologies (GDIT federal IT services and mission systems). Long-dated cost-plus and fixed-price government contracts with a disclosed backlog make forward revenue unusually visible for an industrial.

gate2.note: Genuinely protected where the barriers are physical and political: Electric Boat is one of only two US yards able to build nuclear submarines (with HII Newport News), and the Virginia- and Columbia-class programs are decades-long national-priority commitments; the Abrams line at Lima, Ohio is sole-source; Gulfstream carries a top-two large-cabin brand with a captive global service network and high customer switching cost. Offsetting and preventing a WIDE rating: the customer is a monopsony that sets allowable margins, Gulfstream is deeply cyclical, and federal IT services is a recompete-driven, price-shopped business with no durable advantage.

Mix shifted toward the weakest-moat segment. GD announced the CSRA acquisition on 2018-02-11 and closed it 2018-04-03 for $9.7B including ~$2.8B of assumed debt, folding it into GDIT and taking pro-forma net debt to roughly $10.5B -- making Technologies, the segment with the shortest contract lives and the lowest barriers, the largest by revenue. Visible in reported results from 2018 onward: Technologies showed flat-to-declining organic revenue through 2019 on recompetes, award protests and delayed federal procurements, while the protected marine and combat franchises carried growth. Additional operating evidence at the anchor: COVID-19 travel restrictions blocked 13 completed Gulfstream deliveries in Q1 2020 (reported 2020-04-29, net 11 deliveries lost after pulling two forward), and 4,300 IAM Local S6 machinists struck Bath Iron Works from 2020-06-22 -- eight days before the anchor -- over expanded use of subcontractors (ratified a new contract 2020-08-23, post-anchor).

gate3.note: DISCONTINUITY FLAG -- historically remote, entirely different management. GD was the central corporate subject of the 1980s defense-procurement scandals: Navy suspension of divisions from new contract awards and penalties over improperly billed overhead, congressional investigations of fraud, waste and abuse (see the July 1985 CRS report on GD specifically), and a related federal indictment concerning the DIVAD/Sgt York program that was subsequently dismissed in 1987. This predates the anchor by 35 years and multiple complete management turnovers (William Anders' 1991 restructuring, then Chabraja, Hewson-era peers, Novakovic and Phebe Novakovic as CEO from 2013). Recorded for the record, not as a live character finding at 2020.

Disclosed in GD's own filings: in 2015 Electric Boat received a civil investigative demand from DOJ over potential False Claims Act violations concerning failures of its quality system with respect to allegedly non-conforming parts purchased from a supplier. In 2016 GD learned it was a defendant in a sealed qui tam action, and the Navy's Suspending and Debarring Official issued a SHOW CAUSE LETTER demanding Electric Boat answer concerns about its oversight and management of subcontractor and supplier quality assurance -- a debarment-adjacent step against the crown-jewel franchise. LATER REDUCED/REVERSED: in Q3 2019 DOJ declined to intervene and the relator's complaint was unsealed (investigation stated to be continuing); the relator filed a second amended complaint in Q4 2020; the district court dismissed the complaint WITH PREJUDICE in Q3 2021; and the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal with prejudice on 2023-08-17 (84Partners, LLC v. General Dynamics Electric Boat). At the 2020-06-30 anchor the matter was live and unresolved with DOJ's investigation open.

gate1.note: Sells small-molecule antivirals -- an HIV franchise built on the tenofovir backbone and a hepatitis C franchise -- at near-zero marginal cost under patent protection. Unit economics are net price times treated patients, with the whole edifice resting on patent life and payer willingness to pay. The one non-obvious feature is easy to state: a hepatitis C therapy is a 12-week cure, so it depletes its own market rather than creating an annuity.

gate2.note: The moat is HIV, not hepatitis C. Gilead's tenofovir backbone anchored the majority of first-line US regimens with roughly 80% share, defended by treatment-guideline entrenchment, physician and patient inertia on a lifelong therapy where switching carries clinical risk, and successive lifecycle patents (Viread to Truvada to Complera/Stribild to the TAF-based Genvoya/Descovy to Biktarvy). NARROW rather than WIDE because every element is time-limited by patent expiry rather than by customer captivity, and payers, not Gilead, ultimately set net price.

Class unchanged, but the revenue base underneath it began collapsing and this was visible in reported results before mid-2016. Sovaldi and Harvoni peaked at roughly $19.1B combined in 2015. Q1 2016 results (reported 2016-04-28) already showed hepatitis C revenue declining year over year; Harvoni US net product sales fell to ~$1.5B in Q2 2016 from ~$2.8B in Q2 2015. Full-year HCV: ~$14.8B in 2016, ~$9.1B in 2017 (Harvoni alone -52% year over year), and on 2017-02/2018-02 guidance calls management guided 2018 HCV to just $3.5-4.0B, roughly 60% below 2017. Two independent causes, both dated: the prevalent treatable patient pool depleted after the 2015 warehouse of patients was cured, and competition crushed net price -- Merck's Zepatier (approved 2016-01) and, decisively, AbbVie's pan-genotypic Mavyret (approved 2017-08) at a far lower list price. Consolidated revenue fell $32.6B (2015) to $30.4B (2016) to $26.1B (2017) to $22.1B (2018).

By the anchor the composition has fully inverted and the surviving moat is visible in results. Reported 2019-02 (FY2018) and through 2019: the HIV franchise grew to roughly $14.6B, up about 12%, with Biktarvy -- approved 2018-02 -- becoming the fastest HIV product launch on record in the US, while HCV shrank to a small residual. Total revenue stabilized at ~$22.4B in 2019 versus $22.1B in 2018. Offsetting: the $11.9B Kite Pharma acquisition (announced 2017-08) disappointed -- Yescarta produced only $264M in 2018 and $456M in 2019 against the price paid, and Gilead later took an $820M charge on a Kite anti-BCMA program. Leadership turned over: CEO John Milligan's departure was announced 2018-07 and Daniel O'Day (ex-Roche Pharma) became CEO on 2019-03-01, four months before the anchor -- a new and unproven capital allocator at the anchor date.

gate3.note: 2015-12-01: Senate Finance Committee ranking members Wyden and Grassley released an 18-month investigation concluding that Gilead set Sovaldi's price -- $1,000 per pill, $84,000 per course -- at the level it believed would maximize revenue, with internal documents showing that access and affordability were secondary considerations; the report noted Medicaid programs spent over $1B in 2014 yet treated only about 2.4% of roughly 700,000 infected enrollees. No legal action followed. Graded MINOR because it produced no settlement or regulatory sanction, but it is a direct, documented character finding on how management weighed patients against revenue.

Gilead was swept into the DOJ's industry-wide investigation of pharmaceutical co-pay charities, disclosing the subpoena in its SEC filings by early 2017. RESOLUTION, POST-ANCHOR: on 2020-09-23 Gilead agreed to pay $97M to resolve False Claims Act allegations that from 2007 through 2010 it used the Caring Voice Coalition as a conduit to pay Medicare co-pays for its own pulmonary-arterial-hypertension drug Letairis -- funding a fund that covered co-pays only for Letairis and not competing medicines, while routinely obtaining data from the foundation to calibrate how much to pay. Settled without admission; the effect alleged is defeating the co-pay's cost-control purpose while billing Medicare for the full price.

2018-05: California HIV patients filed personal-injury and class-action suits alleging Gilead knew tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) carried bone and kidney toxicity, and that it deliberately shelved the safer tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) so as to run out TDF's patent life before switching patients. Graded MINOR at the 2019-06-30 anchor because it was unadjudicated private mass-tort litigation that Gilead contested; the allegation itself is serious in kind. LATER DEVELOPMENT: in 2024-02 a California appellate ruling allowed the novel negligence theory -- a duty to develop the safer successor drug -- to proceed, keeping the litigation alive.

2019-05, one month before the anchor: consolidated antitrust class actions were filed in N.D. Cal. (In re HIV Antitrust Litigation) alleging Gilead paid Teva roughly $1B in a 2014 reverse payment to keep generic Truvada and Atripla off the market, and that Gilead imposed 'no-generics' restraints in its combination-pill collaborations with Bristol-Myers Squibb and Janssen; plaintiffs sought about $3.6B. Pure competition-law matter, no deception alleged. LATER LARGELY REVERSED IN GILEAD'S FAVOR: in 2023 a jury unanimously cleared Gilead and Teva of the pay-for-delay claims; separately, in 2023-05 Gilead funded a $246.75M settlement with direct-purchaser and retailer plaintiffs (CVS, Rite Aid, Walgreens) covering purchases from February 2018 to November 2022.

gate1.note: Designs, manufactures and sells GPS-enabled devices across five reported segments -- automotive/mobile, outdoor, fitness, marine and aviation. Vertically integrated manufacturing in Taiwan; unit economics are straightforward consumer and certified-avionics hardware: units times ASP at a gross margin in the low-to-mid 50s, with heavy R&D and no meaningful recurring revenue at this date.

gate2.note: Two real but unequal sources. Aviation is the durable one: panel-mount and integrated flight decks require FAA/EASA certification, are designed into airframe OEM programs with multi-year qualification cycles, and generate long aftermarket and upgrade tails -- a genuine regulatory and switching-cost moat. Elsewhere the advantage is operational rather than structural: vertical integration (Garmin owns its manufacturing, unusual among consumer-electronics firms) sustained gross margins above 50% and a debt-free, large net-cash balance sheet. The consumer personal-navigation-device position was a share lead, not a defensible franchise.

Class holds only because of the segments that were NOT the biggest one; the largest segment's moat was destroyed on a datable day. 2009-10-28: Google announced free turn-by-turn Google Maps Navigation for Android; Garmin fell more than 16% the following day to $30.85 and TomTom fell ~29%. 2010-01-21: Nokia made Ovi Maps navigation free. The substitution then showed up in reported results continuously: total revenue $3.49B (2008) to $2.95B (2009) to $2.69B (2010), with price cuts already visible by December 2009; automotive/mobile fell from 58% of revenue in 2011 to 55% in 2012 and to ~50% by Q2 2013 on North American and European PND unit declines. 2012 total revenue $2.72B, -2%; Q1 2013 revenue $532M, -4% versus $557M. OFFSETTING AND VISIBLE AT THE ANCHOR: outdoor grew ~11% and fitness ~8% in 2012, and aviation grew, so the mix was migrating from the segment with no moat toward the segments that had one -- which is why the company, unlike TomTom, was not broken. Garmin also initiated a $300M repurchase in February 2013 against a large net-cash position.

gate3.note: 2010-08-26: Garmin voluntarily recalled roughly 1.25 million nuvi personal navigation devices over a battery overheating and fire hazard traced to a third-party battery supplier within a defined date-code range and a specific circuit-board design. Fewer than 10 incidents had been reported, with no injuries and no property damage; Garmin described it as an abundance of caution. Read as a positive integrity signal -- proactive disclosure ahead of harm, not a concealment finding.

Ordinary-course patent litigation. Complaint filed 2012-07-24 by Technology Properties Limited, Phoenix Digital Solutions and Patriot Scientific against 24 companies including Garmin entities over US Patent 5,809,336; the ITC instituted a Section 337 investigation 2012-08-21. RESOLVED IN GARMIN'S FAVOR, just after the anchor: on 2013-09-06 the ITC administrative law judge issued an initial determination of no Section 337 violation by any Garmin company.

POST-ANCHOR by weeks. Meyers v. Garmin International, Inc. (D. Kan., No. 13-CV-2416), a putative consumer class action alleging lithium-ion batteries in certain Garmin personal navigation devices were prone to premature failure. Garmin prevailed on summary judgment (announced 2016). No fraud, accounting, bribery, antitrust or regulatory-enforcement matter of any kind was found for Garmin in the years preceding the 2013-06-30 anchor.

gate1.note: MRO distribution is transparent: buy 1.5M+ industrial consumables, hold them in DCs/branches, resell at a markup for same-day availability. Unit economics are gross margin per order less fulfillment and selling cost; the only judgment call is how much of the markup is paid for service versus opacity.

gate2.note: Through FY2013 (10-K filed 2014-02) Grainger showed classic wide-moat marks: gross margin ~43-44%, operating margin 13.7% in 2013, ROIC in the 20s-30s, an unmatched US branch/DC network and KeepStock vendor-managed inventory that embedded it in customer plants. Catalog franchise dating to 1927; unplanned MRO buyers were price-insensitive.

Gross-margin erosion turned into an unbroken multi-year trend beginning Q4 2013 (it ran 21 consecutive quarters of YoY decline through Q4 2018, disclosed 2019-01). Visible pre-2016-06-30: Q1 2016 results (reported 2016-04-18) showed gross margin 41.7%, down 310bp YoY, attributed to price deflation exceeding cost deflation and mix shift to lower-margin large customers; FY2016 guidance was cut/narrowed. Amazon Business had launched 2015-04-28 and was openly targeting industrial supplies. Scale and service still intact, so NARROW not NONE.

Pricing umbrella confirmed gone, but the scale/service moat held. At the 2016-11-11 analyst day management said it would move US list prices to 'market competitive' levels across ~400,000 web SKUs (cuts up to ~25%), conceding roughly 40% of US volume had been priced above market ('we don't need to have the lowest price, we just need to be in the ballpark'). On 2017-02 it announced accelerating the remaining 2018 cuts into Q3 2017. The damage hit reported results BEFORE the 2017-06-30 anchor: Q1 2017 (reported 2017-04-18) adjusted EPS $2.88, down 9% YoY, and FY2017 guidance was cut from $11.30-$12.40 to $10.00-$11.30 and sales growth from 2-6% to 1-4%, explicitly because more volume than expected moved to lower prices. Post-anchor for the record: Amazon Business Prime Shipping launch drove GWW down >3% on 2017-10-24; US volume nonetheless grew 7% in 2017 and operating margin bottomed at 11.1%.

gate3.note: Paid the US $6 million to settle False Claims Act allegations that it sold government agencies special-order items at markups above those allowed by its GSA Multiple Award Schedule contract. Civil, no admission.

Announced 2012-12-27: paid $70 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations on GSA and USPS contracts - GSA IG alleged Grainger failed to disclose the discounts it gave other customers as required for favored-procurement status, and USPS IG alleged USPS was not given promised most-favored-customer treatment. Civil settlement, no admission of liability. A stricter reading (concealing better pricing given to others in order to keep a government price) edges toward deception of a customer; graded SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING because it was civil-only with no admission and no fraud finding.

gate1.note: Oilfield services sells discrete jobs - cementing, pressure pumping/fracturing, drilling fluids, completion tools - priced per well or per stage, so revenue tracks customer E&P capex and rig count and margin tracks equipment utilization. Simple to explain; extremely operationally levered and cyclical.

gate2.note: World #2 in oilfield services with genuine scale in North American pressure pumping and cementing plus proprietary completion technology, but demonstrably a price-taker across cycles: revenue fell about 21% in 2009 with sharp margin compression as customers demanded service-price concessions. Moat is scale/logistics, not pricing power.

Visible before the 2015-06-30 anchor: WTI fell from about $107 (2014-06) to about $53 (2015-01). HAL disclosed roughly 9,000 job cuts (about 10% of headcount) between 2014-12 and 2015-02. Q4 2014 (reported 2015-01-20) and Q1 2015 (reported 2015-04-20) showed North America revenue and margin falling hard on customer-demanded double-digit service price cuts. No ability to hold price. Post-anchor confirmation: Q2 2015 (2015-07-20) revenue down about 26% YoY, FY2016 revenue down about 33% with North America operating losses.

Post-anchor, dated for completeness. The Baker Hughes combination, announced 2014-11-17 (pre-anchor, and at the anchor still pending and defended by management), was sued by DOJ on 2016-04-06 ('unfixable' per AAG Bill Baer) and abandoned 2016-05-01, costing a $3.5 billion reverse break fee paid to Baker Hughes - roughly 18 months of management attention and a capital loss with nothing acquired.

gate3.note: 2004-08-03 SEC settlement: $7.5 million civil penalty over the 1998-1999 disclosure of and accounting for revenue from unapproved claims on long-term construction projects (booking cost overruns as income from 1998-04 without disclosing the change until the 1999 10-K). Settled without admitting or denying; the SEC did not find a GAAP departure, ordered no restatement, and made no fraud finding, but explicitly said the penalty size reflected lapses in the company's cooperation. Graded SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING on the absence of a fraud or GAAP finding; an analyst applying a hard candor test could reasonably grade it higher.

2009-02-11: KBR/Halliburton FCPA resolution, $579 million total - then the largest ever against a US company. Subsidiary Kellogg Brown & Root LLC pled guilty to conspiring to violate the FCPA and paid a $402 million criminal fine; KBR and Halliburton paid $177 million in SEC disgorgement. The scheme bribed Nigerian officials over roughly a decade (1995-2004) to win about $6 billion of Bonny Island LNG contracts, executed through the TSKJ joint venture. Straight bribery, hence DISQUALIFYING. Discontinuity to flag: the conduct occurred while KBR was a Halliburton subsidiary (Cheney was CEO 1995-2000, Dave Lesar from 2000); KBR was spun off in 2007-04, so by the 2015 anchor the offending unit was no longer owned and the responsible management was gone six years before the settlement and 15 years before the anchor.

2013-07-25 DOJ announcement: Halliburton Energy Services agreed to plead guilty to criminal destruction of evidence - it deleted the results of post-blowout computer modeling of the Macondo cement job, i.e. destroyed evidence bearing on its own liability in the Deepwater Horizon investigation. Judge accepted the plea 2013-09-19: $200,000 statutory maximum fine, three years probation, plus a voluntary $55 million contribution to the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (not a condition of the plea). Cementing technology director Anthony Badalamenti separately pled guilty to instructing employees to delete the data. A criminal admission of deceiving investigators - DISQUALIFYING, and only two years before the anchor.
2014-09-02: agreed to a $1.1 billion settlement with Deepwater Horizon private plaintiffs, without admission of liability.

Post-anchor, dated for the record. 2017-07-27 SEC FCPA settlement, about $29.2 million, over Angola: Halliburton steered oilfield-services subcontracts to a local company owned by a friend/associate of a Sonangol official to win Angolan business, with books-and-records and internal-controls violations. Shows the 2009 FCPA resolution did not end the pattern.

gate1.note: Own or license play brands, outsource manufacture (mostly Asia), sell to a concentrated retail channel, and monetize the same characters again through licensing and entertainment. Economics are brand margin plus royalty income against toolings, media spend and royalties paid out; the hit-driven revenue line is the hard part, not the accounting.

gate2.note: Real owned-brand equity - Monopoly, Transformers, Nerf, Play-Doh, My Little Pony, G.I. Joe - with decades of pricing and licensing power, but three structural leaks keep it NARROW: extreme retail concentration (Walmart, Target and Toys 'R' Us together roughly a quarter to a third of revenue), dependence on licensed properties whose royalties must be renegotiated (Marvel, Star Wars), and a hit-driven revenue line. FY2012 (reported 2013-02) revenue $4.09 billion, down about 5% YoY from $4.29 billion in 2011, with a restructuring announced 2013-02 that cut roughly 10% of the workforce - not the pattern of a business that can price through weakness.

Visible after the 2013-06-30 anchor, dated for the record. FY2013 (reported 2014-02) showed the girls category up 26% to $1 billion on My Little Pony, Equestria Girls, Furby and Nerf Rebelle, against a 22% decline in boys - i.e. the franchise machine still worked but was carried by one swinging category. Hasbro then won the Disney Princess/Frozen doll license from Mattel (announced 2014-05, product from 2016), a licensed - and therefore losable - dependency rather than owned equity.

gate3.note: UK Office of Fair Trading decision of 2003-02-19 found Hasbro UK, Argos and Littlewoods had entered price-fixing agreements (resale price maintenance on Hasbro toys and games), entered 1999 and infringing from 2000-03-01 until sometime between 2001-05-15 and 2001-09-14. Hasbro received 100% leniency on that decision for being first to hand over evidence before the investigation opened. Separately, in the related distributor case Hasbro was fined GBP 4.95 million (reduced from GBP 9 million for cooperation) for forcing about ten UK wholesale distributors in the first half of 2001 to contract not to sell below list price, backed by threats of losing access to Action Man and Star Wars lines. Appealed 2003-04-07; the Competition Appeal Tribunal remitted on witness-statement grounds 2003-07-30 but upheld the OFT on liability 2004-12-14. Secret price-fixing, so DISQUALIFYING by the rule - mitigants an analyst must weigh: UK-only, conduct 12-14 years before the 2013 anchor, self-reported by Hasbro, liability upheld not reversed.

2007-07-19 CPSC/Hasbro recall of about 1 million Easy-Bake Ovens after roughly 250 reports of burns including a partial finger amputation, following an earlier and criticized-as-inadequate 2007-02 repair-kit remedy. Ordinary-course product-safety failure.

gate1.note: Regional bank: gather low-cost Midwest core deposits, lend into C&I, auto, RV/marine and mortgage, earn the spread plus payments and wealth fees. Understandable at the unit level; loan-book credit quality is only ever knowable in aggregate, which is a risk, not opacity.

gate2.note: Genuine deposit-franchise density in Ohio and Michigan (long-standing top share in Columbus) with a sticky low-cost core deposit base, but commodity banking economics, high rate sensitivity, and a poor stress record: the 2001-2002 earnings misstatements and restatement, then near-death in the crisis - Franklin Credit exposure, the common dividend cut to $0.01 in 2009, and a large FY2009 loss including goodwill impairment.

Franchise materially stronger but still NARROW. FirstMerit closed 2016-08-16 (announced 2016-01-26), taking Huntington to roughly $100 billion of assets with added Ohio, Michigan and Wisconsin scale; because the first full quarter appeared in Q3 2016 results (reported 2016-10) the change is only visible for anchors from 2017 on. Efficiency ratio improved toward the high 50s and cost synergies were delivered ahead of plan, but returns remained peer-average, not moat-like.

Visible before the 2020-06-30 anchor. CECL adopted 2020-01-01; Q1 2020 (reported 2020-04) provision for credit losses jumped to roughly $440 million from roughly $65 million a year earlier, and management flagged large COVID-exposed books (hotel, retail CRE, auto). Capital held (CET1 in the mid-9s) and the dividend was maintained, so the franchise was stressed rather than impaired - class unchanged.

gate3.note: SEC civil action filed 2005-06-02 against Huntington Bancshares, then-CEO Thomas Hoaglin, former CFO Michael McMennamin and former controller John Van Fleet: the company reported inflated earnings in 2001 and 2002, letting it meet or beat Street EPS estimates and internal EPS targets that determined senior-management bonuses. Huntington paid a $7.5 million penalty without admitting or denying, and restated. The three individuals paid disgorgement, interest and penalties of $667,609, $415,215 and $51,660 respectively. Deliberate accounting manipulation tied to management's own bonus targets - DISQUALIFYING on the conduct. TWO EXPLICIT MITIGANTS an applicator must weigh at a 2020-06-30 anchor: (1) a 15-year gap with no repeat accounting event; (2) full management discontinuity - Hoaglin ceased to be CEO in 2009-01 when Stephen Steinour took over, and the CFO and controller had already left. Nothing in the 2020 management team is connected to the 2001-2002 conduct.

Approved 2017-03: Huntington agreed to a $15.9 million settlement of a class action over overdraft fee practices (high-to-low transaction sequencing) - conduct at FirstMerit BEFORE Huntington acquired it on 2016-08-16. The bank did not admit wrongdoing and maintained the fees were properly charged. Predecessor conduct under different management: graded SERIOUS with the discontinuity flagged; it is acquired-entity behavior Huntington inherited, not its own.

Post-anchor, dated for the record. 2024-08-14: Huntington was among a group of banks and broker-dealers penalized by the SEC (an $81 million round covering U.S. Bank, KeyBank, Huntington and others) for off-channel business communications on personal devices/WhatsApp - recordkeeping violations, with admissions of the failures.

gate1.note: Lodging REIT: own luxury and upper-upscale hotels, hand operations to Marriott, Hyatt and Ritz-Carlton under management agreements, collect hotel EBITDA less a large fixed cost base and heavy recurring FF&E capex. Very easy to explain, very hard to own - a nightly-repriced product against near-fixed costs.

gate2.note: Judged on asset quality the portfolio is close to irreplaceable: about 80 owned hotels concentrated in gateway urban CBDs and destination resorts, largest lodging REIT, blue-chip brand affiliations, investment-grade balance sheet. But the moat stops at the real estate - room rates are reset nightly and Host has no pricing power in a demand shock: RevPAR fell more than 20% in 2009 and the dividend was cut to $0.01 with FFO collapsing. Group/convention-dependent big-box assets are the most demand-elastic part of lodging.

All of this was public BEFORE the 2020-06-30 anchor.
