Q1 2020 (reported 2020-05-07): total revenue and total RevPAR down 24.3% and 21%, comparable RevPAR down 23.3% with March room revenue down about $200 million YoY; 13 hotels had suspended operations by 2020-03-31 and management said about 20 hotels representing roughly 22% of rooms would still be suspended at 2020-06-30; April total RevPAR was guided to fall 90-95%. On 2020-06-19 the board suspended the regular quarterly dividend beginning with the Q2 payment (the $0.20 Q1 dividend had been paid 2020-04-15), preserving about $140 million in the quarter. Asset quality was unchanged - earnings power was not merely at risk, it had gone to roughly zero, so the durable-advantage class is NONE at this anchor.

gate1.note: Regional bank: fund with Ohio, upstate New York and Pacific Northwest deposits, lend mostly commercial and industrial plus commercial real estate, and add fee income from commercial mortgage servicing/agency origination and KeyBanc capital markets. Understandable; the C&I and CRE credit books are only visible in aggregate.

gate2.note: A roughly $100 billion Cleveland-based deposit franchise with real density in Ohio and a differentiated commercial-mortgage/agency servicing platform, but a weak franchise record: large 2008-2010 losses, $2.5 billion of TARP taken 2008-11 and repaid 2011-03, and a persistent inability to earn its cost of capital.

Sub-par economics plainly visible before the 2016-06-30 anchor. FY2015 (reported 2016-01-21) showed return on tangible common equity around 10% and an efficiency ratio in the mid-to-high 60s against a compressing NIM near 2.9% - a bank earning roughly its cost of equity in the best part of the credit cycle has no durable advantage. Capital allocation reinforced this: the First Niagara deal was announced 2015-10-30 (about $4.1 billion, cash and stock) and was immediately criticized for its tangible-book earn-back - Key guided about six years, critics said closer to ten, and activist HoldCo Asset Management later attacked the price paid. TIMING RELATIVE TO ANCHOR: at 2016-06-30 the deal was announced and shareholder-approved (vote 2016-03-23) but NOT closed - Fed approval came 2016-07-12 and closing was 2016-08-01, both AFTER the anchor. So at the anchor First Niagara is a pending commitment and a signal about management's growth options, not a result in the numbers; the earn-back and integration outcome are post-anchor facts.

gate3.note: KeyBank was named a defendant in In Re: Checking Account Overdraft Litigation (MDL, S.D. Fla.), a putative national class action over overdraft ordering practices. Procedural history: the Eleventh Circuit vacated the order compelling arbitration on 2014-06-18, and the district court denied KeyBank's second renewed motion to compel arbitration on 2015-02-03, so the matter was live and unresolved at the 2016-06-30 anchor. Ordinary-course consumer litigation, no finding of wrongdoing.

Post-anchor, dated for the record. 2024-08-14: KeyBank entities were among firms penalized in an $81 million SEC round for off-channel business communications (personal devices/WhatsApp) recordkeeping violations, with admissions of the failures.

gate1.note: Open-air shopping-center REIT: own grocery-anchored strip and mixed-use centers, sign multi-year leases with rent bumps and recoveries, and reinvest in redevelopment. Economics are rent per square foot against tenant occupancy cost, plus leasing and redevelopment capex - straightforward, with joint-venture structures the only real complexity.

gate2.note: Judged on asset quality: the largest owner of open-air, grocery-anchored centers in North America, concentrated in first-ring suburbs of the top US metros where new supply is effectively unbuildable, and anchored by essential-goods grocers rather than apparel. But the tenant base below the anchor is weak credit, e-commerce has pressured occupancy cost for a decade, and the 2009 dividend cut showed the rent stream is not bond-like. NARROW, not WIDE.

Severe COVID stress, all public BEFORE the 2020-06-30 anchor, but the asset-quality case held so the class does not fall to NONE. Q1 2020 results (reported 2020-05-07/08) disclosed April 2020 collections of only 68% of base rent, with 22% deferred and 10% uncollected. The board temporarily suspended the common dividend in 2020-05 (the $0.28 Q2 dividend had been paid in April). Pre-anchor tenant bankruptcies: Pier 1 Imports filed 2020-02-17 (11 Kimco leases), Modell's 2020-03-11 (8 leases), GNC 2020-06-23 (12 leases). Post-anchor, dated for the record: Ascena filed 2020-07-23 (14 leases); Q2 2020 (reported 2020-08-07) carried a $51.7 million uncollectible-receivables charge; collections recovered to 76% in June, 82% in July, 85% in August; Q3 occupancy 94.6% versus 96.4% a year earlier; the dividend was reinstated for Q3 2020 (declared 2020-09-01) at a reduced rate. Grocery anchors traded through the shutdown - stress, not a broken asset.

gate1.note: Buys land, builds houses, sells them at a gross margin, plus attached mortgage/title services and (until 2018) Rialto asset management. A generalist can read the unit economics off community count, deliveries, average selling price and gross margin; the difficulty is cyclicality, not opacity.

gate2.note: Homebuilding is a price-taking commodity business with no customer captivity and no durable pricing power; demand is set by mortgage rates and credit availability. Lennar posted large losses through 2007-2011 and its homebuilding gross margins (~20-21%) track the peer group. Scale in land acquisition and national purchasing is a modest cost edge, not a moat.

CalAtlantic merger (announced 2017-10-30, closed 2018-02-12, ~$9.3B) made Lennar the largest US homebuilder by revenue (~$20.6B FY2018) and delivered synergies above the initial $100M target toward a $380M FY2019 goal. Fully visible in FY2018 results (reported 2019-01-09) and FY2019 quarters: scale showed up as cost synergies, not as a margin premium over peers. Class unchanged.

gate3.note: LandSource Communities Development (Lennar/CalPERS/MW Housing JV formed 2003) filed Chapter 11 on 2008-06-08; CalPERS wrote off roughly $970M-$1.2B. A California False Claims Act qui tam (Citizens Against Corporate Crime LLC v. Lennar), alleging inflated appraisals and misrepresentations that cost CalPERS ~$970M, was later blocked by a Delaware bankruptcy release, affirmed by the 3rd Circuit (opinion reported 2020-12), and cert denied 2021-06-07. Allegations were never adjudicated on the merits; graded MINOR because no finding of wrongdoing exists.

Barry Minkow's Fraud Discovery Institute published reports in January 2009 accusing Lennar of a Ponzi-like scheme; the stock fell from ~$11.57 to ~$6.55. REVERSED AND DISCREDITED: Minkow had shorted the stock, pled guilty on 2011-03-30 to conspiring to manipulate Lennar's share price, was sentenced to five years and ordered to pay $583.5M restitution TO Lennar. Exculpatory for Lennar's management.

Defective Chinese drywall litigation: as of 2009-07-10 Lennar disclosed 41 Florida state suits and two federal class actions from homeowners. Lennar remediated roughly 400 affected homes and itself sued the manufacturers, suppliers and installers. Ordinary-course construction-defect exposure, resolved through the MDL over 2010-2013.

gate1.note: Spend R&D, win a patent, price high for the exclusivity window, lose ~80-90% of the revenue to generics at loss of exclusivity. The accounting is legible even if individual trial outcomes are not forecastable, so this is uncertainty, not opacity.

gate2.note: Patent-protected franchises with global distribution and decades of high returns on capital: Zyprexa peaked near $5.0B/yr and Cymbalta near $5.1B (2013), on total revenue of ~$23-24B. Pricing power inside the patent window is close to absolute.

Zyprexa lost US exclusivity 2011-10; FY2011 revenue $24.3B fell to $22.6B in FY2012, visible in the January 2012 and January 2013 reports. The moat is a rolling series of expiring monopolies, not a permanent one, and Lilly's replacement pipeline was the weakest of the large caps -- the solanezumab Phase 3 failures were announced 2012-08 and the company had frozen salaries in anticipation of the cliff.

Cymbalta lost US exclusivity 2013-12 and Evista in 2014-03. Q1 2014 (reported 2014-04-24) revenue fell 16% to $4.68B with adjusted EPS $0.68 vs $1.14; full-year guidance was set at $19.4-20.0B against $23.1B in FY2013. Still NARROW rather than NONE: Humalog, Alimta, Trajenta and Japan/emerging-market growth held the base. POST-ANCHOR: Trulicity was approved 2014-09-18 and became the growth engine; do not let that colour the June 2014 read.

gate3.note: Lilly pled guilty to a misdemeanor Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act violation and paid $36M in December 2005 over off-label promotion of Evista for uses not approved by the FDA. Establishes that the later Zyprexa case was recidivism, not a one-off.

On 2009-01-15 Lilly agreed to pay $1.415B to resolve DOJ allegations of off-label promotion of Zyprexa, including a GUILTY PLEA to a misdemeanor FDCA charge and a $515M criminal fine -- at the time the largest criminal fine ever imposed on an individual corporation in any US prosecution. Lilly admitted promoting Zyprexa for dementia in the elderly between September 1999 and 2001-03-31, causing false claims to Medicaid, TRICARE and FEHBP. Systematic deception of prescribers and payers, with an admission. Five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement followed.

On 2012-12-20 the SEC charged Lilly with FCPA violations for improper payments by subsidiaries in Russia, Brazil, China and Poland from 1994 through 2009 (Lilly-Vostok routed millions to offshore entities for purported 'marketing services'). Lilly paid $29,398,734 (disgorgement $13.96M, prejudgment interest $6.74M, penalty $8.7M) WITHOUT admitting or denying. Graded DISQUALIFYING under the bribery/FCPA head; note the absence of an admission and that DOJ issued a declination (reported 2015-02).

gate1.note: Sell seats: revenue per available seat mile against cost per available seat mile, times capacity. The airline model is transparent -- it is the economics that are hostile, not the disclosure.

gate2.note: The best-in-class exception inside a bad industry: 47 consecutive profitable years (1973-2019), the lowest unit costs among US majors, a single 737 fleet type, point-to-point network, entrenched positions at Dallas Love, Houston Hobby, Chicago Midway and Baltimore, and the only US airline holding investment-grade ratings from all three agencies. NARROW not WIDE because airlines remain capital-intensive price-takers with no pricing power against a demand shock.

Two dated shocks, both visible in reported results by early 2020. (1) The FAA grounded the 737 MAX on 2019-03-13 after two fatal crashes; Southwest owned 34 MAX aircraft, the largest fleet of the type, and had expected 75 by year-end. On 2020-01-23 Southwest disclosed the grounding cut FY2019 operating profit by $828M and net income by $167M; Q2 2019 alone was reduced ~$175M. Single-fleet economics became single-point-of-failure. (2) COVID: TSA throughput fell ~95% by April 2020 (public daily data) and Q1 2020 (reported 2020-04-28) produced Southwest's first operating loss in 11 years. Core cash burn ran ~$30M/day in April 2020 falling to ~$16M/day in June 2020, disclosed in 8-K investor updates during the quarter (e.g. 2020-05-19). Southwest raised ~$13.9B net in H1 2020 -- $10.0B of financings and sale-leasebacks, $2.2B of common stock (permanent dilution) and $1.6B of CARES Act Payroll Support -- and ended 2020-06-30 with $14.5B of cash and short-term investments. No cost advantage produces pricing power when demand is gone.

gate3.note: FAA proposed a $10.2M civil penalty on 2008-03-06 for operating 46 aircraft on roughly 60,000 flights without required fuselage fatigue-crack inspections; FAA whistleblower inspectors testified before Congress in April 2008 that Southwest's compliance representations were unreliable. Settled for $7.5M on 2009-03-02. Safety-compliance misreporting to the regulator.

DOJ opened an investigation in July 2015 into possible capacity collusion among the four largest US carriers; private class actions were filed from 2015-07 and consolidated in D.D.C. in 2015-10 (In re Domestic Airline Travel Antitrust Litigation). Southwest settled first, in January 2018, for $15M while denying wrongdoing, and agreed to cooperate against American, Delta and United. Pure competition-law matter, no admission and no alleged deception.

Flight 1380 uncontained CFM56 fan-blade failure on 2018-04-17 killed one passenger -- the first US airline passenger fatality since 2009. NTSB's final report (2019-11-19) assigned cause to fan-blade inspection methodology at the engine manufacturer, not to Southwest maintenance. Accident, not misconduct.

DOT Office of Inspector General report released 2020-02-11 after a near-two-year audit found the FAA had not effectively overseen Southwest's safety-risk management. Specific findings: the FAA learned in 2018 that Southwest 'regularly and frequently' transmitted incorrect aircraft weight-and-balance data to its pilots in violation of regulations; and the FAA's Certificate Management Office allowed 88 used 'Skyline' aircraft into service without a comprehensive conformity inspection, with the OIG finding more than 150,000 flights carrying 17.2 million passengers on aircraft in an unknown airworthiness state. Congressional statements followed on 2020-02-12. A regulatory finding of systematic non-compliance; graded SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING because the report documents accepted low-risk justifications rather than proven deception.

POST-ANCHOR (exclude at a 2020-06-30 read). The December 2022 operational meltdown cancelled roughly 16,700 flights over ten days after crew-scheduling systems failed; DOT announced a $140M civil penalty settlement on 2023-12-18, the largest consumer-protection penalty in DOT history.

gate1.note: Designs, manufactures and markets toys under owned brands (Barbie, Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, American Girl) and licensed properties, sold through a concentrated retail channel (Walmart, Target, Toys 'R' Us). Unit economics are legible: gross margin, advertising as a percent of sales, and licence royalties.

gate2.note: Barbie (1959) and Hot Wheels (1968) are among the most durable consumer franchises ever built; gross margins ran roughly 50-54%, and FY2013 was a record at $6.48B of net sales and $903.9M of net income with a long unbroken dividend record.

Three dated facts visible before the 2015-06-30 anchor. (1) On 2014-09-25 Hasbro announced it had won the Disney Princess and Frozen doll licences, ending a roughly 20-year Mattel relationship; the line was ~7% of Mattel's $6.28B FY2015 sales and about $400-500M of revenue, with the handover effective in 2016. (2) FY2014 results (reported 2015-01-30): net sales -7% to $6.02B, net income -45% to $498.9M, gross margin down 380 basis points, Barbie -16% for the year and -12% in the holiday quarter, with Barbie down in eleven consecutive quarters. (3) CEO Bryan Stockton was removed on 2015-01-26 (a later filing confirmed he was fired, not resigned) and Christopher Sinclair took over as interim CEO. Dividends paid in FY2014 (~$517M) exceeded net income.

POST-ANCHOR for a 2015 read. The Disney handover hit in 2016: the girls category fell about 62% in Q1 2016. FY2017 net sales fell 11% to $4.88B with a net loss of roughly $1.05B; Toys 'R' Us filed Chapter 11 on 2017-09-18; the quarterly dividend was cut in February 2017 and eliminated in October 2017, and the credit rating was downgraded to non-investment grade in late 2017.

gate3.note: August-September 2007 recalls of roughly 2 million toys (Big Bird, Elmo, Dora, Sarge, Barbie accessories, GeoTrax) for lead paint and loose-magnet hazards. CPSC announced a $2.3M civil penalty on 2009-06-05 -- the highest ever for CPSC-regulated product violations at the time -- alleging Mattel and Fisher-Price KNOWINGLY imported and sold children's toys violating the federal lead-paint ban: up to 900,000 non-compliant Mattel units (2006-09 to 2007-08) and up to 1.1 million Fisher-Price units (2006-07 to 2007-08). Settled; graded SERIOUS.

POST-ANCHOR. Fisher-Price recalled roughly 4.7 million Rock 'n Play Sleepers on 2019-04-12 after the product was linked to more than 30 infant deaths; a congressional subcommittee report in 2021 found the product had been marketed for overnight sleep without adequate safety validation.

POST-ANCHOR -- must not colour a 2015 read, but is the single most consequential later fact. On 2019-08-06 Mattel learned that PwC had received a whistleblower letter about its accounting for the Thomas & Friends asset, two days before a $250M corporate debt offering was to close. Mattel had understated a tax valuation allowance and overstated tax expense in 2017, forcing a ~$109M restatement in November 2019; the CFO departed. The SEC issued a cease-and-desist order on 2022-10-21 with a $3.5M civil penalty (no admission or denial) and separately charged the former PwC audit partner with improper professional conduct and independence violations.

gate1.note: Cigarettes: a declining volume base (roughly -4% to -5% a year for the industry) more than offset by annual price increases, plus smokeless, wine, and a 10.2% economic interest in Anheuser-Busch InBev. Extremely simple economics, transparently disclosed.

gate2.note: Marlboro held roughly 43-44% US retail share in 2018 with Altria near 50% in total. The 1998 Master Settlement Agreement, by banning most advertising and imposing per-unit payments, entrenched the incumbents and foreclosed brand-building by new entrants -- a regulatory moat. Demonstrated pricing power: Q1 2019 (reported 2019-04-25) net revenue rose 3.2% to $5.4B and adjusted operating income grew even though domestic cigarette shipments fell an estimated 7% adjusted.

Still wide at the anchor, but the erosion rate is accelerating and is visible in reported results. Industry volume fell an estimated 4.5% in 2018 and about 5% in Q1 2019; Marlboro shipments fell 13.5% year over year in Q1 2019 (20,467M sticks vs 23,653M), partly inventory timing. Youth migration to vapour is the mechanism. Price/mix was still fully covering volume at 2019-06-30.

POST-ANCHOR. The JUUL impairments were a capital-allocation failure, not moat destruction: the core smokeable segment continued growing operating income on price. Distinguish the two carefully when reading later data.

gate3.note: Master Settlement Agreement signed 1998-11-23 with 46 states -- roughly $206B over 25 years plus permanent marketing restrictions -- resolving state Medicaid recoupment claims WITHOUT any admission of liability. Context: it followed the 1994 congressional testimony by tobacco chief executives denying that nicotine is addictive.

United States v. Philip Morris: on 2006-08-17 Judge Gladys Kessler issued a 1,683-page opinion holding Philip Morris/Altria and the other defendants liable under RICO for a decades-long scheme to defraud the public about the health effects of smoking, the addictiveness of nicotine, 'light'/low-tar claims, and marketing to children. The court held the First Amendment gave no protection because 'Defendants knew of their falsity at the time and made the statements with the intent to deceive.' AFFIRMED unanimously by a D.C. Circuit panel on 2009-05-22 (liability upheld; most remedies upheld; additional remedies sought by DOJ and public-health interveners denied); Supreme Court denied certiorari in June 2010. Court-ordered corrective statements began running in November 2017. A judicial finding of intentional deception, not a no-admission settlement.

On 2018-12-20 Altria bought 35% of JUUL Labs (non-voting Class C-1 stock) for $12.8B. DISCONTINUITY FLAG: the conduct that drove JUUL's regulatory exposure -- youth-targeted marketing -- predated Altria's investment and occurred under JUUL's own management, with Altria holding non-voting shares. Dated public evidence available BEFORE the 2019-06-30 anchor: FDA inspected/seized documents at JUUL headquarters 2018-09-28; the Massachusetts AG opened an investigation in July 2018; the North Carolina AG sued JUUL on 2019-05-15; San Francisco voted in June 2019 to ban e-cigarette sales. Graded SERIOUS for Altria at the anchor.

POST-ANCHOR, all of it. Altria wrote down JUUL by $4.5B in Q3 2019 (announced 2019-10-31), a further $4.1B in Q4 2019 (announced 2020-01-30, taking total 2019 charges to $8.6B and implying a ~$12B JUUL valuation), and about $4.0B more in Q1 2020. Press reports on 2020-02-20 disclosed an SEC probe of the JUUL transaction. The FTC filed an administrative complaint on 2020-04-01 seeking to unwind the deal as anticompetitive; an ALJ dismissed it on 2022-02-24 and the FTC ended the matter in 2023 after Altria exchanged its non-voting shares. None of this was knowable at 2019-06-30.

gate1.note: Mines phosphate rock and potash and converts them into DAP/MAP and MOP sold by the tonne into a global market. Cost per tonne against realised price per tonne -- about as legible as a business gets.

gate2.note: A pure price-taker in a globally traded commodity with no product differentiation and no customer captivity. DAP fell from its 2008 spike toward roughly $340/tonne by mid-2016; MOP fell from roughly $400/tonne in 2013 to around $200/tonne by mid-2016 after Uralkali publicly quit the Belarusian Potash Company marketing venture on 2013-07-30, ending the two-cartel pricing discipline that had held the potash market. Mosaic sells export potash through Canpotex, a DISCLOSED and legal Webb-Pomerene export association with PotashCorp and Agrium -- not a secret cartel and not a moat. Long-lived low-cost Florida phosphate rock reserves plus ammonia/sulphur integration give a cost position, which is not pricing power.

Nothing changed the class; the cycle simply confirmed it. Realised DAP and MOP prices in the quarters reported through 2016-05-02 were down sharply year over year, potash segment margins compressed toward breakeven at higher-cost mines, and Mosaic curtailed higher-cost potash output. New low-cost supply was already under construction (K+S Bethune, EuroChem), so the price weakness was structural rather than purely cyclical. POST-ANCHOR: Mosaic cut its quarterly dividend roughly 60% in December 2016 and announced the acquisition of Vale Fertilizantes on 2016-12-19 (closed 2018-01-08).

gate3.note: Mosaic agreed in January 2013 to pay $43.75M to settle the consolidated potash antitrust class action (In re Potash Antitrust Litigation II / Minn-Chem, Inc. v. Agrium Inc., N.D. Ill.), pending since 2008, which alleged that Canadian, US, Russian and Belarusian potash suppliers ran a global cartel setting artificially high prices and restricting supply from 2003. Settled without admission of liability; Agrium separately paid $10M. Pure competition-law matter, no alleged deception of customers.

On 2015-10-01 Mosaic Fertilizer settled with EPA, DOJ, Florida and Louisiana over RCRA hazardous-waste claims covering eight phosphate fertilizer facilities -- 60 billion pounds of hazardous waste, the largest quantity ever covered by a federal or state RCRA settlement, ending a case EPA had pursued for about a decade. The allegation was improper classification and disposal of hazardous acid wastes into phosphogypsum stacks. Total value roughly $2B, structured as a $630M initial financial-assurance trust growing toward $1.8B for long-term care and closure, plus corrective measures and civil penalties. Environmental non-compliance; no fraud alleged.

POST-ANCHOR (do not apply at a 2016-06-30 read). A sinkhole roughly 100 feet wide opened beneath the New Wales phosphogypsum stack at Mulberry, Florida on about 2016-08-27, draining approximately 215 million gallons of contaminated process water into the Floridan Aquifer. Mosaic notified Florida DEP and EPA but did not inform Polk County or the public until mid-September 2016, after a local TV investigation broke the story; a Mosaic vice-president apologised at a September 2016 county commission meeting without explaining the delay. Resident and shareholder suits followed. The disclosure delay -- not the geology -- is the governance fact.

gate1.note: Three legible pieces: refining (buy crude, sell products, earn the crack spread across ~1.8 million barrels/day of capacity), Speedway retail (roughly 2,730 company-owned convenience stores earning fuel and merchandise margin), and a midstream MLP, MPLX, earning fee-based pipeline, terminal and gas-processing revenue. Spread-driven and volatile, but not opaque.

gate2.note: Spun off from Marathon Oil on 2011-07-01. Refining itself has no pricing power -- the crack spread is set by the market on both sides -- but the asset base is hard to replicate: large Gulf Coast complexes at Garyville (~522 kbpd) and Galveston Bay (bought from BP, closed 2013-02-01), a dominant Midwest logistics position (Kentucky's own 2015 antitrust complaint alleged Marathon held 90-95% of the state's wholesale reformulated-gasoline supply), the Speedway retail network, and MPLX's fee-based midstream, materially enlarged by the MarkWest merger completed 2015-12-04. NARROW rather than NONE because roughly 40% of segment earnings came from retail and fee-based midstream rather than the crack spread.

The 2016 refining downcycle -- record US product inventories and sharply narrower crack spreads through H1 2016, visible in the Q1 2016 report on 2016-04-28 -- collapsed Refining & Marketing earnings while Speedway and MPLX held up. This is confirmatory rather than a re-rating: it demonstrates precisely where the durable earnings sit and that the refining core is a price-taker. Class unchanged.

gate3.note: Kentucky Attorney General Jack Conway filed a federal antitrust suit against Marathon Petroleum on 2015-05-12 (W.D. Ky.) alleging abuse of a 90-95% share of Kentucky's wholesale reformulated-gasoline market -- notably exclusive contracts requiring independent retailers to buy 100% of their RFG from Marathon -- and claiming Louisville wholesale prices ran roughly 25 cents/gallon above comparable St. Louis. Kentucky sought more than $173.6M. Pure competition-law claim with no alleged deception. DISMISSED: in June 2020 Judge David J. Hale excluded the Commonwealth's only expert and granted summary judgment to Marathon on the federal antitrust claims, leaving state-law claims open for refiling.

MarkWest Liberty Bluestone, an MPLX subsidiary, received an EPA Consent Agreement and Final Order on 2016-02-17 for Clean Air Act violations at the Sarsen gas-processing facility (Keystone Complex, Pennsylvania) found in a July 2012 inspection; it agreed in principle to a $95,000 penalty and leak-monitoring enhancements. Inherited from the MarkWest merger closed 2015-12-04, i.e. conduct under prior management.

On 2016-06-09 EPA and DOJ announced the first amendment to the 2012 US v. Marathon Petroleum Clean Air Act consent decree: Marathon will spend about $319M installing flare gas recovery systems at refineries in Illinois, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan and Ohio, plus $15.55M on mitigation projects, and pay a civil penalty of $326,500. Calibration: the punitive component is trivial ($326,500) and the $319M is injunctive capital spending under an industry-wide EPA refinery enforcement initiative that swept up essentially every major US refiner; no deception alleged. Material by dollar size, so graded SERIOUS, but it is not evidence of a dishonest culture.

Marathon paid Kentucky $22.5M in July 2019 to settle a suit originally filed in 2007 by then-Attorney General Greg Stumbo alleging that Marathon and its Speedway stations illegally raised pump prices after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005. Settled without admission. The suit was public and pending throughout the 2016 anchor date; only the resolution is post-anchor.

gate1.note: Sells per-seat and OEM licenses for Windows, Office and server software: near-zero marginal cost on each incremental license, so revenue per installed seat and seat count are the whole model. A generalist can explain it; FY2012 (reported 2012-07-19) showed ~76% gross margin on $73.7B revenue.

gate2.note: At 2013-06-30 the franchise economics were intact and visible in filed results: FY2012 10-K (2012-07-26) revenue $73.7B with segment operating income of $11.5B on Windows & Windows Live ($18.4B rev), $15.7B on Microsoft Business/Office ($24.0B rev) and $5.6B on Server & Tools ($18.7B rev) - three separate businesses each earning utility-like returns on almost no capital. Windows ran ~90% of PCs and Office was the de facto document standard; enterprise agreements and Software Assurance made revenue annuity-like. Q3 FY13 (reported 2013-04-18) still showed Server & Tools +11% and Business +5%. Countervailing evidence already public: Windows 8 (launched 2012-10-26) was poorly received and IDC reported on 2013-04-10 that Q1 2013 PC shipments fell 13.9% - the steepest decline since it began tracking in 1994 - explicitly blaming Windows 8; Microsoft had also written off $6.19B of aQuantive goodwill (announced 2012-07-02), and Online Services was loss-making. Judged on FY2013 economics the moat was WIDE in the OS/productivity/server core, with the PC-unit tailwind already gone.

Class unchanged, but the adjacent hardware/mobile bets failed visibly: $900M Surface RT inventory writedown disclosed with Q4 FY2013 on 2013-07-18 (just after the anchor, and the first quarter Microsoft ever took such a charge on its own device), then a $7.6B impairment of the Nokia phone business announced 2015-07-08 with ~7,800 job cuts. The core stayed wide - FY2015 (reported 2015-07-21) Office and server annuities held while commercial cloud grew - so the writedowns dated the failure of the device adjacency, not of the licensing franchise.

gate3.note: US v. Microsoft. District court found illegal monopoly maintenance (conclusions of law 2000-04-03) and ordered a breakup (2000-06-07); the DC Circuit on 2001-06-28 affirmed the monopoly-maintenance liability, VACATED the breakup remedy, and disqualified the trial judge for extrajudicial statements creating an appearance of bias. Settled with DOJ 2001-11-02; final judgment approved 2002-11-01. Graded SERIOUS, not DISQUALIFYING: pure competition law (tying, exclusionary dealing with OEMs), no finding of fraud or of deceiving customers about the product.

SEC settled administrative cease-and-desist order, 2002-06-03. The Commission FOUND that Microsoft maintained seven reserve accounts that did not comply with GAAP because they lacked adequately substantiated bases, held between $200M and $900M of unsupported and undisclosed reserves from July 1995 to June 1998, and thereby MISSTATED ITS INCOME BY MATERIAL AMOUNTS in periodic filings covering 1994-07-01 through 1998-06-30 - i.e. 'cookie jar' reserve smoothing. Graded DISQUALIFYING because the rubric's core case is accounting manipulation and the SEC made an affirmative finding of material income misstatement. Mitigating facts for the applicator: no fine was imposed, no individuals were charged, Microsoft consented without admitting or denying, the conduct ended in FY1998 - 15 years before the anchor - and there is no repeat accounting finding in the following 15 years.

European Commission decision 2004-03-24: EUR 497.2M fine for abuse of dominance (withholding server interoperability information and tying Windows Media Player). Upheld almost in full by the Court of First Instance 2007-09-17. Competition law only; no deception element found - SERIOUS.

Non-compliance penalties on the 2004 decision: EUR 280.5M periodic penalty 2006-07-12, then EUR 899M on 2008-02-27 for charging unreasonable interoperability royalties. The General Court reduced the 2008 penalty to EUR 860M on 2012-06-27 (partial annulment on legitimate-expectation grounds). Still competition law - SERIOUS.

European Commission fined Microsoft EUR 561M on 2013-03-06 for BREACHING ITS OWN LEGALLY BINDING COMMITMENT - the browser 'ballot screen' made binding by the 2009-12-16 commitment decision. The screen was absent from Windows 7 Service Pack 1 from May 2011 to July 2012, so ~15M users never saw it, and Microsoft filed compliance reports asserting compliance during that window. First time the Commission ever fined a company for breaching a commitment decision. Grading rationale, honestly stated: this is the closest of Microsoft's antitrust matters to a dishonesty finding, because inaccurate compliance reporting to a regulator is a deception-adjacent element. It is graded SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING because the Commission attributed the lapse to a technical error in a Windows build, made no finding of intent to deceive, Microsoft acknowledged responsibility and did not contest the breach, and the underlying matter is a tying remedy - pure competition law. An analyst who weighted the false compliance reports more heavily could defensibly go higher.

FCPA exposure became public 2013-03-19 (WSJ) - DOJ and SEC examining kickback allegations from a former Microsoft China representative plus reseller/consultant relationships in Romania, Italy, Russia and Pakistan (gifts and trips to procurement officials, bribes to win Romanian ministry contracts). At the anchor this was an OPEN INVESTIGATION with no finding, which is why it is SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING. Microsoft confirmed the inquiries publicly the same week.

POST-ANCHOR resolution of the above: 2019-07-22 Microsoft Hungary entered a DOJ non-prosecution agreement paying $8.75M criminal penalty and Microsoft settled SEC FCPA books-and-records/internal-controls charges for ~$16.6M (total ~$25.3M), for discounts channeled through resellers to fund improper payments to Hungarian government officials 2013-2015, with related conduct in Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Thailand. Conduct partly post-dates the 2013 anchor; the finding is dated 2019-07 and must be excluded at 2013-06-30.

gate1.note: Sells P25 mission-critical two-way radios and the network infrastructure behind them to police, fire and government agencies, then collects multi-year service, maintenance and system-integration fees on the installed base. Unit economics are a hardware sale plus a long services tail against a multi-year backlog - simple to explain.

gate2.note: At 2015-06-30 the switching-cost case was strong and visible. Public-safety LMR is a standards-bound (APCO Project 25), interoperability-critical installed base with 15-20 year replacement cycles, heavy sole-source and incumbent-favoured procurement, and a buyer whose cost of a failed radio call is measured in lives, not dollars - Motorola's share of US public-safety LMR was routinely described as roughly 70-80%. Economics corroborated it: FY2014 non-GAAP operating margin 18.2% of sales, rising to 20.5% in FY2015 (reported 2016-02-04) DESPITE falling revenue - pricing held while volume fell, which is the signature of real switching costs. The revenue decline visible at the anchor was mostly portfolio and budget, not share: the Enterprise (rugged handheld/barcode) business was sold to Zebra, closing 2014-10-27, taking revenue from $8.7B (FY2013) to $5.88B (FY2014), and Q1 2015 (reported 2015-04-30) sales fell ~11% on North American government budget pressure. The live threat at the anchor was the FirstNet nationwide public-safety LTE network authorised by the Feb 2012 spectrum act - a potential long-run substitute for LMR that had not touched reported results.

Class unchanged and the moat confirmed in reported results after the anchor: Airwave (the UK national public-safety network) acquired 2016-02-19, growth resumed with FY2017 revenue $6.38B, +8% (reported 2018-02-01), and the software/services mix and backlog grew rather than shrank - LTE proved additive, not substitutive. Separately, a federal jury on 2020-02-14 awarded Motorola Solutions $764.6M against Hytera for trade-secret theft and copyright infringement of its DMR source code, evidence that the product advantage was proprietary rather than merely incumbent.

gate3.note: SEC Section 21(a) Report of Investigation re Motorola, Inc. (Rel. 34-46898, 2002-11-25) concerning selective disclosure to analysts under Regulation FD. A report, not an enforcement action - no penalty, no finding of fraud. Predecessor-entity conduct: Motorola, Inc. was renamed Motorola Solutions on 2011-01-04.

Silverman v. Motorola, Inc. securities class action (filed 2007-08-09, N.D. Ill.; class period 2006-07-19 to 2007-01-05) settled for $200M cash - announced December 2011, agreement signed 2012-02-01, $150M funded by insurers. The complaint alleged false statements concealing Motorola's inability to deliver competitive 3G handsets after Freescale failed to supply working 3G chips, AND two 'sham' intellectual-property transactions with Freescale and Qualcomm in Q3 2006 that were allegedly not properly disclosed and violated GAAP in order to hide the earnings impact - i.e. accounting-manipulation allegations. Graded SERIOUS, not DISQUALIFYING, on three grounds: settled with no admission, there was NO restatement and NO SEC enforcement action, and the alleged conduct was in the Mobile Devices handset business under then-CEO Ed Zander. DISCONTINUITY FLAG: Motorola Solutions is the same legal entity (renamed 2011-01-04) and therefore carried the liability, but the handset business was spun off as Motorola Mobility on 2011-01-04 and the management responsible had left - Greg Brown, MSI's CEO at the 2015 anchor, did not become co-CEO until 2008-01.

POST-ANCHOR. UK Competition and Markets Authority referred the Airwave network to a market investigation on 2021-10-26 and on 2023-04-05 imposed a price control, finding Motorola Solutions was earning excess profits from a network the Home Office had no realistic alternative to. Pure competition/economic-regulation matter with no deception element and no finding of misconduct - SERIOUS by the rubric's competition-law rule.

gate1.note: A plain commercial bank: gather low-cost core deposits in dense upstate New York and Mid-Atlantic markets, lend them to regional commercial and CRE borrowers, earn the spread less credit losses and operating cost. A generalist can explain the P&L; the hard part is judging credit quality, not the model.

gate2.note: At 2020-06-30 the evidence for a durable but bounded franchise was in the 2019 10-K (filed 2020-02-20): net income $1.93B, ROA 1.73% and ROTCE around 19% on $119.9B of assets, an efficiency ratio in the mid-50s (top-decile among US regionals), and a deposit base concentrated in markets where M&T held #1 or #2 share - Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse, Baltimore. M&T had also been profitable in essentially every quarter since 1976 and Berkshire had been a long-term holder (Buffett's relationship with the late Robert Wilmers, CEO 1983-2017, who died 2017-12-16). NARROW rather than WIDE because a deposit franchise confers cost advantage, not pricing power: loan pricing is set by competitors, net interest margin is hostage to the Fed (already visible - the Fed cut to zero on 2020-03-15 and M&T's Q1 2020, reported 2020-04-20, showed NIM compression plus a $290M provision), and the balance-sheet leverage of ~7.6x equity means the moat is underwriting discipline, which is a management property rather than a structural one.

Class unchanged. The COVID credit cycle passed without impairing the franchise (2020 full-year provision ~$800M, reported 2021-01-21, with hotel and CRE concentrations the main worry), and M&T then agreed on 2021-02-22 to acquire People's United Financial in an all-stock deal (~$7.6B, closed 2022-04-01), roughly doubling New England presence - scale added, but the same cost-advantage-not-pricing-power character.

gate3.note: Public 2013-04-12/15: M&T and Hudson City Bancorp disclosed that the Federal Reserve would not approve their August 2012 merger because examiners had identified deficiencies in M&T's Bank Secrecy Act / anti-money-laundering compliance program. The deal, originally slated to close Q2 2013, was pushed out repeatedly (termination date extended to 2014-12-31, then 2015-04-30, then further) and did not close until 2015-11-01. Graded SERIOUS: a supervisory finding of program deficiencies and a blocked transaction, with no allegation that M&T deceived anyone.

Written Agreement between M&T Bank Corporation, Manufacturers and Traders Trust Co. and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, dated 2013-06-06 and made public 2013-06-17, requiring a revised firm-wide BSA/AML compliance risk management program, customer due diligence and suspicious-activity monitoring overhaul. Remediation reportedly cost M&T more than $400M over four years. The Federal Reserve TERMINATED the agreement on 2017-07-28 - i.e. fully cured three years before the anchor.

Wilmington Trust - PREDECESSOR CONDUCT, DISCONTINUITY FLAGGED. The SEC charged four former Wilmington Trust officers (CFO David Gibson, President/COO Robert Harra, controller Kevyn Rakowski, chief credit officer William North) in 2015 with intentionally understating past-due loans - omitting roughly $351M of matured loans 90+ days past due from Q3 2009 disclosures and ~$330M in Q4 2009 - and federal prosecutors indicted Wilmington Trust Corporation itself, which M&T publicly responded to on 2016-01-08. All of the conduct occurred in 2009-2010, BEFORE M&T acquired Wilmington Trust in May 2011, and related solely to Wilmington Trust's own commercial banking operations under its own management; M&T's public position was exactly that. Resolution: WTC settled civilly for $60M on 2017-10-09 (including $16M previously paid to the SEC) with no admission of liability and no finding of wrongdoing against the entity; the four executives were convicted at trial in May 2018, but the Third Circuit VACATED the fraud convictions in January 2021, holding prosecutors had not shown the bank's past-due reporting interpretation was the only reasonable reading of the regulations. Graded SERIOUS per the predecessor-conduct rule, not DISQUALIFYING, despite the underlying allegation being securities fraud.

2016-05-13: M&T Bank agreed to pay $64M to resolve DOJ False Claims Act allegations that from 2006-01-01 to 2011-12-31 it certified for FHA insurance mortgage loans that did not meet HUD underwriting requirements and failed to follow FHA quality-control requirements. Originated from a whistleblower suit by a former M&T employee (Keisha Kelschenbach). This is M&T's own conduct, not a predecessor's, and the government's theory was knowing certification - but it was a civil FCA resolution in the industry-wide FHA sweep that caught nearly every large originator, resolved without a litigated finding of fraud. SERIOUS.

gate1.note: Four simple revenue lines: per-share transaction fees on trades matched, annual fees from listed companies, subscriptions for market data and indexes, and licensed trading technology sold to other exchanges. Explaining it requires no specialist knowledge.

gate2.note: At 2013-06-30 the business was two halves with opposite economics. Durable half: the listings franchise is effectively a duopoly with NYSE (switching venue is rare and reputationally loaded), and market data and technology are recurring - FY2012 (reported 2013-01-31) net exchange revenue was $1,652M, and by FY2013 the mix was 41.0% Market Services, 12.0% Listings, 23.3% Information Services, 23.7% Technology Solutions, i.e. roughly 59% of net revenue was NOT transaction-dependent. Commodity half: US cash equity matching is a price-taking business fought on fee/rebate schedules - Nasdaq's matched share sat around 18-20% with BATS's two venues alone at roughly 19% of daily US equity volume and a large share of flow going to dark pools and internalisers, and volumes were falling industry-wide. Operational fragility was also already public: the 2012-05-18 Facebook IPO cross failure. NARROW - a real but partial moat, resting on listings/data rather than on trading.

Class unchanged, competitive facts sharpened. BATS and Direct Edge announced their merger 2013-08-26 (completed 2014-01-31), creating a venue larger than Nasdaq by US equity volume and pushing Nasdaq to third - confirming that the trading half had no pricing power. Nasdaq's answer, visible in dated transactions, was to buy recurring revenue: eSpeed (announced 2013-04-01, closed 2013-06-28) and the Thomson Reuters investor-relations, PR and multimedia businesses (announced 2013-12-16, closed 2013-05-2014).

POST-ANCHOR re-rating. By FY2019 (reported 2020-01-29) roughly three-quarters of Nasdaq's net revenue was non-transactional and largely subscription/annuity - index licensing built on the Nasdaq-100, market data, listings, and market technology sold to scores of other exchanges and regulators - with annualised recurring revenue disclosed as a headline metric. That mix, plus the index franchise's brand-level pricing power, supports WIDE from around 2020; it is not visible in FY2012-13 results and must be excluded at the 2013 anchor.

gate3.note: 2013-05-29: SEC settled charges against NASDAQ Stock Market LLC and NASDAQ OMX for securities-law violations during the 2012-05-18 Facebook IPO; $10M penalty, the largest ever imposed on an exchange at the time. Findings: a design limitation in the IPO cross order-matching system left more than 30,000 Facebook orders stuck in the system for over two hours; senior leadership convened a 'Code Blue' call, removed a few lines of code, and chose to open secondary trading WITHOUT having understood the root cause; Nasdaq violated its own price/time-priority rule and assumed an unauthorised ~$10.8M proprietary position in an error account, functioning outside its own rules. Nasdaq consented without admitting or denying the findings, and separately paid a $62M accommodation fund to harmed members (SEC-approved 2013-03-22, up from an initial $40M). Graded SERIOUS, not DISQUALIFYING: the SEC's findings are of poor systems and poor real-time decision-making, not of deceiving members or the Commission. This is one month before the anchor and therefore squarely in the anchor's information set.

POST-ANCHOR. 2013-08-22 'flash freeze': a connectivity failure between NYSE Arca and Nasdaq's Securities Information Processor halted trading in all Nasdaq-listed securities for roughly three hours. SEC Chair White summoned exchange leaders on 2013-09-12; no penalty or enforcement action against Nasdaq resulted. Operational, not integrity - MINOR.

gate1.note: PASS, but two very different businesses under one holding company and the split matters. Florida Power & Light is a rate-regulated monopoly utility serving ~4.6M customer accounts: it invests capital in rate base and the Florida PSC lets it earn an allowed return, so earnings are essentially allowed-ROE times rate base - trivially explainable. NextEra Energy Resources is the largest US wind generator plus merchant nuclear and gas, and its economics run through PPAs, production tax credits, tax-equity partnerships and a power/gas hedging book; that arm is materially harder to read but not opaque, since contracted output and PTC eligibility are disclosed.

gate2.note: At 2013-06-30 the REGULATED half looked wide-moat but is not one in the pricing-power sense: FPL has a legal service-territory monopoly, the lowest typical residential bill among Florida utilities, and Florida's constructive regulatory regime - the FPSC issued its final order in January 2013 approving the 2012 rate agreement, granting a $350M annualised base-revenue increase and an allowed regulatory ROE of 10.50% with a +/-100bp band (FPL may seek relief below 9.50%, intervenors may seek review above 11.50%) through 2016. That is a moat granted and capped by a political body, which can be reset at the next rate case - a regulator-set return, not pricing power. The UNREGULATED half (NEER, then ~10+ GW of wind plus merchant nuclear/gas) competed on levelised cost and depended on the production tax credit - extended only one year at a time (the 2013-01-02 fiscal-cliff extension) - while low natural gas prices in 2012-2013 compressed merchant spark spreads and NEER's marginal-unit economics. Combined verdict NARROW: durable but externally determined on the regulated side, cost-competitive but subsidy- and commodity-exposed on the merchant side.

Class unchanged, mix improved. The regulated share grew (Gulf Power acquired 2019-01-01) and NEER's output became overwhelmingly long-term contracted with a multi-gigawatt signed backlog disclosed each year, so merchant commodity exposure shrank. Still NARROW, because returns on both halves remain set by regulators and by tax policy rather than by the customer's willingness to pay.

gate3.note: In January 2010 the Florida PSC granted only a small fraction of FPL's ~$1.27B base-rate request, against the backdrop of a 2009-2010 controversy over improper closeness between the PSC and the utilities it regulated (PSC staff socialising with FPL officials, undisclosed contacts, retained BlackBerry PIN messages); two commissioners were subsequently denied reappointment in 2010. Graded MINOR because at the time there was NO enforcement action or legal finding against FPL itself and the amounts were rate-case outcomes rather than penalties. Later reporting (e.g. February 2016) alleged FPL had run an aggressive behind-the-scenes campaign in 2009 to investigate PSC commissioners and circulate negative material about then-Governor Crist and other critics - that characterisation became public in 2016, not 2010, and must not colour the earlier date.

NRC imposed a $140,000 civil penalty on FPL (reported 2012-04-11) for two Turkey Point violations: the Technical Support Center's ventilation power supply was disconnected 2010-12-04 to 2011-07-13 and again 2011-10-10 to 2011-10-28 without adequate compensatory measures, and FPL FAILED TO NOTIFY the NRC within the required eight hours of the resulting major loss of emergency-assessment capability. Contains a failure-to-report-to-regulator element, which is why it is flagged, but graded MINOR: low-to-moderate safety significance and a $140k penalty against a company with ~$14B of revenue - immaterial by any financial measure.

POST-ANCHOR. From October 2020 the Miami Herald and other Florida outlets reported that 'ghost' no-party candidates had been run in three 2020 Florida Senate races (Jestine Iannotti, SD9; Alex Rodriguez, SD37; Celso Alfonso, SD39) to siphon votes from Democrats, financed through a chain of nonprofits controlled by Jeff Pitts, then CEO of Matrix LLC - a consulting firm working for FPL. At this date the link to FPL was reported but not documented and FPL denied involvement, so SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING.

POST-ANCHOR. NRC enforcement (proposed penalty $150,000, letters dated 2021-04-06, announced 2021-04-08) concerning FALSIFIED maintenance records by staff at Turkey Point; FPL said it would pay. Deliberate falsification of records by site personnel is a dishonesty element, but it is localised employee misconduct with a trivial penalty rather than management-level or systemic deception - SERIOUS.

POST-ANCHOR. In July 2022 internal Matrix LLC documents leaked to the Orlando Sentinel and Floodlight showed FPL CEO Eric Silagy communicating with consultant Jeff Pitts - who controlled the dark-money vehicle Grow United - using the PSEUDONYM 'Theodore Hayes', and directing pressure on a sitting state senator, tying FPL leadership directly to the covert 2020 ghost-candidate and dark-money operation. Graded DISQUALIFYING: the pseudonymous channel and the layered nonprofits are deliberate concealment of a company's political operation, which is dishonesty in the Gate 3 sense even though it is not accounting fraud or bribery. Counter-facts the applicator should weigh: NextEra commissioned an internal investigation (disclosed around January 2022) that concluded no law was violated, no enforcement action was ever brought against FPL or NextEra, and the only criminal conviction was of former state senator Frank Artiles (September 2024), who was not an FPL employee. Silagy retired abruptly in January 2023.

gate1.note: Sells storage arrays whose value sits in the ONTAP operating software, then collects high-margin multi-year hardware and software maintenance on the installed base. Product gross margin, services attach rate and installed-base renewals are the whole economic story - readily explainable.

gate2.note: At 2015-06-30 the case for stickiness was real but the numbers were already soft. ONTAP was an entrenched data-management platform - snapshots, replication, admin skills and application certifications all make migration painful - and NetApp was the clear #2 in external storage at roughly 11-12% share. But FY2015 (fiscal year ended 2015-04-24, reported 2015-05-20) net revenue was $6,122.7M, DOWN 3% year over year, with product revenue falling faster than total, gross margin around 61% but GAAP operating margin only in the high single digits to ~10%; declining OEM revenue (IBM, Fujitsu) and friction in migrating customers from 7-Mode to clustered ONTAP compounded it. Two competitive attacks were visible: all-flash entrants (Pure Storage, EMC XtremIO) undercutting performance-tier arrays, and public-cloud object/block storage substituting at the low end and for new workloads. Management confirmed the deterioration - on the FY2015 call the CEO said he was not satisfied with performance and the company disclosed plans to cut ~500 jobs, following an earlier reduction in February 2015; the board then replaced 10-year CEO Tom Georgens with George Kurian, announced around 2015-05/06-01. NARROW, and thinning.

POST-ANCHOR. FY2016 (reported 2016-05-25) settled the question for a period: revenue $5.55B, DOWN 9%; Q4 revenue $1.38B, down 10.4%, with an $8M net LOSS for the quarter; product revenue down about 10% through the first three quarters; and external-storage-systems share fell nearly a full point, from almost 12% to just over 11%. Losing price, volume and share simultaneously while running at a loss is the absence of a moat, not a narrow one.

POST-ANCHOR. The all-flash pivot worked: FY2018 (reported 2018-05-23) revenue $5.91B, +7% - the first growth in three years - with gross margin back above 63%, restored operating margin, all-flash array run-rate growing at triple-digit rates off a small base, and cloud-adjacent products (ONTAP Cloud / Cloud Volumes on AWS, Azure and GCP) converting the cloud from pure substitute into a channel. Back to NARROW; not WIDE, because share never returned to its former level and the array market kept commoditising.

gate3.note: 2009-04-15: NetApp Inc. and NetApp U.S. Public Sector Inc. agreed to pay the United States $128M plus interest to resolve DOJ False Claims Act allegations - at the time the largest contract-fraud recovery GSA had ever obtained. The allegations: NetApp knowingly failed to give GSA current, accurate and complete information about its commercial sales practices and discounts, and knowingly failed to comply with the price-reduction clauses of its GSA schedule contracts by not passing on the deeper discounts it gave commercial customers. Whistleblower Igor Kapuscinski, a former NetApp procurement manager, received $19.2M (15%). NetApp neither admitted nor denied the allegations. GRADING NOTE, stated honestly: the government's theory was knowing nondisclosure to a government customer over a period of years, which is deception-adjacent and an analyst could argue toward DISQUALIFYING. It is graded SERIOUS because it resolved without admission or any litigated finding, it is a defective-pricing/contract-compliance matter under a clause that has snared much of the IT industry (Oracle settled the same theory for $199.5M in 2011), and there was no allegation of falsified financial statements or of deceiving NetApp's own shareholders. Six years before the anchor, with no repeat matter since.

gate1.note: Sells perpetual database and middleware licenses, then collects annual support at roughly 22% of license value with renewal rates above 90%, plus applications and (post-Sun) hardware. The economics reduce to license bookings feeding a compounding, ~90%-plus-margin support annuity - easy to explain and easy to see in the segment disclosure.

gate2.note: At 2015-06-30 the database franchise still had the strongest switching costs in enterprise software - roughly 40-48% of the relational database market, mission-critical applications certified against Oracle, and a support annuity customers renew because dropping support means no patches on systems that run the business. FY2015 (fiscal year ended 2015-05-31, reported 2015-06-17) showed software license updates and product support revenue near $18.9B at ~94% segment margin and total GAAP operating margin around 37% on $38.2B of revenue - the marks of a wide moat. BUT the first crack in the licensing engine was ALREADY in reported results at the anchor and must be dated pre-anchor: FY2015 new software license revenue was $8.54B, DOWN 9.4% for the year, with Q4 new licenses down 16.7% to $3.14B; total revenue was flat in dollars (up 4% in constant currency) and the quarter missed on both revenue and earnings. Cloud revenue was growing ~28% year over year but off a base too small to offset it, and hardware was shrinking. So: WIDE at the anchor, with cloud/SaaS substitution visible in the top line as of 2015-06-17 - not later.

POST-ANCHOR. FY2016 (reported 2016-06-16) confirmed the trend rather than reversing it - total revenue about $37.0B, down ~3%, new software license down double digits again, hardware down - while AWS and Azure took the new-workload decision and Salesforce, Workday and others took new applications spend. The support annuity kept cash flow enormous, which is why the class is NARROW rather than NONE, but Oracle had visibly lost the ability to set the terms on incremental enterprise spending.

POST-ANCHOR. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and AI-training demand re-widened the moat in reported results: FY2024 (reported 2024-06-11) revenue about $53B with cloud infrastructure growing over 50% and remaining performance obligations of roughly $98B, rising to roughly $138B a year later - a contracted backlog that is itself a switching cost. Excluded at the 2015 anchor.

gate3.note: 2011-10-06: Oracle Corp. and Oracle America agreed to pay the United States $199.5M plus interest - then the largest False Claims Act recovery GSA had ever obtained - over a 1998 GSA Multiple Award Schedule contract. DOJ alleged Oracle knowingly failed to give GSA current, accurate and complete information about its commercial sales practices and discounts, KNOWINGLY MADE FALSE STATEMENTS to GSA about those practices, and violated the price-reduction clause by not passing on deeper commercial discounts. Whistleblower Paul Frascella, a former Oracle employee, received $40M. Settled without admission of liability. Graded SERIOUS rather than DISQUALIFYING - the 'false statements' language is a government allegation resolved civilly with no litigated finding, and this was the industry-wide GSA price-reduction theory (NetApp settled the same theory for $128M in 2009) - but the deception allegation is flagged explicitly because it is not merely a technical pricing dispute.

2012-08-16: SEC settled FCPA charges against Oracle Corporation for $2M civil penalty. Oracle India, from 2005 to 2007, allowed distributors to park roughly $2.2M of proceeds in unauthorised 'side funds' held off Oracle's books, some of which went to phony vendors; the SEC charged violations of the FCPA's books-and-records and internal-controls provisions. Settled without admitting or denying. Graded DISQUALIFYING because the rubric places FCPA/bribery matters in that category and the mechanism was deliberate off-book concealment by company personnel. Facts that cut the other way and the applicator should weigh: the charges were books-and-records and internal controls ONLY - no bribery or anti-bribery charge - the amount was trivial ($2M penalty, $2.2M of funds), Oracle VOLUNTARILY DISCLOSED the conduct, cooperated, fired the employees involved and upgraded its compliance program, and the conduct was five to seven years stale at settlement. What is NOT available at a 2012 or 2015 anchor, but is worth recording: the SEC charged Oracle a SECOND time on 2022-09-27, imposing $23M and expressly labelling it a recidivist, so with hindsight 2012 was not an isolated lapse.

POST-ANCHOR. Securities class action filed August 2018 alleging Oracle executives made misleading statements about cloud revenue growth, concealing that growth was being driven by coercive sales tactics tied to license audits rather than organic demand. Private litigation with no regulatory finding, and it did not produce a restatement - MINOR. Relevant to the 2015 anchor only as a later data point on how the cloud transition was managed.

POST-ANCHOR but with PRE-ANCHOR-ADJACENT CONDUCT - date carefully. 2022-09-27: SEC charged Oracle a second time under the FCPA and Oracle paid about $23M ($8M disgorgement plus ~$15M penalty) over slush funds used by subsidiaries in India, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates to pay foreign officials. The SEC described conduct running from roughly 2014 to 2019 - i.e. some of it had begun by the 2015-06-30 anchor - but NONE of it was publicly known until 2022-09, so Gate 3 at the anchor cannot use it. Recorded here so the timeline is honest about what was true versus what was knowable.

gate1.note: Two-step distribution: buy dental and animal-health consumables and equipment, warehouse them, resell to solo/small dental practices and vet clinics through a field sales force plus an equipment service-technician network. Unit economics are simple and legible (FY2018 sales ~$5.5B on low-single-digit operating margin, working-capital and receivables heavy), so a generalist can explain them even though the two end markets differ.

gate2.note: Real but modest advantages: three distributors (Schein, Patterson, Benco) held >85% of US distributor sales of dental products (FTC, 2018-02-12); Patterson had exclusive US distribution of Sirona CAD/CAM (CEREC) equipment from 2005, expanded by agreement announced 2012; ~1,600 dental sales reps and a captive equipment service network create switching friction for small practices; Animal Health International (acquired 2015-06, ~$1.1B) added vet scale. Economics were never franchise-like: thin operating margins, no pricing power over branded consumables.

The exclusivity leg was removed and the share leg cracked. Dentsply Sirona declined to renew the exclusive US technology distribution arrangement; exclusivity ended 2017-09, and Patterson announced replacement non-exclusive lines (3Shape TRIOS scanners and others) in 2017-08/09. On 2018-03-01 Patterson reported FQ3 FY2018 with earnings down 26%, cut FY2018 guidance (GAAP $1.90-2.05 to $1.67-1.77), blamed 'sales force disruption', and disclosed its CFO's departure; the stock fell ~23-24% in one day. The FTC's 2018-02-12 complaint alleges the incumbents' buying-group margins were held by agreement rather than by advantage, which is the opposite of a moat.

gate3.note: Private federal antitrust class action consolidated in E.D.N.Y. (In re Dental Supplies Antitrust Litigation, No. 1:16-cv-00696) alleging Patterson, Henry Schein and Benco conspired to fix dental-supply prices and to boycott lower-cost channels; a related private suit by dental e-commerce entrant SourceOne Dental had already been filed in E.D.N.Y. in 2015. Patterson agreed on 2018-09-28 (post-anchor) to pay $28.3M to settle, without admission.

FTC administrative complaint filed 2018-02-12 (Docket 9379) charging Benco, Patterson and Henry Schein with an unlawful horizontal agreement to refuse discounts to, or otherwise compete for, dentist buying groups - i.e. a concealed group boycott among firms holding >85% of the market, not a unilateral abuse-of-dominance theory, which is why this is graded as dishonesty rather than as a pure competition-law matter. At the 2018-06-30 anchor only the complaint existed. Post-anchor: the ALJ's initial decision (announced 2019-10) held Benco and Patterson conspired and that the agreement was a per se violation of Section 5 while dismissing the complaint against Schein; Benco and Patterson declined to appeal in 2019-11, making that decision final, and Patterson settled with the FTC on those terms.

Securities class actions filed in D. Minn. beginning 2018-03 after the 2018-03-01 earnings collapse and CFO exit, alleging Patterson made false statements about its antitrust compliance and the sources of its margins for the class period 2013-06-26 to 2018-02-28. Class certified 2021; Patterson agreed to a $63M settlement announced 2022 (post-anchor), without admission. Investor-facing allegation, unproven at the anchor - but it points at the same conduct as the FTC case.

Texas Attorney General agreed final judgment announced 2018-04-20, following a three-year state investigation into an alleged joint effort by Patterson, Schein and Benco to thwart the Texas Dental Association's lower-cost online supply venture. Patterson paid $200,000, accepted antitrust training and injunctive terms; no admission of liability. Same boycott conduct as the FTC matter, resolved cheaply and pre-anchor.

Post-anchor: grand jury subpoenas to Animal Health International concerning sales of prescription animal-health products to unlicensed locations; Patterson entered a tolling agreement in 2018-08 and disclosed the matter in the 10-Q filed 2018-09 while cooperating with the U.S. Attorney's Office. Regulatory/criminal inquiry into distribution licensing; no charge against Patterson followed at that time.

gate1.note: Engineered motion-and-control components - hydraulics, pneumatics, seals, filtration, instrumentation, aerospace systems - sold largely through ~13,000 independent distributor outlets and to OEMs, with a large replacement/MRO aftermarket. Enormous SKU breadth makes it wide, not opaque: the unit economics (small high-mix parts, price/mix and decremental-margin discipline over a cyclical volume base) are explainable in a paragraph.

gate2.note: Evidence of durable but bounded advantage as of the 2016-06-30 anchor: FY2016 (ended 2016-06-30, reported 2016-08-04) sales fell to $11.36B with Q3 down 11% and Q4 down 6% y/y, yet adjusted segment operating margin held essentially flat at ~14.8% (decremental margin ~17%) - real pricing and cost discipline. Sources of advantage: replacement demand specified into installed industrial equipment, distributor density and same-day parts availability, and aerospace content that is certified and often sole-source with multi-decade aftermarket streams. Bounded by fragmented, capable competition (Eaton, Bosch Rexroth, Danaher, IMI) and mid-cycle ROIC only around 10-12%, with severe end-market cyclicality (oil and gas, mining, ag, construction). Not wide.

gate3.note: Marine hose cartel became public: the EC's 2006-12 leniency application by Yokohama led to surprise inspections and to an FBI-recorded cartel meeting in Houston on 2007-05-02, with Parker ITR's oil-and-gas business unit manager arrested in Houston in 2007-05. The cartel (bid rigging, price fixing, market and customer allocation for marine oil-and-gas hose) ran from at least 1986 to 2007-05. Critical for the discontinuity test: Parker acquired the ITR Rubber marine-hose business in 2002, so roughly five years of the conspiracy ran under Parker ownership - this is not purely predecessor conduct, though the conspiracy began long before Parker bought the unit.

European Commission decision of 2009-01-28 fined five groups a total of about EUR 131.5M; Parker ITR was fined about EUR 25.6M with Parker-Hannifin held jointly and severally liable for roughly EUR 8.3M. Later modified on appeal: the General Court (T-146/09, judgment 2013-05-17) cut the fine on economic-continuity/personal-liability grounds; the Court of Justice (C-434/13 P, judgment 2014-12-18) set that judgment aside and remitted the case; on remand in 2016-07 the General Court re-imposed a fine at a level between the two (roughly EUR 19M, with Parker-Hannifin jointly liable for a smaller share). Net: reduced, never annulled.

US criminal resolution: DOJ announced on 2010-02-16 that Parker ITR S.r.l. agreed to plead guilty to a one-count felony (S.D. Tex.) for conspiring to rig bids, fix prices and allocate market shares of marine hose from as early as 1999 until as late as 2007-05-02, and to pay a $2.29M criminal fine (US commerce affected at least $15.3M). Investigation ran jointly with DCIS, NCIS and the FBI because the US Navy was among the victims.

Romano Pisciotti, a former manager of Parker ITR's Oil & Gas business unit, was extradited from Germany to the United States in 2014-04 (the first successful extradition on a pure antitrust charge) and pleaded guilty in 2014-04 to the marine hose bid-rigging conspiracy, receiving a prison term. Individual conduct, but it kept the cartel record live and public within two years of the 2016 anchor.

Post-anchor: DOJ filed an antitrust suit on 2017-09-26 alleging Parker-Hannifin's $4.3B acquisition of CLARCOR (announced 2016-12-01, closed 2017-02-28) created an effective monopoly in EI-qualified aviation ground fuel filtration systems and elements sold to US customers. Settled by consent decree requiring divestiture of the aviation ground fuel filtration business, announced 2017-12-19. Pure competition-law/merger matter, no deception element alleged.

gate1.note: Buy and entitle land, build houses to order or on spec, sell them, and originate the mortgage through a captive finance arm; inventory-heavy, cyclical, and entirely legible to a generalist. Three brands segment the customer (Centex entry-level, Pulte move-up, Del Webb active adult) but the economics are one business.

gate2.note: Homebuilding has no pricing power - price is set by local comparable sales and by the buyer's monthly payment, i.e. by mortgage rates. Land is the input and the balance sheet is inventory (~$7B+ of house and land inventory in 2018), so returns swing violently: PulteGroup lost money every year from 2007 through 2011 and earned record profits in 2017-2018. The only durable edges are scale purchasing, land-position access, and the Del Webb active-adult brand (acquired in the 2001 Del Webb merger; Centex added 2009-08-18) - none of which survives a downturn as pricing power. Q2 2018 (reported 2018-07) showed a healthy peak-cycle print, not a moat.

gate3.note: Governance, not misconduct: founder's grandson Bill Pulte, with Jim Grosfeld, ran a public campaign demanding CEO Richard Dugas's removal (13D and public letters from 2016-03/04; activist counsel Olshan retained 2016-04). Company announced on 2016-04-04 that Dugas would retire at the 2017 annual meeting; on 2016-09-08 the board named Ryan Marshall CEO effective immediately, with Dugas staying as executive chairman until the 2017 meeting. No allegation of dishonesty; a performance and board-composition fight, and Bill Pulte joined the board in 2016.

Post-anchor and therefore NOT available at the 2018-06-30 anchor: the Florida Attorney General filed and simultaneously settled an action (complaint dated 2018-12-28, publicly announced 2018-12-31 through 2019-01-05) charging Pulte Home Company under Florida's Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act with building more than 23,000 Florida homes between 2008 and 2016 with improperly installed stucco that did not meet code, failing to disclose those defects to buyers, denying warranty claims without adequate inspection, and withholding deposits. Total package about $78.7M: >$64M of repairs already made during the investigation, >$10M on materials/training, $4.7M homeowner restitution, plus an obligation to repair homes up to 10 years old. Settled without admission, hence SERIOUS - but note the explicit concealment-from-buyers allegation, which is dishonesty in substance. The investigation was opened in 2016 after Orlando-area officials flagged Windermere townhomes and ran roughly two years non-publicly.

gate1.note: Four legible pieces: refine crude and capture the crack spread, move hydrocarbons for fees (midstream/PSXP), sell branded fuel through marketing, and own 50% of Chevron Phillips Chemical. A generalist can explain each; what is hard is forecasting the refining spread, which is a predictability problem rather than an understandability problem.

gate2.note: Refining is a price taker on both sides: crude in at market, products out at market, margin set by the crack spread. Phillips 66 ran 100% refinery utilization in Q2 2016 and still saw Q2 2016 earnings fall to $496M from about $1.6B in Q2 2015 (reported 2016-07-29), and full-year earnings fell from $4.2B (2015) to about $1.6B (2016) almost entirely on margin - operational excellence with no pricing power. The genuine cost advantages exist but do not add up to a moat at this anchor: no new US refinery has been permitted since 1977 (an entry barrier that protects capacity, not spreads); Gulf Coast complexity allows advantaged crude runs; and the CPChem JV enjoys a real US ethane feedstock cost advantage (Chemicals contributed $190M in Q2 2016 and was building new Gulf Coast cracker/polyethylene capacity). Fee-based midstream was still too small at 2016-06-30 to carry the whole. Judged honestly: NONE.

gate3.note: EPA Notice of Violation received 2014-07 alleging flaring-related violations at the Wood River refinery for 2009-2013, followed by a second NOV in 2014-09 alleging a hazardous-air-pollutant violation at Wood River in 2014. Ordinary-course environmental enforcement for a refiner; resolved post-anchor by a proposed Clean Air Act consent decree lodged by DOJ on 2018-08-10 (United States and Illinois v. WRB Refining LP and Phillips 66 Company, S.D. Ill.). Phillips 66's US refineries were already operating under two earlier Clean Air Act consent decrees with EPA, six states and one local air agency.

Voluntary settlement with the Illinois EPA in 2016-10 over alleged wastewater violations at Wood River, after a Sierra Club notice of intent to sue: capital projects plus a $125,000 payment. Small, ordinary course.

Disclosed in the FY2016 10-K (filed 2017-02): the California Air Resources Board issued four Notices of Violation alleging fuel-specification violations at the Los Angeles refinery and Torrance tank farm, with a proposed total penalty of $190,000. Immaterial in dollars; relevant only as a pattern of routine environmental/product-spec non-compliance.

Post-anchor: a $39M settlement announced in 2017-04 resolved MTBE groundwater-contamination claims against ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. Discontinuity flagged - the MTBE conduct predates the 2012-05-01 spin-off of Phillips 66 from ConocoPhillips and occurred under ConocoPhillips/Phillips Petroleum management; the plaintiffs' theory (that the industry marketed a product it knew would contaminate groundwater) has a deception element, so this is graded SERIOUS on predecessor-conduct grounds rather than dismissed as ordinary product liability. No enforcement action alleging fraud, price fixing, or bribery by Phillips 66 as a standalone company was found in the pre-anchor record.

gate1.note: Two halves that are easy to state: QCT sells Snapdragon baseband/application processors at hardware margins, and QTL licenses the 3G/4G standard-essential patent portfolio at a royalty rate applied to the whole handset selling price, earning ~85% operating margins on almost no incremental cost. The legal architecture holding QTL together is complex, but the unit economics are not.

gate2.note: As originally underwritable: ownership of CDMA and LTE standard-essential patents that every handset maker must license, royalties charged on the device price rather than the chip price, and simultaneous chipset leadership - a rare combination that produced licensing operating margins near 85% and made QTL the majority of company profit. Barriers: two decades of accumulated SEPs, 3GPP standard participation, and the practical need for licensees to keep chip supply.

First structural concession, visible in reported results: China's NDRC resolution of 2015-02-09 (RMB 6.088B, about $975M) came with a rectification plan under which Qualcomm licensed Chinese device makers on a royalty base of 65% of net device selling price and unbundled portfolios. The royalty rate architecture survived - hence still WIDE - but the precedent that a regulator could reset the base was now on the record, and the EU opened two formal proceedings in 2015-07 (Apple exclusivity payments; alleged predatory pricing of baseband chips), reviving scrutiny that had lapsed when the earlier EU case closed in 2009-11.

By the 2017-06-30 anchor the licensing moat was visibly breached, not merely challenged. KFTC's 2016-12-28 decision (KRW 1.03 trillion, about $854-865M, its largest ever fine on one company) ordered Qualcomm to license SEPs to rival chipmakers and to renegotiate coercive licence terms - a direct attack on the 'no license, no chips' structure. The US FTC sued on 2017-01-17 on the same theory. Apple sued on 2017-01-20 for about $1B of withheld rebates, alleging retaliation for its cooperation with the KFTC, and by 2017-04 Apple's contract manufacturers had stopped paying royalties altogether, which Qualcomm disclosed with reduced guidance in 2017-04. QTL revenue actually fell. The chipset franchise (QCT) remained strong, so NARROW rather than NONE.

gate3.note: KFTC fined Qualcomm about KRW 260B (roughly $208M) in 2009-07 for abuse of dominance through conditional/loyalty rebates favouring buyers of its chipsets. Pure competition-law matter, no deception element. Largely upheld on appeal (Seoul High Court 2013, Korean Supreme Court 2019).

China's NDRC concluded its investigation (opened 2013-11) on 2015-02-09 with a RMB 6.088B fine (about $975M) and a rectification plan changing Qualcomm's Chinese licensing terms. Abuse-of-dominance/licensing matter; Qualcomm did not contest and no deception was alleged - graded SERIOUS, not disqualifying, but it materially reset the economics of the largest handset market.

The one genuine dishonesty item in the pre-anchor record, and it is not an antitrust matter: on 2016-03-01 Qualcomm settled SEC FCPA charges for $7.5M (cease-and-desist order plus two years of self-monitoring and self-reporting). The SEC found Qualcomm and its Chinese subsidiary hired relatives of officials at Chinese state-owned telecom customers and provided gifts, travel and entertainment to influence them, and recorded those benefits in its books as legitimate business expenses. Charged under the FCPA's internal-controls and books-and-records provisions rather than the anti-bribery provision; DOJ closed its parallel investigation without action. A later Delaware Caremark suit against the board over the same conduct was dismissed.

KFTC decision announced 2016-12-28: KRW 1.03 trillion (about $854-865M) plus corrective orders requiring Qualcomm to license standard-essential patents to competing chipset makers and to renegotiate licences with device makers. Abuse-of-dominance/FRAND matter with no deception element, so SERIOUS - but the corrective orders, not the fine, were the threat to the business model. Post-anchor: the Seoul High Court upheld the core of the decision in 2019-12 and the Korean Supreme Court upheld it on 2023-04-13.

FTC sued Qualcomm in N.D. Cal. on 2017-01-17 for monopolization of baseband processor markets ('no license, no chips', refusal to license SEPs to rival chipmakers, exclusivity payments to Apple).
